pages.text: Incredibly, many wild animals knew to run inland before the 2004 Asian tsunami hit land. However, pets and farm animals did not fare so well. Many people in the areas hit by the tsunami depended on working farm animals. Large numbers of these animals were killed, and many others were injured or left in places without food when the tsunami struck. The Humane Society International and others help the animals, and the people who care for them, get their lives back on track. A man carries his daughter and dog to safety after the tsunami in December 2004.
pages.brief: A man carries his daughter and dog to safety after the December 2004 tsunami. Many wild animals ran inland before the tsunami hit, but pets and farm animals suffered. The Humane Society International helps animals and the people who care for them get their lives back on track.

pages.text: Conclusion Rehabbers often use animals that cannot go back to the wild as ambassadors to help teach people to respect wildlife. Children and adults learn about wildlife that live in their area and about respecting the land so that wild animals can continue to find food and shelter. Wildlife rehabbers do important work in caring for injured wild animals and returning many of them to the wild. You can help rehabbers’ efforts by respecting wildlife and by calling a rehabber if you see an animal in trouble. One phone call could give a wild animal the opportunity to grow up and live a free and healthy life. This bird of prey acts as an ambassador to teach children about animals in their area.
pages.brief: A bird of prey acts as an ambassador, helping children learn about wildlife that lives in their area. The children learn to respect the land so wild animals can find food and shelter. Rehabbers care for injured animals and return many to the wild; a phone call can help an animal in trouble.

books.title: The Case of the Disappearing Honeybees
books.art_why: The book is about modern honeybees, beekeepers, farms, scientists, and cities, all real subjects today that can be photographed.

pages.text: A healthy honeybee colony Who Took My Strawberries? Think of your favorite fruit. Now imagine a world in which that fruit— or any other fruit, or many nuts, vegetables, or flowers—is extremely rare. Without honeybees to pollinate the flowers of these plants, our diets would be very bland and boring. In fact, one in three bites of the food you eat is thanks to bees. Yet, in 2007, honeybees began to vanish around the world. The reasons have puzzled scientists for a long time. Although the problem slowed over time, the reason behind it is still a mystery. Scientists are still working today to help save the honeybees.
pages.brief: A healthy honeybee colony covers a honeycomb, with many bees crowded on its cells. Nearby are flowers, fruit, nuts, and vegetables that depend on pollination. The scene suggests how much food comes from bees, while scientists still work to understand why honeybees began vanishing around the world in 2007.

pages.text: Missing in Action In October 2006, an American beekeeper arrived at one of his apiaries, or beeyards, in Florida to pick up four hundred hives. Three weeks before, the hives had appeared healthy, but now he found the hives nearly empty. Food, baby bees, and a few queens were all that was left. The beekeeper looked for dead bodies, but twenty million bees had disappeared. This beekeeper was not alone. Reports of other losses began to surface across the United States, Europe, Argentina, China, and other countries. During the winter of 2006–2007, roughly 750,000 of the estimated 2.4 million colonies in the United States had vanished. On average, U.S. beekeepers lost 38 percent of their colonies. In 2008, the largest occurred in the almond tree groves of California. Two billion bees vanished there. Both farmers and desperate for science to shed some light on A honeybee colony before and the mystery. after the bees vanished.
pages.brief: An American beekeeper stands at a Florida beeyard beside rows of nearly empty hives. He has come to pick up four hundred hives and finds only food, baby bees, and a few queens. Twenty million bees have disappeared, with no dead bodies; losses are also reported across the United States, Europe, Argentina, China, and other countries.

pages.text: On the Case Scientists named the problem colony collapse disorder (CCD) and quickly determined the symptoms. CCD happens in a matter of weeks when what seems to be a healthy hive collapses, yet few, if any, dead bees can be found. The only bees remaining are the very young and the queen—members of the colony that normally would never be left alone. Honeybee scientists from around the country started working to find out what was killing the honeybees and stop it. Reaching that goal has proven far more complicated than anyone expected. CCD scientists surveyed beekeepers and took samples of wax, pollen, and live and dead bees (when they could find them). The samples were shipped to laboratories to be studied. When scientists dissected the bees, they found that the bees had many diseases. It seemed that their immune systems were compromised — A scientist takes samples from but why? a hive with CCD.
pages.brief: A scientist in protective clothing takes samples from a hive affected by colony collapse disorder. Nearby, other researchers survey beekeepers and collect wax, pollen, and live or dead bees for laboratories. Inside a hive, only very young bees and the queen remain, while dissected bees show many diseases and compromised immune systems.

pages.text: Average Annual Hive Loss by State, 2020–2021 The scientists investigated the usual suspects that might damage honeybees’ immune systems. These included several parasites, such as a mite that feeds on bee blood, transmits viruses, and lays eggs in the same hive cells as baby bees. They looked at fungal bacteria that make it difficult for bees to eat and leave them too weak to forage. Scientists also found a virus that causes paralysis in a large number of CCD hives. While these are all extremely dangerous to bees, researchers decided that none were the cause of CCD, so their investigation turned to farming practices.
pages.brief: Scientists examine a tiny mite on a honeybee, fungal bacteria that weaken bees, and a bee affected by a paralysis virus. The mite feeds on bee blood, transmits viruses, and lays eggs in hive cells with baby bees. Researchers decide none of these suspects caused colony collapse disorder and turn to farming practices.

pages.text: A truck sprays pesticide over plants. Just One Crop Once upon a time, farms were small and grew many different crops. Today, most farms are massive and grow a single crop, such as wheat, corn, or soybeans. This arrangement is called a monoculture. Some farmers like a monoculture because it’s very efficient, but bees can’t survive on such a farm for long because once the single plant crop stops blooming for the year, the bees starve to death.
pages.brief: A large farm field grows a single crop such as wheat, corn, or soybeans. A truck sprays pesticide over the plants. The scene shows a monoculture: efficient for farmers, but bees cannot survive long once the single crop stops blooming and they starve.

pages.text: Monocultures present bees with other complications, too. Because pests love monocultures, farmers must spray chemical pesticides to eliminate them. In American agriculture, a large portion of the food we eat is treated with pesticides. According to the Environmental Protection Agency, more than a billion pounds of these chemicals are used on our crops annually. It’s challenging for farmers to find chemical pesticides that kill harmful insects but leave the beneficial ones, such as bees, alone. Pesticides spell trouble for many creatures, bees in particular. So farmers try to spray crops at times when plants aren’t blooming and bees are less likely to be nearby. Still, scientists found pesticides in the samples they’d collected from hives with CCD. Also, a new class of pesticides has some scientists particularly concerned. These pesticides are systemic, which means that the seeds are treated with chemicals that then infiltrate every part of a plant as it grows. A single treatment lasts a long time and kills various crop pests, which is a seemingly good thing. However, the bee losses coincide with the appearance of these new pesticides.
pages.brief: Farmers spray chemical pesticides over a large monoculture field, trying to kill pests without harming beneficial insects such as bees. Scientists found pesticides in samples from hives with colony collapse disorder. They are especially concerned about systemic pesticides: treated seeds grow into plants with chemicals in every part, and bee losses coincide with these pesticides.

pages.text: Pesticides might weaken the bees’ immune systems. This lets diseases like the paralysis virus take hold. Beyond this, though, systemic pesticides target the nervous system. They might affect the bees’ ability to learn, remember, and navigate, all of which would contribute to the bees’ failure to return to the hive after foraging. If bees can’t find their way back to the beehive, they die. Scientists found evidence that systemic pesticides exist in beehives that have had CCD. Also, the timing of the introduction of these new pesticides coincides with the appearance of CCD. They cannot, however, state conclusively that these pesticides cause the disease. Still more factors must be considered. What Lawns Lack While colony collapse disease is slowing, another bee crisis has come. Many native bees are now in danger of extinction. Manicured lawns are partly responsible for wild bee decline. Certain types of bees rely on certain plants to there are fewer native plants and which farmers move to pollinate crops— wild bees are having trouble finding food and shelter.
pages.brief: A honeybee navigates among flowers; systemic pesticides may affect its nervous system, learning, memory, and ability to return to the hive. Elsewhere, a manicured lawn with few native plants shows why wild native bees struggle to find food and shelter, as some native bees face extinction.

pages.text: Do You Know? Ancient Egyptians floated beehives on rafts down the Nile River to follow the bloom. Today, trucks transport hives all over the country. Keep On Trucking Bees have been buzzing around the world for 150 million years. However, in the last 10,000 years, the relationship between bees and humans has transformed. Humans went from foragers of naturally pollinated foods to using bees for monoculture farming. Since honeybees are excellent pollinators, moving them into a field while crops are blooming is a great way for farmers to ensure a plentiful crop. Once bees began to live in hives constructed by humans, the hives became mobile. Today in the United States, trucks drive hives all over the country. The honeybees they carry annually pollinate $15 billion worth of food in the United States alone.
pages.brief: A truck carries stacked beehives down a highway, while another scene shows ancient Egyptians floating beehives on rafts along the Nile. The page explains that humans once foraged naturally pollinated foods and now truck mobile hives across the United States to pollinate crops worth $15 billion each year.

pages.text: The thought of trucking a million bees down the highway may seem strange, but it helps production with modern monocultures. Farmers might need bees to pollinate one crop in February and another one across the country in April. Almond trees, for example, are completely dependent on honeybees for pollination. In California, almond farmers require the use of 1.4 million colonies of honeybees. That’s about 60 percent of all managed honeybee colonies in the United States. Around Valentine’s Day, bees are trucked to the California groves, and when the almond trees start to bloom, they go to work. For two weeks, those 600,000 acres (242,811 ha) of blooming trees are a busy and beautiful sight. For the other fifty weeks of the year, those groves are a terrible habitat for bees. There’s nothing to eat then. Transport isn’t great for the bees, either. Millions of bees die from the stress each year. Also, once they’re on the road, the bees don’t have access to natural food sources. What beekeepers feed them instead, some scientists liken to junk food. Bringing in bees from different parts of the country (or the world) also spreads pests quickly.
pages.brief: Trucks carry beehives to California almond groves around Valentine’s Day, where 600,000 acres of blooming almond trees need honeybees for pollination. For two weeks the groves are busy and beautiful, but for the other fifty weeks they offer bees nothing to eat. Transport stress and junk food kill millions of bees, and moving hives spreads pests.

pages.text: A beekeeper is on his way to check on the more than 100,000 honeybees that live in the garden on top of City Hall in downtown Chicago. Help the Bees Because of the complexity of CCD, scientists have yet to find an exact cause or a complete cure. However, scientists have found some promising treatments. As a result, the rates of CCD have dropped over time—though not as much as scientists would like. Solving the case of the disappearing honeybees will require additional research. In the meantime, we can use what we do know to create bee- friendly environments that will benefit plants, bees, and people.
pages.brief: A beekeeper heads toward the rooftop garden on City Hall in downtown Chicago, where more than 100,000 honeybees live. The page says colony collapse disorder has no exact cause or complete cure, though promising treatments have reduced its rates; bee-friendly environments can benefit plants, bees, and people while research continues.

pages.text: Anyone with outdoor space can help bees by keeping the kinds of plants they need. One thing honeybees need is lots of different wildflowers. To answer this need, honeybee sanctuaries full of blooming plants are springing up. In these places, bees can escape pesticides and find plenty to eat. Some major cities have also made it legal to keep bees. Beekeepers in cities keep fewer hives and don’t truck them around. Even monoculture farmers can take a small portion of their land and grow plants that would sustain bees all year long, not just for a couple of weeks each year. They might also use different pesticides, or none at all. Bees are small but important for the health and well-being of many species, including humans. Taking action to protect them helps not only the bees but us as well.
pages.brief: People with outdoor space plant many different wildflowers, and honeybee sanctuaries full of blooming plants appear so bees can escape pesticides and find food. Some cities make beekeeping legal, with urban beekeepers keeping fewer hives and not trucking them. Monoculture farmers can also grow bee-sustaining plants year-round, use different pesticides, or none at all.

books.title: Laura Ingalls Wilder
books.art_why: Laura Ingalls Wilder is a named famous person, so cartoon art fits the biography.

pages.text: Where Laura Lived Minnesota South Dakota Wisconsin St. Paul Pierre De Smet (1879–1894) Pepin Walnut Grove (1867–1869, (1874–1876, 1871–1874) 1878–1879) Madison Iowa Nebraska Des Moines Lincoln Illinois Springfield Missouri Topeka Jefferson Kansas City KEY Independence (1869–1870) Laura’s homes Mansfield Oklahoma (1894–1957)
pages.brief: A map of the central United States shows the many places Laura Ingalls Wilder lived, from Wisconsin and Minnesota to Kansas, Dakota Territory, Iowa, and Missouri. Towns and states spread across the prairie and plains, tracing her family’s moves between 1867 and 1957.

pages.text: Introduction Three-year-old Laura Ingalls awoke near dawn to Pa’s gentle voice inquiring, “Do you girls want to head out to the Indian camp for a picnic?” Laura and her older sister, Mary, leaped out of bed excitedly. It wasn’t often they could spend a day with Pa, who was usually busy with farm chores. The girls packed a lunch and followed their father across the vast, rolling prairie. Warm wind stirred Laura’s hair, and insects and birds sang in the rippling grass. The Osage people had left their camp for the season. The girls picnicked near their fire pits and collected colorful beads in the grass. On the walk home, the sunset stained the sky pink and gold.
pages.brief: At dawn, three-year-old Laura and older sister Mary leap from bed when Pa asks if they want a picnic at the Indian camp. They pack lunch and follow him across the rolling prairie. They picnic near empty Osage fire pits, collect colorful beads in the grass, and walk home under a pink-and-gold sunset.

pages.text: Did You Know? The Osage tribe lived in the Kansas area for centuries before white settlers arrived. In the late 1800s, the U.S. government violently forced Osage people from their lands and moved them to Indian Territory, modern-day Oklahoma. Four-year-old Laura watched sadly as the prairie receded behind their covered wagon. She was too young to remember living in Wisconsin as a baby, but when they returned, she discovered another wonderful new world. The big woods were dark, wild, and mysterious. Laura loved being outdoors, whether throwing snowballs with her cousins or collecting firewood and doing other chores. On long winter evenings, Pa played his fiddle for the family. His music accompanied the happiest days of Laura’s childhood.
pages.brief: An Osage camp in Kansas is shown before the Osage are forced to Indian Territory. Four-year-old Laura watches the prairie recede from a covered wagon, then finds a dark, wild world in Wisconsin’s big woods, where she throws snowballs with cousins, gathers firewood, and hears Pa’s fiddle on winter evenings.

pages.text: Hard Times “Everything from the little house was in the wagon, except the beds and tables and chairs. Pa could always make new ones.” —Laura Ingalls Wilder Pa Ingalls was a restless man, and he longed to return to the open space of the prairies. He made plans to relocate his young family to Minnesota. They faced difficulties even before they left. Laura caught scarlet fever, so the family bundled her in every blanket they owned before nestling her in the back of the covered wagon. Seven-year- old Laura watched her silent, snow-covered home disappear behind her. In Minnesota, Laura and Pa were happy to be back on the wide-open prairie. First, they moved into a sod house constructed from dense mats of grass roots, which appeared from a distance to be nothing more than a gentle hill rising from the banks of a creek. Later, Pa constructed a wood house and planted wheat near the town of Walnut Grove. Laura and Mary went to school, where Laura loved reading, writing, and reciting. Ma was expecting another baby.
pages.brief: Pa Ingalls, restless for open prairie, moves the family to Minnesota. Seven-year-old Laura, bundled in blankets after scarlet fever, watches their silent, snow-covered home disappear from the covered wagon. They first live in a sod house by a creek; later Pa builds a wood house and plants wheat near Walnut Grove, where Laura and Mary attend school.

pages.text: After a few months of happiness, hardship struck. Grasshoppers, descending in swarms as big as thunderclouds, devoured the family’s wheat. Having lost their crop, the family moved into Walnut Grove and took odd jobs. Even little Laura cleaned and waited tables in a hotel. Then they lost their new baby brother, Freddie, to a fever. Their spirits lifted a little when another baby, Grace, arrived in 1877, but times remained tough. Mary fell ill, and either the illness or a stroke damaged the nerves of her eyes. No one knows for sure what caused the damage, but Mary would be blind for the rest of her life. Pa decided it was time to head west in search of a new start. Laura, right, stands beside her sisters Carrie, left, and Mary around 1880.
pages.brief: Grasshoppers descend like thunderclouds and devour the wheat. The Ingalls move into Walnut Grove and take odd jobs; little Laura cleans and waits tables in a hotel. Baby Freddie dies, baby Grace arrives, and Mary falls ill and becomes blind. Pa decides to head west. Laura stands beside sisters Carrie and Mary around 1880.

pages.text: Settling in Dakota Territory The family boarded a train in Walnut Grove and rode west to join Pa, who had gone ahead to Dakota Territory to work. Eleven-year-old Laura described the hulking, smoking train, the ornately decorated cars, and the golden blur of wheat fields speeding by as Mary hung on every word. When they got off the train, there was no settlement— just a railroad stop. The Ingalls family and a few other white families were the first citizens of what would later become the town of De Smet, South Dakota. Pa built some of the first buildings, including the first store. As more settlers arrived, the Ingalls family acquired a homestead a few miles outside of town, and Pa built a cabin, a stable, and a garden. When winter came, the family resided above their store in town, where the girls would be closer to school. Did You Know? The U.S. government encouraged white settler-colonists to move west and offered homesteads, or nearly free living space, on land stolen from Native people. At that time, the U.S. government did not consider Native people citizens. Like many white settler-colonists, Laura had racist views of the Native people on whose land she lived. Her books often erase or present Native peoples in a negative way, while glorifying the white settler-colonists.
pages.brief: Eleven-year-old Laura rides a hulking, smoking train west with her family, watching wheat fields blur past while Mary hangs on every word. They step off at a bare railroad stop in Dakota Territory, on land taken from Native people. Pa builds some of the first buildings, including a store, and the family settles on a homestead outside De Smet.

pages.text: It was a lucky decision because one blizzard after another hammered the new town. The snow was so blinding that the girls couldn’t find their way to school. Trains couldn’t deliver food, and some families nearly starved. Laura and her sisters spent hours grinding raw wheat into flour by hand. A young man named Almanzo Wilder trudged through the snow to the only established farm in the area. He returned bearing all the wheat the farmer could spare, saving the settlers’ lives. It was not the last time Laura would hear about this good man.
pages.brief: One blizzard after another hammers the new town, blinding the girls so they cannot find their way to school. Trains cannot deliver food, and some families nearly starve. Laura and her sisters spend hours grinding raw wheat into flour by hand. Almanzo Wilder trudges through snow to the only established farm and returns with wheat that saves the settlers’ lives.

pages.text: Young Lady Laura “Suffering passes, while love is eternal.” —Laura Ingalls Wilder At last the long winter broke, and the family returned to their homestead on the blooming Dakota prairie. Their farm, and the new town, soon thrived. Mary had heard about a college for blind students in Iowa, and she wanted more than anything to attend. Laura was now old enough to teach school, and she knew the income would help Mary pay for college. She accepted a teaching job in a settlement twelve miles from De Smet. Sixteen-year-old Laura bravely said goodbye to her family, but she dreaded being away from home for an entire semester. When the first week of school ended, she got a wonderful surprise. Almanzo Wilder, the young man who had helped save De Smet, pulled up to the schoolhouse in a beautiful horse-drawn sleigh, offering to bring Laura home on weekends. During their long drives across the prairie, their friendship blossomed into love. One night, Almanzo asked Laura to marry him. She said yes.
pages.brief: The long winter breaks, and the family returns to its homestead. Mary wants to attend a college for blind students, so sixteen-year-old Laura accepts a teaching job twelve miles from De Smet. After the first week, Almanzo Wilder arrives in a horse-drawn sleigh and offers to bring Laura home on weekends. Their friendship becomes love, and she agrees to marry him.

pages.text: Laura and Manly, as she moved to his De Smet, and soon a daughter, Rose. Unfortunately, the young family was then hit with a string of bad luck. A hailstorm Laura stands next to Almanzo Wilder in 1885, shortly after their marriage. wheat crop, and then Laura and Manly contracted a dangerous infection. Laura recovered fully, but Manly would walk with a limp for the rest of his life. Laura gave birth to a baby boy, but he only survived for two weeks. Then their house burned to the ground. Still a settler, Laura searched for a new place where they could get a fresh start, and it wasn’t long before she found her home. Sickness in Settler Days Before the twentieth century, people had few vaccines and very few effective medicines, so diseases were common and serious. Many members of Laura’s family were touched by illness, which was not unusual for the times.
pages.brief: Laura stands beside Almanzo Wilder in 1885, shortly after their marriage. Bad luck strikes the young family: a hailstorm ruins the wheat crop, Laura and Manly contract a dangerous infection, and Manly will walk with a limp for life. A baby boy survives only two weeks, and their house burns down. Laura searches for a new place to start again.

pages.text: Happiness at Rocky Ridge “It is the sweet, simple things of life which are the real ones after all.” —Laura Ingalls Wilder One day, a visitor presented Laura with a gleaming red apple from the Ozark Mountains. Twenty-seven-year-old Laura set out once more in a covered wagon, but this time, she headed east, toward the land of that beautiful apple. Laura and Manly bought an unassuming farm near Mansfield, Missouri, in the foothills of the Ozarks. It was rough, wooded, and rocky, but Laura instantly knew it was home. It took years of chopping trees, hauling rocks, plowing, building, and planting, but Rocky Ridge grew into a beautiful, prosperous farm. After a lifetime of wandering, Laura was content in her home. Rose, Laura’s daughter, inherited Pa’s restless spirit. Intelligent and ambitious, she moved away to San Francisco, where she became a respected journalist. One summer, Laura visited her adult daughter in California. She wrote to Manly, describing the towering redwoods, the glittering city, and the thundering Pacific Ocean. Rose was making a living at something Laura had always loved—writing. Now that life on her farm was comfortable, could Laura do the same?
pages.brief: A visitor gives Laura a gleaming red apple from the Ozark Mountains. Twenty-seven-year-old Laura travels east with Manly and buys a rough, wooded, rocky farm near Mansfield, Missouri. Years of chopping, hauling rocks, plowing, building, and planting turn Rocky Ridge into a prosperous farm. Their daughter Rose becomes a journalist in San Francisco, and Laura wonders if she could write.

pages.text: The Little House Books Once home, Laura began to pour her memories onto the page, sometimes staying up all night writing at a little desk that Manly built for her. Soon she had written an entire book about her early years under the towering trees of Wisconsin, which she titled Little House in the Big Woods. Rose sent it to a publisher. Sixty-four-year-old Laura didn’t think much would come of it. After all, it was the 1930s. People had cars, electricity, radio—who wanted to hear about doing backbreaking chores in a dark forest? The book was an immediate sensation. Laura brought to life the howling winter wind, the crackling fire, and the joyful skip of Pa’s fiddle. She captured the thrill of meeting animals in the wilderness, and she evoked the joy that a simple rag doll could bring to a settler girl who lived in a rough log cabin. The mailbox at Rocky Ridge overflowed with letters from young readers begging for more. Laura recounted her time on the Kansas prairie in Little House on the Prairie and near Walnut Grove in On the Banks of Plum Creek. The frightful winter in De Smet became The Long Winter, and the town’s recovery became Little Town on the Prairie.
pages.brief: At home, Laura pours her memories onto page after page, sometimes staying up all night at a little desk Manly built. Her first book becomes an immediate sensation, astonishing sixty-four-year-old Laura. Young readers send letters begging for more, and she writes more books about her prairie, Plum Creek, and the frightful De Smet winter.

pages.text: Laura Ingalls Wilder smiles as she signs copies of her books 1940. Laura loved answering letters from her fans and traveling to readings and book signings, but she was always happy to return home to Manly and Rocky Ridge Farm. The couple both lived into their nineties. After Laura’s death in 1957, her books lived on, even becoming a TV series in 1974. Laura Ingalls Wilder’s stories of settler life still captivate young readers today. Her life has become part of American history.
pages.brief: Laura Ingalls Wilder smiles as she signs copies of her books in 1940. She loves answering letters from fans and traveling to readings and book signings, but is always happy to return to Manly and Rocky Ridge Farm. The couple live into their nineties. After Laura’s death in 1957, her books live on, becoming a TV series in 1974.

pages.text: Freaky, Fabulous Frogs No bigger than a pea, the Matang narrow- mouthed frog is one of the smallest known frogs in the world. It was discovered on Borneo, an island in Southeast Asia, in 2010. Although examples of these frogs are found in century-old museum collections, scientists simply thought they were juveniles of a different species. They learned otherwise when they heard the frogs calling at dusk from pitcher plants. Since only adult frogs make calls, scientists concluded that these tiny frogs must be full-grown. Matang narrow-mouthed frog Narrow-mouthed frog tadpoles in a pitcher plant Do You Know? Pitcher plants are important to the Matang narrow- mouthed frog because female frogs deposit their eggs on the sides of the pitcher and tadpoles grow in the liquid that gathers inside the plant.
pages.brief: On Borneo, a tiny Matang narrow-mouthed frog, no bigger than a pea, sits at dusk on the rim of a pitcher plant. Nearby, tadpoles swim in the liquid inside another pitcher plant, and eggs rest on the plant's inner side. The frog is shown small among rainforest plants.

pages.text: The long-nosed tree frog is also known as the spike-nosed tree frog. A herpetologist discovered another frog species, the long-nosed tree frog, during an expedition to the Foja Mountains of New Guinea in 2010. The area is so remote, and so recently explored, that it has been nicknamed the “Lost World.” This tree frog is notable not for its size but rather for its long, unique nose. When the male frog calls, its nose points upward like a spike, and when the frog is done calling, its nose falls. No one knows why it does this. The frog was nicknamed the Pinocchio frog due to its long nose. The herpetologist spotted it sitting on a bag of rice in his campsite.
pages.brief: A herpetologist in the remote Foja Mountains of New Guinea spots a long-nosed tree frog sitting on a bag of rice in a campsite. The male frog's long nose points upward like a spike as it calls. Dense, recently explored rainforest surrounds the campsite.

pages.text: Sazima’s tarantulas are only found in the tabletop mountains of Brazil, which have a different climate than the surrounding area. Interesting Invertebrates Scientists estimate that vertebrates—animals with backbones—represent only 3 percent of all species. They include those species that are the most familiar (and similar) to us: amphibians, reptiles, birds, fish, and mammals. The remaining 97 percent of animal species known to science are invertebrates—animals without backbones. Tarantulas can be one of the more frightening invertebrates. They’re big and hairy, come in about nine hundred species, and are predators. The largest species can kill small mammals, lizards, and birds. Sazima’s tarantula, however, has a special beauty. Its dark blue body almost glows. This fantastic arachnid has an extremely limited habitat, only living high in the mountains of Brazil.
pages.brief: High in the tabletop mountains of Brazil, a Sazima’s tarantula rests on rocky ground. Its dark blue body almost glows against the landscape. The big, hairy spider sits in its extremely limited mountain habitat, where the climate differs from the surrounding area.

pages.text: Like most insects, planthoppers go through stages of development. This young planthopper is just beginning to develop wings. The “troll-haired” planthopper, discovered in 2013 in the rainforest of South America, may not be good-looking, but at least it has good hair. The wild hair isn’t hair at all, but instead waxy secretions from the insect’s belly. The theory is that when a predator attacks it, the “hair” breaks off and the planthopper can jump to safety, but scientists have yet to confirm this theory.
pages.brief: In a South American rainforest, a troll-haired planthopper clings to a leaf. Wild-looking waxy strands stick out from its belly like messy hair. A younger planthopper nearby is just beginning to develop wings. The insect is ready to jump if a predator attacks.

pages.text: The Gorgon’s head starfish is named for the Gorgons from Greek mythology, which had hundreds of snakes on their heads instead of hair. Underwater Wonders Scientists discovered the Gorgon’s head starfish in 2010, about half a mile (800 m) beneath the surface of the North Atlantic Ocean. The Gorgon’s head, a species of basket star, has five curly, branching arm-like appendages that split off from its body. The five appendages include as many as five thousand tips. The tips help this basket star feed on plankton and shrimp floating by in the water. It also uses its appendages to walk along the seabed. They even protect the animal when it’s disturbed by curling around it to form a tight ball. Since Earth’s oceans are vast, large portions have yet to be explored. However, that’s not the reason it took until 2013 to discover the walking bamboo shark.
pages.brief: Deep beneath the North Atlantic Ocean, a Gorgon’s head starfish rests on the seabed. Its five curly, branching arm-like appendages spread out, with many tips helping it feed on plankton and shrimp. The basket star can also walk along the seabed and curl into a tight ball.

pages.text: The walking bamboo shark has different patterns of spots and bands than other bamboo sharks. Like most sharks, the walking bamboo shark is no threat to humans. It lives off the coast of Indonesia. Scientists discovered it because its coloration differs from that of other bamboo sharks. This new species is thought to reach about 30 inches (80 cm) in length. It uses its fins to push itself along the ocean floor in search of food. The wiggling movement makes it look as though the shark is walking. Because these sharks are so rare, the government of Indonesia is taking steps to protect them.
pages.brief: Off the coast of Indonesia, a walking bamboo shark rests on the ocean floor. Its spotted and banded pattern is visible. It uses its fins to push itself along the seabed, wiggling as if walking. The rare shark is about 30 inches long and is not a threat to humans.

pages.text: Olinguitos tails than the mistaken for. Hiding in Plain View The olinguito (oh-lin-GEE-toh) managed to escape notice for so long by being mistaken for something else. In 2013, researchers discovered that for more than a hundred years, the olinguito had been wrongly identified. This mammal, which looks a lot like a teddy bear, leaps through trees at night. The smallest member of the raccoon family, the olinguito can be found in Ecuador and Colombia. It is the first species of this type to be discovered in the Americas in thirty-five years. Mistaken Identity Humans may encounter an unidentified species for years while mistaking it for a familiar species. This often happens because the two species look similar, at least on the outside. These are called cryptic species. They are only found to be distinct when scientists study their genetic code. As DNA technology is used more and more, reports of distinct new species are on the rise.
pages.brief: At night in Ecuador and Colombia, a small olinguito leaps through tree branches. It looks like a teddy bear and is the smallest member of the raccoon family. Similar-looking animals are also shown, suggesting how an unidentified species can be mistaken for a familiar one.

pages.text: The Cambodian tailorbird is hard to find because it lives in dense brush. Finding new species of birds is almost as rare as finding new mammals. Finding one in a major city is rarer still. Yet in 2009, researchers discovered the Cambodian tailorbird in and around Phnom Penh—including in the middle of a road construction site. A detailed set of tests revealed that this tailorbird was a separate, new species. Besides studying its genes and feathers, scientists studied its pretty song. While all tailorbirds warble, no two species sound quite the same. Sure enough, the song of the Cambodian tailorbird sets it apart from all the rest.
pages.brief: In dense brush near Phnom Penh, Cambodia, a Cambodian tailorbird perches and sings. The small bird is shown in and around a road construction site, where researchers found it in 2009. Its pretty song and feathers help set it apart from other tailorbirds.

pages.text: Introduction When you hear the words North Pole, do you think of a cold, empty place out in the middle of nowhere? Yes, it’s cold and remote, but it’s far from empty. Actually, the North Pole and the area around it—the Arctic region—are filled with natural wonders. Who should those treasures belong to— separate countries, all people, or the planet itself? Several countries are competing to own parts of the Arctic region beyond their own borders. These grabs for Arctic resources will affect not only the North Pole but all of Planet Earth. Sea ice surrounding the North Pole is visible from outer space.

Carbon dioxide and other gases in the atmosphere trap the Sun’s heat energy, preventing it from escaping into space. Scientists know this warming is linked to human activity because, currently, the climate is heating up about ten times faster than it heated up in other, naturally occurring warming periods. There are many different effects of climate change. Some places will experience droughts and extremely high temperatures, while other places will get more rainfall and hurricanes. In the ocean, coral reefs will die because coral can’t survive in high temperatures. And in the Arctic, climate change is causing glaciers and polar ice caps to melt and sea levels to rise.
pages.brief: Scientists in the Arctic measure the September sea ice at its lowest level for the past century. Beside them, a map shows a smaller white ice area compared with an earlier average outlined by a dashed line.

pages.text: As of early 2014, 165 countries plus the European Union had ratified, or approved, this agreement. After approval, a country has ten years to file a request if it believes it deserves any areas beyond its exclusive economic zone (EEZ). If a country’s request is approved, all resources in the larger area belong to that country. Why might a country want to expand its territory? Carving Up the Arctic Circle The area measuring 200 nautical miles out from each country’s coastline is called an exclusive economic zone (EEZ). Exclusive: not shared by others Economic: related to buying and selling Zone: an area with a special purpose or set of rules Beyond those EEZs, some areas in the Arctic Circle belong to no one—at least for now.
pages.brief: A map-style scene of Arctic coastlines shows exclusive economic zones stretching 200 nautical miles from each country into the sea. Beyond these zones lie open Arctic areas that belong to no one—at least for now.

pages.text: Why the North Pole Is Valuable The Arctic region is the area north of the Arctic Circle. It has a wealth of natural resources. One of the ones people are most dependent on is petroleum, which includes both oil and natural gas. Although located under the Earth’s surface, petroleum is easier to reach now than in the past. That’s because the Arctic ice cap is melting. Right now, the Arctic region provides about 10 percent of the world’s oil and 25 percent of its natural gas. Experts estimate that an even larger supply of each may be discovered near the North Pole in the future. According to the Environmental Protection Agency, using petroleum-based energy causes a lot of pollution and is the main cause of climate change. Many climate scientists think that in order to reduce this pollution, countries will have to stop using petroleum-based energy immediately. However, petroleum products are the main energy sources around the world. We depend on them for more than half our energy. They’re nonrenewable, meaning they will run out someday—possibly as soon as forty to fifty years from now. As a result, many countries are scrambling for new supplies of petroleum. We could decrease our dependence on petroleum by using other energy sources, such as wind, solar, and electric power.
pages.brief: An Arctic drilling operation extracts oil and natural gas from beneath the seafloor in icy water. The scene shows petroleum resources that the Arctic region supplies to the world, now easier to reach as sea ice melts.

pages.text: Beyond natural resources, the Arctic offers the promise of new shipping routes. Right now, most of those routes can be used only during warmer months, when much of the sea ice melts. However, with continued melting, routes may be open during much more of the year. For example, a ship recently traveled from northern Russia to China during February for the first time ever. Dangerous Business Obtaining natural resources in the Arctic region is riskier and more expensive than in most other parts of the globe. Here’s why: • Regular equipment can’t always handle the climate. Special equipment must be used (or, in some cases, developed) that can work in the extreme cold, wet conditions. • Transporting materials and people to and from such a remote location is expensive. • Higher wages need to be paid to people to work in such a remote place. • If accidents happen, the distance from search-and- Oil spills are hard to clean up. Animals, rescue facilities might such as this sea otter, end up coated in oil. mean additional loss of life or increased damage to equipment or the environment. • Regular clean-up equipment can’t handle Arctic oil spills. Cleaning up oil spills in sea ice is much harder than in liquid water.
pages.brief: A sea otter coated in oil floats in cold water after an Arctic oil spill. In the background, a ship travels through a partly frozen route, showing the risks of dangerous business in the region.

pages.text: Scientists and environmental groups argue that the Arctic region is valuable not only to humans. It’s also valuable because of the natural environment and the wide variety of life forms it supports. These include tundra vegetation, caribou, polar bears, whales, and seals. Using more Arctic resources could upset the natural environment in many ways. Polar bears are already in danger of extinction, because of polar ice melt. Many scientists think that most polar bears will die out between 2050 and 2100. Scientists are also concerned that drilling for petroleum could negatively impact caribou and bird populations. Roads, trucks, power lines, and drilling cause noise and other disruptions for wildlife, which might impact migratory and mating patterns. A caribou and calf graze on the autumn tundra in Arctic Canada.
pages.brief: A caribou and its calf graze on the autumn tundra in Arctic Canada, surrounded by low vegetation. Their presence highlights wildlife that could be disrupted by roads, trucks, power lines, and drilling in the region.

pages.text: Indigenous Peoples of the Arctic Indigenous peoples make up about 10 percent of people living in the Arctic. The Arctic is home to forty distinct Indigenous ethnic groups, including the Saami (SAH-mee) and the Inuit. While all Arctic Indigenous tribes, nations, and groups are different, they are similar in that their cultures and survival are built on Indigenous knowledge. Indigenous knowledge has been developed over thousands of years, through observation of the Arctic’s unique environment and traditions that reflect the surroundings. Inuit people, both in the past and today, rely on wildlife such as caribou, seals, walruses, and whales. They use every part of these animals, such as bones, teeth, fat, and skins. These resources provide them with food, clothing, boats, and tools. Because the lifestyle of Arctic Indigenous peoples relies so much on the environment, they are uniquely hurt by climate change. When ice melts, it is more difficult for members of these groups to hunt the animals that are important to their way of life. Some Indigenous peoples are at risk of hunger because hunting provides much of their food. Changes in the environment also make water less safe to drink.
pages.brief: Inuit people use caribou, seals, walruses, and whales for food, clothing, boats, and tools, using every part of the animals. Their culture and survival depend on Indigenous knowledge developed over thousands of years in the Arctic environment.

pages.text: Who Wants the North Pole? Four countries—Norway, Russia, Canada, and Greenland—have filed requests for larger territories than they now own. In other words, those four countries want more of the Arctic region than just their EEZ. In some cases, they want territory all the way to the North Pole. Russia’s Arctic coastline is about 4,300 miles (7,000 km) long. It has the longest coastline of any country bordering the Arctic Ocean. In 2007, Russia sent a small research ship to the seafloor at the North Pole. The ship gathered samples of soil and water from an underwater land feature called the Lomonosov Ridge. Scientists hoped to prove that the ridge is part of Russia and should belong to Russia. Ownership would give Russia the right to any natural resources found there. In 2021, Russia claimed even more of the seabed, adding 705,000 square kilometers to its claims. However, across the Arctic Ocean, the Lomonosov Ridge connects to Canada, which has the second-longest Arctic coastline. Canada also claims this underwater mountain ridge as part of its seabed. Denmark, too, seeks ownership of the ridge because it has a historic relationship with Greenland.
pages.brief: A small Russian research ship sits in icy Arctic water above the North Pole, lowering equipment toward the seafloor. Below, the Lomonosov Ridge stretches underwater across the Arctic Ocean, linking toward Canada. Russia hopes the ridge is part of its territory.

pages.text: The North Pole Neighborhood The bright blue on the map indicates shallower water, and the dark blue is deep water. The Lomonosov Ridge is the bright blue line just left of the North Pole. It is 1,110 miles (1,800 km) long. Canada and the United States disagree about ownership of the Beaufort Sea. This body of water is north of both western Canada and Alaska. All these disputes have to do with mineral rights as well as control of shipping routes.
pages.brief: A map of the Arctic Ocean shows shallow water in bright blue and deep water in dark blue. The long Lomonosov Ridge runs just left of the North Pole, and the Beaufort Sea lies north of western Canada and Alaska.

pages.text: Russia, Norway, and possibly other nations are also interested in expanding their territories for military purposes. They are worried that they might someday need to defend their Arctic resources. They also want good locations for military bases in case of a war between Eastern and Western Hemisphere countries. Arctic routes would shorten travel distances for military planes and ships to reach their targets. No decisions have been made yet about countries’ requests to own more of the Arctic region. Each country believes it has good reasons to expand its territory. The disputes continue to set the countries at odds with each other. Could there be a different plan for the changing Arctic region? What About the South Pole? The South Pole is at the other end of Earth’s axis. It is also a place of extreme cold. An international agreement prevents any country from owning Antarctica or using its resources. The continent is set aside for scientific research and peaceful purposes only. No military activity is permitted there. Should those same guidelines be applied to the Arctic A 165-foot (50 m) dome covers the Amundsen- region? Scott South Pole Station in Antarctica.
pages.brief: A large 165-foot dome covers the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station in Antarctica, standing on a vast icy landscape. The station represents an international agreement that sets the continent aside for peaceful scientific research only, with no military activity permitted.

pages.text: Conclusion Fifty or one hundred years from now, should any country own the Arctic region, including the North Pole? Some people believe that Indigenous groups, and their Indigenous knowledge, should be given greater consideration in these debates. Six Arctic Indigenous groups are considered permanent participants in the Arctic Council. This group encourages nations and groups that share Arctic concerns to work together to solve problems. Through the Arctic Council, these Indigenous groups have a voice in policies and laws that affect the Arctic. The countries that want to expand their areas of control in the Arctic region face important decisions. Which path will win: peaceful cooperation or competition for control?
