pages.brief: A woman of the Inuit people cooks on the tundra, using traditional knowledge and the Arctic environment. Around her, the open landscape reflects the cultural traditions that Indigenous groups bring to debates over the North Pole’s future.

books.title: Elephants: Giant Mammals
books.art_why: Elephants are living animals that can be photographed today.

pages.text: How Big Can They Get? African elephant Human height: 6 feet (1.8 m) 13 feet (4 m) weight: 175 pounds (79.4 kg) 14,000 pounds (6,350 kg) Asian elephant 10 feet (3 m) weight: 11,000 pounds (5,000 kg) Big and Brainy Without a doubt, elephants are the most gigantic land animals living on Earth today. To find a more immense walking creature, you would have to go back to the age of dinosaurs! Elephants aren’t just huge. They’re also highly intelligent, have many ways to communicate with one another, and are clever enough to work together to get things done.
pages.brief: An African elephant and an Asian elephant stand beside a human, showing the elephants’ enormous height and weight. The African elephant is the largest, the Asian elephant is a little smaller, and the human is tiny by comparison, making the elephants look like gigantic land animals.

pages.text: Interesting Elephant Facts An African elephant’s ears are twice as big as an Asian elephant’s. Young elephants drink milk from their mothers for up to three years. An elephant uses its trunk to pick up food, and more. An elephant’s big, round feet have soft pads on the bottom. Elephants are mammals. All mammals: • have a backbone • are warm-blooded • have hair on their bodies • produce milk to feed at some time in their lives.
pages.brief: A young elephant nurses from its mother while an African elephant shows ears twice as wide as an Asian elephant’s. Nearby, an elephant curls its trunk around food, and another stands on big, round feet with soft pads underneath.

pages.text: African and Asian Elephants The two main species of elephants are African and Asian. It is simple to tell them apart if you know what continent you are in, but there are other clues as well. African elephants are greater in size than their Asian relatives, with males measuring 13 feet (4 m) tall and weighing up to 14,000 pounds (6,350 kg). Females are shorter and lighter, at around 9 feet (2.7 m) tall and up to 10,000 pounds (4,540 kg). Male Asian elephants are around 3 feet (0.9144 m) shorter and about 3,000 pounds (1,360 kg) lighter than African males. Females are even smaller and, unlike African females, often have no tusks at all. An African elephant’s appearance differs from its Asian counterpart in other ways, too. Its floppy ears are often twice as large as those of an Asian elephant. The back of an African elephant also dips down in the middle, unlike an Asian elephant’s. If you inspected the animal even more thoroughly, you would see two “fingers” at the end of its jumbo trunk. These handy flaps grab food and small objects.
pages.brief: A large male African elephant stands beside a smaller Asian elephant. The African elephant has huge floppy ears, a back that dips in the middle, and a trunk with two finger-like tips; the Asian elephant has smaller ears and a body that is shorter and lighter.

pages.text: African Asian Elephants use their tusks to dig, fight, or move things around. African elephants also use their tusks to dig for water. In addition to having smaller ears, Asian elephants have large, round bumps on the tops of their huge heads. Spotting these bumps is a clear way to identify the species. The bumps are often the tallest point on an Asian elephant. Their backs are flat or arched, and we can’t forget their trunks, which have just one “finger” at the end instead of two.
pages.brief: An Asian elephant stands with large, round bumps on top of its huge head, while an African elephant uses its tusks to dig. The Asian elephant’s back is flat or arched, and its trunk ends in one finger-like tip; the African elephant’s trunk has two.

pages.text: Elephant Hangouts Elephants are adaptable enough to live in many different types of habitats, as long as they can find enough food and water. In Africa, elephants live in hot, dry grasslands, rainforests, and even deserts. They can live at sea level or high in the mountains. Asian elephants live in wet rainforests and swamps as well as in other more arid forests with long dry seasons. Because of their hulking size, even ferocious lions and tigers rarely threaten elephants. Humans, however, often illegally hunt elephants for their ivory tusks and shoot them for harming crops. As human population increases, elephants’ natural habitats are disappearing. Humans build more roads, plant more crops, and cut down more trees all the time. Less and less land is available for wild animals—especially ones that need large amounts of food and space. Elephants once roamed almost all of Africa and South Asia, but today their habitats have shrunk a great deal.
pages.brief: Elephants stand in hot, dry African grassland and in wet Asian rainforest and swamp. A lion and tiger watch from a distance, while roads, crop fields, and cut trees edge closer to the elephants’ shrinking natural habitat as more land is taken by people.

pages.text: Where Elephants Live ASIA Asian elephant range EUROPE AFRICA African elephant range.
pages.brief: A broad map of the world shows wild elephants spread across Africa and Asia. African elephants stand in many parts of Africa, while Asian elephants occupy smaller areas of Asia. Europe is visible between them, and the elephants’ separate places show where each kind lives.

pages.text: No Meat, Thanks Elephants are herbivores and therefore eat only plants. Other than that, they aren’t picky. They’ll chow down on grass, leaves, branches, tree bark, seeds, and fruits. The most important thing is that there is a lot of food to eat. An adult elephant can eat more than 300 pounds (136 kg) of food every day and slurp about 20 to 60 gallons (75.7–227.1 L) of water, using its handy trunk like an enormous straw. Then, the elephant sprays the water from the end of its trunk into its mouth. Only about 44 percent of the food elephants eat is digested.
pages.brief: An adult elephant stands among grass, leaves, branches, tree bark, seeds, and fruits, using its trunk to gather food. It lifts a trunkful toward its mouth and sprays water from its trunk into its mouth, with plenty of plants around it to eat.

pages.text: Wowser! • Elephant pregnancies last eighteen to twenty-two those of any other animal. • One of the elephant’s closest living relatives is the hyrax—a small, cute, furry animal. You might never think they’re related! • Elephants are closely related to woolly have been extinct for more than ten thousand years.
pages.brief: A pregnant elephant stands with a rounded belly, showing a long pregnancy. Beside her is a small, cute, furry hyrax, and a woolly mammoth appears as an extinct relative that has been gone for more than ten thousand years.

pages.text: This Asian elephant mother uses her trunk to spray water. On sunny days, she might roll in sand or dirt to not get sunburnt. The Elephant Family Elephants, especially female elephants, are social animals. Adult females live together in family groups, most often led by the oldest among them. The herd might be made up of a grandmother elephant, her grown-up daughters, and the daughters’ calves. They take care of each other and eat, bathe, and play together. From the moment an elephant is born, the whole herd helps the mother care for her 250-pound (110 kg) calf. Adult elephants work together to drive away predators. Other adults will even nurse the calf if it’s hungry.
pages.brief: An Asian elephant mother sprays water over her back with her trunk on a sunny day, while another elephant rolls in sand or dirt to avoid sunburn. Female elephants and calves stay close as a family herd, eating, bathing, and playing together, with adults caring for a 250-pound calf.

pages.text: Young elephants have an extra-long childhood. They nurse from their mothers for up to three years. During this time, and for several years later, elephants learn vital survival skills, including where to find food and water, and how to use their trunks. They aren’t mature adults until they’re ten to fifteen years old. Then, males and females go their separate ways, with males leaving the herd to live alone or with other male elephants. Females stay with the herd and eventually raise their own calves. If an adult trouble, it can live for sixty to seventy years. Sometimes an elephant lives so long that it runs out of teeth! It only grows six sets in its lifetime, and once they’re gone, the elephant can’t chew its food well anymore. Older elephants often stay in marshes. They find softer plants to chew there.
pages.brief: A young elephant nurses from its mother and stays close as the herd teaches it where to find food and water and how to use its trunk. Older elephants stand in a marsh, chewing softer plants, and a grown male walks apart from the female herd.

pages.text: Giant Friends It’s hard not to feel a connection to nature’s king-sized elephants. We know they’re brainy and caring, and they like to have fun. Their awesome size and distinctive personalities make them impossible to ignore. If we all work to protect elephants, these giants of nature will roam the Earth for a long time to come. African elephants on the Samburu National Reserve in Kenya, Africa.
pages.brief: A herd of African elephants stands together on the Samburu National Reserve in Kenya, Africa. The brainy, caring elephants gather in the open landscape, their great size and distinctive personalities making them impossible to ignore as people work to protect them.

books.title: Condors: Giant Birds
books.art_why: Condors are real animals alive today, so photographs fit.

pages.text: Meet the Condor Weighing over 30 pounds (13.5 kg), an enormous bird lifts off high in the majestic Andes Mountains of South America. Its powerful wings, measuring an amazing 10.5 feet (3.2 m) across, propel the bird to a dizzying height of 15,000 feet (4,600 m). This is the largest flying bird in the world—the giant Andean condor. As it glides along, it uses its impressive wingspan and extra-keen eyesight to search for food far below. How Big Is It?
pages.brief: A giant Andean condor lifts off high in the Andes Mountains of South America, its enormous wings spread wide as it glides. The huge bird searches for food far below, using its impressive wingspan and keen eyesight over the mountain landscape.

pages.text: Where Condors Live Condors are fascinating animals. This book explores the habitats, eating habits, appearance, and offspring of these giant birds. Vibrant images help bring this book to life. Life on Wind and Rock Andean condors live in the western parts of South America, and California condors live in the American Southwest. All condors need a wide-open habitat so that when they spot food, they have enough space to fly down with their huge wings and land. Condors also need sufficient wind currents to enable them to climb high and fly long distances. These birds can fly as far as 150 miles (240 km) in one day to find food and may reach speeds of up to 50 miles Written by Charlotte Welton per hour (80 kmph).
pages.brief: Andean condors soar over the western parts of South America while California condors fly over the American Southwest. Both birds use wide-open habitat and wind currents to climb high, glide long distances, and search for food across mountains and open land.

pages.text: Some condors live near the sea, and perch high up on cliffs, which provide an excellent view of the shoreline. Most condors, however, live in dry places where they can soar above rocky canyons, deserts, and mountains. Condors prefer to nest on elevated landforms. Lofty nests help keep condor eggs safe from potential predators on the ground. Condors don’t use twigs and feathers to make an inviting, cozy nest. Instead, they nest directly on rocky cave floors or jagged outer ledges. Some California condors nest in large holes near the top of the world’s tallest trees—the towering California redwoods.
pages.brief: A condor perches high on a sea cliff with a clear view of the shoreline. Other condors soar above rocky canyons, deserts, and mountains. One nests on a jagged ledge or rocky cave floor, while another rests in a hole near the top of a towering California redwood.

pages.text: A condor can devour up to 4 pounds (1.8 kg) of food in one day and then go for days without eating. Condors have a special diet that you wouldn’t find very tasty. They only eat carrion —dead and decaying animals. California condors eat small mammals such as rabbits and gophers. However, they prefer to eat larger mammals such as deer and cattle. Condors feeding near the ocean clean the beaches of all kinds of seafood, from small fish to huge whales that have washed ashore. Decomposing animals can be filled with harmful bacteria that can cause disease. Condors, though, have special digestive systems and are not in danger from bacteria. Condors play an important role in nature. They do an expert job of gobbling up rotting flesh and helping to keep ecosystems a little more germ-free.
pages.brief: A condor feeds on carrion, tearing at a dead animal in an open landscape. Nearby lie a rabbit, gopher, deer, and cattle remains, showing the kinds of dead mammals it may eat. Another condor stands on a beach beside a washed-up whale and fish, cleaning the shoreline.

pages.text: Condors do not have a good sense of smell, but their excellent eyesight is an important tool when hunting for food. They can see their food from very high in the sky. Condors sometimes see other carrion-eating birds circling nearb y—a sure sign that they’ve found food. This sight often leads to a condor’s next meal. The condor will simply swoop in and eat the food that other birds have found.
pages.brief: High in the sky, a condor scans the ground with its excellent eyesight. Far below, other carrion-eating birds circle near a dead animal. The condor sees the circling birds as a sign of food, then swoops down to eat the meal the other birds have found.

pages.text: What Makes a Condor a Bird? All birds • have a backbone • have a bill • • • •.
pages.brief: A condor stands on a rocky perch in a natural mountain setting, its large bill and feathered bird body clearly visible. The bird has a backbone and a bill, basic features shared by all birds.

pages.text: Check Out the Condor There are definite similarities between adult male and female California condors—both have black feathers and fluffy black “collars” or necks. Andean males and females both have black feathers and white necks. Andean males, however, have large, fleshy lumps on their heads called combs. California condors don’t have combs, so when deciding which species of bird you’re looking at, check for a comb. If it’s present, it’s a male Andean condor.
pages.brief: An adult male Andean condor stands with black feathers, a white neck, and large fleshy combs on his head. Beside him, a female Andean condor has black feathers and a white neck. Two California condors show black feathers and fluffy black collars, with no combs.

pages.text: Storks are one of the closest relatives of condors. They look nothing alike, though! Condors are very clean birds. After eating, they clean their heads on rocks and tree branches. They also bathe in water and then spend hours smoothing their feathers. All condors have a bald head—a very useful adaptation. Being feather-free from the neck up makes grooming simpler for condors, especially after they stick their heads in decaying animals to feed. Condors have hardly any feathers for the messy stuff to stick to.
pages.brief: A condor cleans its bald head by rubbing it against a rock and a tree branch after feeding. Nearby, another condor bathes in water, then smooths its feathers for hours. A stork stands nearby, a close relative that looks nothing alike. The feather-free neck and head make grooming easier.

pages.text: A One-Egg Nest A female condor produces just one egg every two years, so it’s crucial that the egg be protected. The female and male each sit on the egg, which hatches in about fifty-six days. As the chick matures, its feathers gradually turn from gray to black. The young bird starts to fly when it is around six months old. If they’re lucky, wild condors usually live about sixty years, and condors in zoos or refuges can live for more than seventy-five years. Most animals, including condors, live longer in captivity. In these protected environments, condors are pretty pampered! In the wild, though, condors face many hazards. Sadly, one of the most damaging influences on condors has been human beings.
pages.brief: A female condor sits on a single egg on a rocky nest ledge while a male condor stands nearby. The egg is protected, and later a gray chick grows black feathers. The young bird starts to fly around six months old, with wild and refuge condors shown at different ages.

pages.text: Condors in Trouble Andean condors and California condors are endangered. Their numbers are much lower today than they were two hundred years ago. The trouble began when people started moving into areas where condors lived. Many people in North and South America didn’t like the big birds, so they shot them. People also didn’t like coyotes and wolves, so they left poison out to kill them. When the condors ate the dead animals, they died from the poison, too. Many condors died of lead poisoning, too. They would feast on animals people had shot and sometimes accidentally eat lead bullets. In more recent times, electrical power has also proved a danger to condors. As sharp as condors’ eyesight is, they can’t always see power lines, so they fly into the wires and die. In 1987, California condors were dangerously close to extinction—only about ten were alive in the wild. Scientists captured the wild birds and brought them to refuges. There, the scientists could protect them and help the birds raise their young.
pages.brief: A California condor flies near electrical power lines in an open landscape. On the ground, a coyote and wolf are near poison bait, and a dead animal lies nearby. In a refuge, scientists gently capture a wild condor to protect it and help it raise young.

pages.text: After five years of hard work and dedication, scientists began releasing California condors back into the wild. By May 2013, over 230 California condors were flying free again. Since 1973, similar efforts have been made in South America to save Andean condors. Organizations there have set aside land for condors. Today, their numbers are rising, and it’s estimated that a few thousand birds live in the wild.
pages.brief: Scientists release California condors from a refuge back into the wild, and the huge birds fly free over protected land. By May 2013, more than 230 California condors soar again, while in South America people set aside land for Andean condors and their rising numbers.

pages.text: A Truly Giant Bird Can you imagine what it would be like to see such a gigantic bird fly overhead? It’s an amazing sight since a condor’s wingspan measures twice as wide as an eagle’s and five times as wide as a falcon’s! Many California condors live in protected reserves, which is one of the only places left where the huge birds fly. Serious dangers remain for condors. But if people continue to protect these giant, high-flying birds and their environments, they will keep us in awe for centuries to come.
pages.brief: A gigantic condor flies overhead with wings fully spread above a protected reserve where many California condors live. Below, an eagle and a falcon appear much smaller, showing the condor's wingspan is twice as wide as an eagle's and five times as wide as a falcon's.

books.title: Genetics at Work
books.art_why: Modern genetics, farms, labs, zoos, and scientists are real-world subjects that can be photographed.

pages.text: Family members look alike because they share the same inherited traits. Introduction Do you sometimes wonder what you want to be when you grow up? Have you ever thought about being a doctor or a detective, or working with animals? All these jobs have one thing in common— genetics. What is genetics? Genetics is the field of science that studies how all living things pass traits from one generation to the next. Traits are features such as hair color, finger length, and nose shape. Understanding genetics is important in many jobs. Farming, breeding animals, curing diseases, preventing possible illnesses, and solving crimes are just a few examples.
pages.brief: A family stands together in a bright living room, their faces showing similar hair color, finger length, and nose shape. A young girl in the family looks thoughtful, as if imagining future work as a doctor, detective, or animal expert.

pages.text: Scientists also use genetic techniques with animals. For example, they use genetic breeding techniques to create chickens that lay more eggs. They create cows that grow faster and produce more milk. Genetics sounds great for farming. Why wouldn’t we want crops that grow faster and taste better? Why not help cows milk? Some say Selectively bred piglets grow up faster changing our crops than their wild cousins. and animals will damage their genetic diversity. By only breeding for a select group of traits, many other useful plant and animal traits may be lost forever. The lack of genetic diversity among crops and animals may also leave them vulnerable to a single virus that could wipe out an entire species. People in favor of using genetics in farming want to improve food production. Those against it are concerned about the unknown effects it might have on our environment and our health.
pages.brief: A scientist in work clothes examines plump chickens and healthy cows on a sunny farm. In a grassy field nearby, selectively bred piglets stand beside wild-looking cousins. The scene contrasts animals bred for more eggs and milk with their wild relatives.

pages.text: Animal Breeding Animal breeders use some of the same genetic techniques as plant scientists. These include selective breeding and hybridization. Hybridization is also known as crossbreeding. It involves breeding different varieties or even species to combine the best characteristics of both. For example, female horses can be bred with male donkeys to produce mules. Mules are a hybrid of horses and donkeys. They are tough like donkeys, but agile like horses. They make very good work animals. A donkey (top) crossed with a horse (left) yields a mule (right).
pages.brief: A female horse and a male donkey stand in a sunny farmyard beside a sturdy mule. The mule has a horse-like build and donkey-like toughness, standing calmly in the open yard. The three animals show how crossbreeding combines traits from different animals.

pages.text: Many dog breeders raise dogs only for show. However, many dog breeds are bred for specific purposes, such as hunting, herding, or guarding. Some of the Border collies are excellent herders. earliest hunting dogs were spaniels. Spaniels such as springer and cocker spaniels were first bred in Spain to hunt water birds like ducks or land birds like pheasants. Dog breeders determine the traits they want in a dog. Then they select parents that, when bred, will pass on those traits to their offspring. Herding is another desirable trait that is bred into some dogs. Herding dogs are used to protect and round up cattle and other livestock. Border collies and Australian shepherds are popular herding dogs. They have been so well bred that they continue to herd animals even if they aren’t trained to. Many people who own border collies report that their dogs attempt to herd cars and even people! The border collie breed was developed hundreds of years ago. It was first used to herd cattle and sheep along the border between England and Scotland.
pages.brief: A border collie stands alert in a green field, guiding a small group of sheep. Nearby, a springer spaniel walks through tall grass with its nose low, as if following the scent of ducks or pheasants. Both dogs show traits people bred for herding and hunting.

pages.text: The Australian shepherd was developed from several herding breeds, including the border collie, which English settlers brought with them to Australia. These shepherds are still widely used in Australia. Cattle and other livestock there are raised in open fields. Some dogs are bred as guard dogs. The Doberman pinscher and the German shepherd are two common guard dogs. The Doberman was first bred by a German watchman named Louis Dobermann in the late 1890s. The breed has a reputation for being dangerous. However, recent breeders have worked hard to make the Doberman more calm and friendly. Many dogs are hybrids—crosses between two or more breeds. Some people believe that hybrids make the best pets because they combine the best traits of both parents. Mutts combine the best traits of many breeds.
pages.brief: An Australian shepherd works cattle in a wide open field under a clear sky. Nearby, a German shepherd and a calm Doberman pinscher stand alert, while a mixed-breed dog rests in the grass. The scene shows herding, guarding, and hybrid dogs.

pages.text: Giant pandas have been helped by captive-breeding programs. Animals in Zoos Many zoos perform animal research and provide education and entertainment. Some zoos use genetics in their research. This research is conducted to ensure that animal species survive well into the future. Genetics play an important role in protecting many endangered and threatened animal species.
pages.brief: A giant panda sits in a zoo enclosure, calmly chewing bamboo. Nearby, zoo visitors watch while a zoo scientist observes the panda. The scene shows how zoos use research and education to help endangered species survive.

pages.text: One technique that zoo scientists use to increase the populations of endangered species is captive breeding. Captive breeding is the breeding of animals that are living in captivity (such as in zoos). The purpose is to maintain genetic diversity within a species. Some offspring bred in captivity are released into wild populations. They introduce different genes that give the wild animals a better chance at survival. This type of captive breeding is only successful if the animals can survive and reproduce on their own once they are released into the wild. Captive breeding is being used with certain endangered and threatened species. These include the red wolf, gorilla, giant panda, cheetah, and rhinoceros. Another type of captive breeding is often done with species that are nearly extinct and cannot survive in the wild. It gives the animals a chance to reproduce in a protected environment. Although captive breeding is important, it cannot replace animals living and breeding in the wild. Zoo employees also try to educate people about the importance of protecting the habitats of endangered and threatened species. If wild animals such as rhinoceroses and tigers are not protected, future generations of people will only be able to read about those animals in books.
pages.brief: Inside a zoo breeding center, a red wolf rests in a protected enclosure while a cheetah stands nearby. A gorilla and a rhinoceros are in separate pens, and a giant panda eats bamboo in the background. The animals show species helped by captive breeding.

pages.text: Solving Crimes When crime solvers put on their detective hats these days, they have more to work with than a magnifying glass. Police, detectives, and lawyers now use genetics and DNA to help them solve crimes. All genes contain DNA. DNA Today, detectives have carries the code that determines more clues to work with than ever before. an organism’s genetic traits. Like fingerprints, every organism’s DNA is different. By fingerprinting criminals, police can keep a database of fingerprints. Fingerprints at a crime scene can then be matched with the fingerprints of known criminals in the database. Since DNA, like fingerprints, is unique, we use the term DNA fingerprinting for the use of DNA to solve crimes. The advantage of using DNA is that you do not need to find a fingerprint. To get a DNA fingerprint of a criminal, all you need is a small bit of skin, a single hair, or a drop of fluid such as blood or saliva. It is almost impossible for a criminal not to leave behind a trace of skin, hair, or fluid. Everywhere a person goes, he or she leaves microscopic traces of DNA.
pages.brief: A detective in a police office studies a magnifying glass beside a computer showing DNA patterns. On a table, a single hair, a small skin flake, and a drop of blood are laid out as clues. The scene shows how tiny traces can help solve crimes.

pages.text: For example, imagine that investigators find skin cells under a victim’s fingernails. They can determine the DNA of the skin cells. They then take a DNA sample from the suspect. If the two samples match, the investigators are closer to solving the crime. A lab agent works on DNA evidence. Law enforcement agencies are now building databases of DNA samples, much like collections of fingerprints. These databases contain the DNA fingerprints of convicted criminals. They also store other evidence found at crime scenes. DNA also has been used to free people who were wrongly convicted of crimes. DNA fingerprinting has helped solve many crimes since it was first used in 1985. However, some people are concerned about possible contamination affecting the accuracy of DNA testing as well as its possible misuse. Even so, DNA fingerprinting will continue to be used as long as it helps identify criminals and solve crimes.
pages.brief: In a crime lab, a lab agent in gloves examines skin cells under a victim’s fingernails and compares them with a suspect’s DNA sample on a computer screen. Nearby, another investigator studies a DNA database printout.

pages.text: Health Genetics is also used by many medical and health-care scientists. Genetics is used to diagnose, treat, and prevent diseases as well as to develop new medicines. Medical scientists are now discovering many genes that cause specific diseases. Identifying genes that cause a specific disease helps scientists develop medicines and vaccines to cure or prevent the disease. Genetics counselors also use genetics. They help parents and future parents figure out the odds of passing on genetic disorders to their children. Parents use this information to help them decide whether to have children. They also consider how to cope with the possibility of caring for children with genetic disorders. Some common genetic disorders that may be passed on from parents to their children are cystic fibrosis, Huntington’s disease, and breast cancer. Do You Know? In 2000, scientists completed the Human Genome Project, a full map of the location of every human gene. Humans have about twenty-four thousand genes arranged in a specific order on our chromosomes. It took powerful computers ten years to count and locate them all. Many diseases are caused by genes that are missing or in the wrong place.
pages.brief: A genetic counselor sits with two parents in a bright office, pointing to a simple chromosome chart on a desk. In the background, a medical scientist studies a computer screen filled with gene data. The scene connects family health choices with gene research.

pages.text: A scientist compares DNA fingerprints on a computer screen. Conclusion The field of genetics offers many job opportunities. Genetics is an exciting and relatively new branch of science. It brings new developments and new opportunities almost daily. Whether in plant and animal breeding, medicine, the study of crime, or some other field, many career opportunities are linked to genetics. Check the library or the Internet for more information about this exciting field of science.
pages.brief: A group of workers stands together in a bright science center: a plant breeder with seedlings, a doctor in a white coat, a detective, and an animal breeder with a dog. A young student nearby looks at a library shelf and a computer.

books.title: Hoover Dam
books.art_why: Most of the book recreates 1930s construction work and the 1905 flood, moments that cannot be photographed today.

pages.text: On guided tours, visitors go inside the dam to get a behind-the-scenes look at how the dam works.
pages.brief: A small group of visitors follows a guide through a concrete passageway deep inside Hoover Dam, pausing beside the machinery and pipes that keep the dam working, their faces turned up as the guide points out the behind-the-scenes equipment around them.

pages.text: From the western side of Hoover Dam, visitors can look across the dam to Arizona (left). Kayaking is popular on Lake Mead (right). Water in the Desert Every summer in parts of the southwestern United States, temperatures often exceed 100°F (38°C). Much of the region receives less than 10 inches (25.4 cm) of rainfall each year. So why do millions of people visit the area every year? Why do they come to fish, boat, water-ski, and swim in an enormous refreshing lake? How is this possible in such a dry, sun-baked place? The U.S. Southwest was transformed when Hoover Dam was built in the 1930s. Construction of this iconic landmark brought water and power to parched desert lands. The dam allowed cities, agriculture, and recreation to grow.
pages.brief: From the western rim above Hoover Dam, visitors lean out to look across the long concrete crest toward Arizona, while below on the right two kayakers paddle across the bright blue water of Lake Mead under a dry desert sky.

pages.text: Colorado River floodwaters filled much of Imperial Valley in 1905 and created the Salton Sea. It took two years to get the water under control. The Colorado River winds through the southwestern United States, bringing life-giving water to an otherwise dry region. People have lived along the Colorado’s banks for centuries. They used its water to irrigate crops. However, the Colorado was a fluctuating source of water long ago. Each spring, the river grew with snowmelt, often to the point of flooding farmlands. Later in the year when it shrunk to a trickle, crops would die. Early settlers were discouraged by the changeable water supply, so some people sought a way to control the river. In 1901, a private company built the Alamo Canal just north of the Mexican border. The canal’s purpose was to divert the Colorado’s flow westward to provide irrigation to California’s Imperial Valley. As a result, farming did very well. However, severe flooding in 1905 destroyed the canal’s control gates and ruined much of Imperial Valley.
pages.brief: Brown floodwater from the Colorado River spreads wide across the farmland of Imperial Valley in 1905, swallowing fields, fences and farm buildings, while stranded farmers stand on a small rise and watch the muddy water creep toward them.

pages.text: Imperial Valley residents wanted a larger canal. Arthur Powell Davis was chief engineer of the government agency that manages water in the West. He thought that constructing a dam along the river would be a better solution. It would get more water to more people. After studying the Colorado, he reported his findings to Congress in 1918. Ten years later, Congress approved construction of Hoover Dam along with a canal to provide irrigation to Imperial Valley. In 1930, President Hoover authorized spending for the project. The Great Depression began only eight months before the Hoover Dam project was approved. It was a time of great economic hardship in the United States. Millions were out of work. In total, 21,000 people flocked to southern Nevada for the construction jobs. President Hoover wanted to put as many people to work as possible. He ordered construction to begin before housing, drinking water, a hospital, or other facilities were in place. At first, some workers and their families lived in camps that lacked electricity and running water. Homes were tents, and people bathed in the Colorado River.
pages.brief: Arthur Powell Davis, chief engineer, stands in a paneled room before seated members of Congress, one hand on a large map of the Colorado River, reporting what he learned from studying the river and urging them to approve a dam.

pages.text: Hoover Dam is considered an arch- gravity dam. A Massive Dam Hoover Dam was the tallest dam in the world when it was built. Constructing the dam was an amazing engineering feat that required the skills of six different companies working together. Hoover Dam combines the features of a gravity dam and an arch dam. A gravity dam relies on its own weight to resist the force of stored water. An arch dam, which curves upstream, causes most of the water to flow against the canyon walls. The flow of water squeezes the arch, which compresses and strengthens the dam. Hoover Dam’s power plant converts the energy of moving water into electricity. Lake Mead, the dam’s reservoir, is the largest human-made lake in the United States.
pages.brief: Hoover Dam curves upstream between the dark walls of Black Canyon, holding back the wide blue water of Lake Mead, while the dam's power plant sits at the base of the concrete face and tiny figures on the crest show the dam's enormous scale.

pages.text: Parts of Hoover Dam Top is 45 feet (13.7 m) thick Four intake towers, each 395 feet (120.4 m) tall, control the power plant’s water supply. Height: 726.4 feet (221.4 m) rock to crest Width: 1,244 feet (379 m) across Black Canyon at the top Weight: more tons (5,987,419 mt) Base is 660 feet (201 m) thick.
pages.brief: Seen from downstream in Black Canyon, the enormous concrete face of Hoover Dam rises from a thick base to a slimmer top, and four tall intake towers stand in the blue reservoir behind it, making the boats below look tiny.

pages.text: Hoover Dam Diversion Map Arizona Nevada Constructing the Dam In order to build Hoover Dam, the dam site first had to be dry. The enormous task of diverting the Colorado’s water began in May 1931. Workers used dynamite to blast two tunnels on each side of the canyon to carry the Colorado’s water around the site. Once the tunnels were completed, they were lined with concrete. Creating the diversion tunnels was extremely dangerous. Workers were exposed to falling rocks and fumes from the use of gasoline-powered vehicles in the tunnels. Above the ground, other workers built watertight barriers called cofferdams above and below the dam site. The higher cofferdam would divert water into the tunnels. The lower one, along with a rock barrier, would keep water from flowing back upstream and flooding the construction site.
pages.brief: Workers crouch behind rocks as dynamite blasts tunnels into both canyon walls beside the Colorado River; others line the new tunnels with concrete, while watertight cofferdams stretch across the water above and below the dry dam site.

pages.text: At the same time, “high scalers” removed loose rock from canyon walls and cut grooves where the dam would attach. These workers often dangled high above the river on wooden swings in 120°F (49°C) heat while using jackhammers and dynamite. Other projects were taking place at the same time. Boulder City was being built so workers would have homes, a hospital, and other facilities. Railroad tracks were installed near the dam site so supplies could be delivered. A road was built between Boulder City and the dam site. In addition, workers installed a power line 222 miles (357 km) long from San Bernardino, California, to Black Canyon to provide power for the dam’s construction. High scalers had perhaps the hardest jobs at Hoover Dam. Dozens of workers lost their lives as a result of falling rocks and tools. Almost one hundred men in total died of industrial accidents during the dam’s construction.
pages.brief: High above the river, high scalers dangle from ropes on wooden swings against the canyon wall, gripping jackhammers and dynamite in blazing heat to knock loose rock free, while below a railway track and a road run past the dam site toward new buildings.

pages.text: Once the diversion tunnels were finished, the site was pumped dry. The dam had to sit on solid bedrock, which was buried under 135 feet (41 m) of silt and stones. The last of that material was excavated on June 6, 1933—about two years after work had begun on the tunnels. Finally it was time to build the dam. Workers lowered huge buckets of wet concrete into block-shaped molds, called forms. Other workers smoothed the concrete and got rid of air bubbles before the concrete hardened and more layers of concrete were added. Narrow steel pipes carried cold water through the forms to cool the concrete quickly. Once the concrete had hardened, the wooden form was taken apart and put back together on top of the finished block. After that block was finished, another one was built on top of it. When the columns of blocks reached their final height, the spaces between them were The dam was built from concrete filled with grout. blocks that were stacked to form columns.
pages.brief: Workers guide a huge bucket of wet concrete down into a block-shaped wooden form on the dry riverbed, while others smooth the surface and chase out air bubbles; nearby, stacked columns of finished concrete blocks rise in steps and steel pipes carry cold water.

pages.text: After the dam was complete, workers built passages called spillways to carry high water around the dam. This would help if the Colorado River ever flooded. Then they built the power plant and the four intake towers that would control water flow to the power plant. By February 1, 1935, the work was finally completed. Workers plugged the diversion tunnels that had been allowing the Colorado’s waters to bypass the dam site. Water started rising behind the dam, overflowing the cofferdam, and forming Lake Mead. By the time the project was finished, more than 21,000 men had worked on it, with an average of 3,500 each day. The project cost $165 million, which is equal to $3 billion or more today. • Hoover Dam, along with its power plant and other structures, contains enough concrete to pave a highway from San Francisco to New York City. • The construction of Hoover Dam used over 5,000,000 President Roosevelt dedicated barrels of cement. That the dam on September 30, 1935. amounts to between He called it “the greatest dam 7,500 and 10,800 barrels in the world.” each day.
pages.brief: President Roosevelt stands at a podium to dedicate the finished Hoover Dam, while behind him the Colorado River rises against the concrete wall, spreading into the new Lake Mead and covering the plugged diversion tunnels below the dam.

pages.text: Visiting the Dam Hoover Dam has welcomed visitors since 1937. Millions of people visit the dam each year. Close to a million take tours of the dam and power plant. The visitor center has displays about the region’s natural history as well as the history and construction of the dam. If you go, be prepared to be impressed. Visitors describe their experience with words like spectacular, amazing, and incredible. Fishing, boating, picnicking, and hiking are available year-round at Lake Mead. The area has nine wilderness areas, five hundred types of animals, and nine hundred types of plants. From inside the visitor center, tourists get a bird’s-eye view of Hoover Dam. Guided tours give behind-the-scenes details of the dam.
pages.brief: From a high window inside the visitor center, tourists look down on the full length of Hoover Dam spread below them; outside, families boat, fish and picnic on Lake Mead, and hikers follow a trail through the desert scrub of a wilderness area.

pages.text: In 1930, Las Vegas was a railroad hub with only about 5,000 residents. After Hoover Dam was built, the city’s population swelled. As of 2013, Las Vegas had over 600,000 residents. Changing the Southwest The Colorado River is the main source of water in the southwestern United States. Hoover Dam controlled the Colorado for the first time in history. It supplied farmers in Arizona, Nevada, and California with a trustworthy source of irrigation. The dam also provided drinking water and affordable electricity, which allowed Los Angeles, San Diego, Las Vegas, Phoenix, and other cities in the Southwest to grow. In addition, Hoover Dam provided jobs for thousands of men and became a symbol of hope during a very hard time. The difficult and dangerous task of building Hoover Dam took place over seventy-five years ago. The dam’s last known construction worker died in 2014. Yet the stories live on in every ton of concrete in one of America’s most remarkable landmarks.
pages.brief: A modern city skyline of glass towers rises from the desert where the railroad town of Las Vegas once stood, its streets spreading far across the valley, with green irrigated fields and river water reaching distant farms and homes.

books.title: Mythical Creatures of Ancient Greece
books.art_why: Ancient Greek myths and fifth-century BCE artworks cannot be photographed, so drawings suit the topic.

pages.text: Heracles (HAIR-uh-kleez), a Greek hero, greets Cerberus, the two- or three-headed guardian dog of the underworld on this vase from the fifth century bce. Introduction People in many cultures have myths. Myths are stories that explain important ideas, such as good and evil, in ways people can understand. A myth can take many forms. It can be a lesson, an explanation of a historical event or natural phenomenon, or even a warning. In ancient Greece, myths were an important part of religion. They weren’t told as entertainment. Rather, stories about gods and goddesses had deep meanings that Greek people used as guidelines for their lives. While gods, goddesses, heroes, and villains are the stars of Greek myths, On this vase, the goddess Athena helps Heracles fantastic creatures often play attack the Hydra, a monster a central role as well. composed of many snakes.
pages.brief: On a fifth-century vase, the Greek hero Heracles greets Cerberus, the two- or three-headed guardian dog of the underworld. On another vase, the goddess Athena helps Heracles attack the Hydra, a monster made of many snakes.

pages.text: Ixion indeed fell in love with the cloud, thinking it was Hera. The cloud gave birth to the first Centaur, and angry Zeus punished Ixion by forcing him to rotate around and around Centaurs are often shown winning on a blazing wheel forever. against Greeks in battle, as in this sculpture from the Parthenon, a Pictures of battle fifth-century bce temple in Athens. scenes showing Greeks fighting Centaurs were commonplace in ancient Greece on everything from drinking cups to stone temples. The Greeks rarely showed current events in their art. Rather, they used pictures of myths to express how they felt about what was happening in the world around them. For example, the Greeks connected one of their greatest enemies, the Persians, with the wild nature of the Centaurs. They portrayed great battles with Greeks fighting the Centaurs to show their superiority over the Persians. Do You Know? Honoring the relationship between a guest and his or her host was an important part of ancient Greek culture. The myth about Ixion and the first Centaur shows the importance of this relationship through Ixion's disrespect of Zeus, his host. Zeus's punishment was a lesson about the consequences of breaking this accepted custom.
pages.brief: A fifth-century BCE sculpture from the Parthenon temple in Athens shows Greeks fighting Centaurs in battle, with Centaurs often shown winning. Similar battle scenes appear on drinking cups and stone temples. In the myth, Ixion falls in love with a cloud he thinks is Hera, and Zeus punishes him on a blazing wheel.

pages.text: Sirens Like Centaurs, Sirens were hybrid creatures. Sirens were women with the wings, legs, and bodies of birds. They represented the importance of self-control. They lived on an island in the middle of the sea, where they sang beautiful songs to lure sailors. The sailors would lose control of their ships and crash onto the island’s rocky shores. According to myth, the Sirens had once been human maids to the goddess Persephone (pur-SE-fuh-nee). Hades, god of the underworld, abducted Persephone to make her his wife. Their wings helped the Sirens search for Persephone. Unsuccessful in their search, they settled on the island.
pages.brief: Sirens are shown as women with the wings, legs, and bodies of birds. They live on an island in the middle of the sea, singing beautiful songs to lure sailors. Sailors lose control of their ships and crash onto the island’s rocky shores. The Sirens had once been human maids to Persephone.

pages.text: The Sirens killed many unsuspecting sailors, but a few sailors passed by them alive. The famous Greek musician Orpheus (OR-fee-uhss) played music so loud that it drowned out the Sirens’ song. The Greek king Odysseus, on his journey home from fighting in the Trojan War, instructed his sailors to tie him up tightly to the mast of his boat. His sailors plugged their own ears so that they wouldn’t be tempted to stop rowing. The Greeks prided themselves on their restraint. Resisting the Sirens’ the strength of will that ancient Greeks valued. This fifth-century bce Greek vase shows Odysseus tied to the mast of his ship so he could hear the Sirens' song... and remain alive. Word Wise The mythological Sirens are connected to the word siren, which is a device that gives off a loud warning sound. They also inspired the meaning of a siren song. That’s something so appealing that it makes you want it, even if it is dangerous.
pages.brief: The Greek musician Orpheus plays music so loud that it drowns out the Sirens’ song. Odysseus is tied tightly to the mast of his boat while his sailors plug their ears and row past. A fifth-century BCE Greek vase shows Odysseus bound to the mast, hearing the Sirens’ song and staying alive.

pages.text: Medusa While the Sirens were known for their beauty, Medusa was famous for her frightening appearance. Greek artists usually showed the Gorgons—Medusa and her two sisters—with large, round heads and huge, staring eyes. Snakes instead of hair grew out of their skulls. Pointed tusks, flared nostrils, and tongues sticking out of their mouths completed their features. Although Medusa’s sisters were immortal, she was mortal. This made her vulnerable to humans. She had her own defense against attacks, though. She could turn people to stone once they looked directly into her eyes.
pages.brief: Medusa and her two sisters, the Gorgons, have large round heads, huge staring eyes, snakes instead of hair, pointed tusks, flared nostrils, and tongues sticking out. Medusa is mortal while her sisters are immortal. She can turn people to stone when they look directly into her eyes.

pages.text: The myth about Medusa began with an evil king who was in love with the mother of a boy named Perseus. To get Perseus out of his way, the king tricked Perseus into promising that he would bring anything the king wished. The king sent Perseus to kill Medusa and return with her head. The king thought this deed would be impossible. With the help of gods and goddesses, Perseus cut off Medusa’s head. From her body, two creatures sprang forth. They were Chrysaor (kriss-AH-or), a giant whose name means “golden blade,” which could refer to grain, and Pegasus, a winged horse whose name refers to springs of water. Some people think the killing of Medusa symbolized the ending of a drought, and that Chrysaor and Pegasus represented the good things that came afterward— thriving crops and flowing water. Wowser! The ancient Greeks believed that the frightening faces of the Gorgons would protect them and ward off evil. They put pictures of Gorgons everywhere, including on their shields.
pages.brief: An evil king who loves Perseus’s mother sends Perseus to kill Medusa and bring back her head. With help from gods and goddesses, Perseus cuts off Medusa’s head. From her body spring Chrysaor, a giant, and Pegasus, a winged horse. The frightening Gorgon face is shown on shields to ward off evil.

pages.text: The Minotaur The Minotaur was another hybrid creature. It had a bull’s head and a man’s body. Its name came from Minos, the king of Crete, where the Minotaur lived, and taurus, the Greek name for a bull. The monster was so destructive that it was kept in a twisted maze called the Labyrinth beneath the king’s palace. After Athenian boys killed the king’s son, Minos sought revenge by attacking the city of Athens. To stop the attacks, the people of Athens agreed to send seven boys and seven girls every year to the terrible Minotaur.
pages.brief: The Minotaur has a bull’s head and a man’s body. It lives in a twisted maze called the Labyrinth beneath King Minos’s palace on Crete. The monster is so destructive that Athens agrees to send seven boys and seven girls every year to the terrible Minotaur.

pages.text: A brave Athenian boy named Theseus volunteered to be one of the victims. When Theseus arrived in Crete, he was put in a cage with the other victims. It was then that the princess of Crete, Ariadne (ah-ree-AHD-nee), saw Theseus and fell in love with him. Ariadne didn’t want the Minotaur to kill Theseus. She asked the man who built the Labyrinth how Theseus could escape. She was told that she should give Theseus a ball of yarn to unwind as he made his way through the Labyrinth. She also gave Theseus a sword so he could kill the Minotaur. After Theseus killed the Minotaur, he followed the trail of yarn back out of the maze. The Minotaur myth was popular after the Greeks took over Crete. Just as Centaurs often represented the Persians, bulls could stand for Crete. Bulls were considered sacred to an important goddess in Crete. Theseus defeating the Minotaur could have symbolized the Greek conquest of Crete.
pages.brief: Theseus, a brave Athenian boy, arrives in Crete and is put in a cage with the other victims. Princess Ariadne sees him and falls in love. She gives him a ball of yarn to unwind through the Labyrinth and a sword to kill the Minotaur. Theseus follows the yarn back out of the maze.

pages.text: Typhon The fierce Minotaur was tiny compared to the giant Typhon (TY-fon), a winged monster with one hundred heads that represented the destructive forces of weather. Typhon had one human head and ninety-nine heads of other creatures, including lions, bulls, boars, snakes, and dragons. Below the knees, his legs were giant snakes. Instead of fingers, fifty serpent heads coiled forth from each hand. Fire flashed in his eyes, and flames whipped out of his mouth.
pages.brief: Typhon is a giant winged monster with one hundred heads: one human head and ninety-nine heads of lions, bulls, boars, snakes, and dragons. Below the knees his legs are giant snakes. Fifty serpent heads coil from each hand instead of fingers. Fire flashes in his eyes and flames whip from his mouth.

pages.text: Only Zeus, the king of the gods, could match Typhon in battle. When Typhon threatened to take over the world, Zeus used thunder and lightning to combat Typhon’s fire and wind. Their battle shook the whole world. Zeus set all one hundred of Typhon’s heads on fire. He then imprisoned the monster beneath Earth. The ancient Greeks blamed Typhon for stirring strong winds that spread across land and sea during great storms. They also blamed him for sending forth lava from volcanoes. People were comforted by the idea that Zeus could defeat the destructive natural forces that Typhon represented.
pages.brief: Zeus, king of the gods, battles Typhon with thunder and lightning against the monster’s fire and wind. Their battle shakes the whole world. Zeus sets all one hundred of Typhon’s heads on fire and imprisons him beneath Earth. The Greeks blame Typhon for strong storm winds and lava from volcanoes.

pages.text: Conclusion Mythical creatures did not simply entertain or terrify the ancient Greeks. These creatures and the myths about them had deep meanings that helped people understand the world around them at the time and cope with challenges they faced. Mythical creatures played significant roles in ancient Greek culture, and they’re still popular today. Children and adults remain fascinated by their amazing stories. Mythical creatures of ancient Greece inspired some famous logos for major businesses, including Medusa's head for the fashion label Versace (vur-SAH-chee), Pegasus for Mobil Gas, and a Siren for Starbucks Coffee Company.
pages.brief: Ancient Greeks did not use mythical creatures only to entertain or terrify. The creatures and their myths had deep meanings that helped people understand the world and cope with challenges. Their stories still fascinate children and adults today. Medusa’s head, Pegasus, and a Siren inspired logos for Versace, Mobil Gas, and Starbucks Coffee Company.

pages.text: Arizona’s Barringer Meteorite Crater shows how space rocks striking Earth create amazing landforms. Introduction What makes something a natural wonder? A wonder is a natural structure so amazing and beautiful that it makes you ponder how it was formed. Natural wonders are landforms that have been created by nature, not by humans. Some of these wonders are created in a few years. Others take millions of years to form. Our planet is home to many natural wonders. In this book, we will learn about five of them: • A layered canyon carved by a river • A young volcano that took over a village • A breathtaking waterfall • An immense coral reef • A towering mountain.
pages.brief: Arizona’s Barringer Meteorite Crater lies in a desert landscape, a huge bowl showing how a space rock struck Earth. The scene introduces natural wonders made by nature, not humans, some formed in a few years and others over millions of years.

pages.text: Colorado River The layers of rocks that form the canyon walls show geologists what happened in the area over a period of two billion years. These rocks make up the layers in the canyon walls. The top of the canyon, where most visitors enjoy their first view, is the youngest layer of the canyon. The bottom layer, near the river, is the oldest. Scattered rocks located at the bottom of the canyon date back as long ago as two billion years. The Grand Canyon is a great place to study rocks and the Earth’s history because the rock layers are so easy to see and reach. Geologists often visit the site. One of the first geologists to visit was John Newberry, who traveled to the canyon in 1858. Newberry was the first scientist to record the canyon’s layers. He identified many of the geologic layers, although he wasn’t the first to see them.
pages.brief: The Grand Canyon’s layered rock walls rise above the Colorado River. A geologist studies the visible layers, noting the youngest rock at the top and the oldest near the river. In 1858, John Newberry traveled to the canyon and recorded its geologic layers.

pages.text: Rattling Reptiles More than forty-seven different kinds of reptiles live in the Grand Canyon. While most of these reptiles are harmless, visitors should keep an eye out for snakes. Although they rarely bite humans, the Grand Canyon rattlesnake and the diamondback rattlesnake are venomous. In the winter, rattlesnakes hibernate in dens. Hundreds of rattlesnakes may live in one den. This is one of the only times rattlers live together. In the spring when the weather warms up, the snakes come out of their dens and go their separate ways. In late summer, females give birth to live babies. The babies only stay in the area where they were born for about seven to ten days. Then they shed their first baby skin, add their first rattle, and move on in search of food. As a rattlesnake grows, it sheds its skin at least once a year. It adds a new rattle to its tail with each shed. A mature diamondback may grow to be 2 meters (about 6.5 ft.) long and weigh up to 6.8 kilograms (15 lb.). Rattlers can live to be years old.
pages.brief: In the Grand Canyon, a Grand Canyon rattlesnake and a diamondback rattlesnake lie among rocks. One raises its rattle. The page shows snakes that hibernate together in winter dens, emerge in spring, and in late summer females give birth to live babies.

pages.text: Native Americans lived in and around the Grand Canyon for more than four thousand years before European explorers arrived. These early groups of people hunted local animals and gathered edible plants. By 1150, most of the original tribes had moved away. Only the Havasupai people remained. Some of them still live and work in the Canyon. Every year, millions of people travel to Grand Canyon National Park to hike, raft, and see this majestic wonder of nature. Havasu Falls is on the Havasupai Reservation. It is an example of how water continues to carve the western Grand Canyon.
pages.brief: Havasupai people live and work in the Grand Canyon, continuing a long Native American presence. Havasu Falls drops over rock on the Havasupai Reservation. In the canyon, visitors hike and raft in Grand Canyon National Park, drawn by the majestic natural wonder.

pages.text: Paricutín Many of nature’s creations are millions of years old. They began forming long before humans lived on Earth. Other creations have formed in modern times. The Paricutín (pah-ree-koo-TEEN) volcano in Mexico is one such formation. Paricutín began forming in 1943 in a field. That year, GULF OF MEXICO MEXICO a farmer discovered a fissure (FISH-ur), Paricutín or opening in the PACIFIC ground, in his OCEAN cornfield. The crack was about 1.8 meters (6 ft.) long. Soon more fissures appeared. Black smoke came from the holes, and ash piled up on the ground, forming a cone. In about twelve hours, the cone had grown to 10 meters (33 ft.) high. After a day, it had grown to 50 meters (164 ft.). The volcano continued to grow, reaching a height of 100 meters (328 ft.) in just a week. The brand-new volcano grabbed the attention of news organizations all over the world. Paricutín volcano erupts in 1943.
pages.brief: In a Mexican cornfield in 1943, a farmer discovers a fissure in the ground. Black smoke rises from the opening as ash piles into a cone. The new Paricutín volcano grows quickly, reaching 100 meters in a week and drawing news organizations from around the world.

pages.text: A church steeple is all that remains visible after ash and lava covered the town of Paricutín. The people of Paricutín hoped that their village would be safe, but after a few months, the cone had grown so large that the slow-moving lava started to reach their town. The villagers had to evacuate, leaving behind their homes and farms. Over a nine-year period, lava and ash eventually covered the entire village of Paricutín and most of the nearby town of San Juan. In the end, all that was left of Paricutín was the church steeple rising out of the black rock as a reminder of nature’s power.
pages.brief: A church steeple rises from black volcanic rock where the town of Paricutín once stood. Ash and slow-moving lava covered the village and most of nearby San Juan over nine years. The villagers evacuated, leaving homes and farms behind as a reminder of nature’s power.

pages.text: Volcanoes such as Paricutín are called cinder cones. They are the simplest type of volcano because they appear suddenly, erupt, and then go dormant for decades or centuries. Cinder cones are formed when lava, which is under pressure inside Earth, shoots out from a central vent in the ground. As the lava explodes into the air, it cools and breaks into small pieces that harden and fall as rocks and ash, or cinders, around the central vent to form a cone. Most cinder cones have a bowl-shaped crater at the top. Because Paricutín volcano is young, scientists have been able to observe its growth since it first appeared. Today, the volcano stands about 424 meters (1,391 ft.) tall and covers 26 square kilometers (10 sq. mi.). Its development has allowed scientists to better understand the powerful forces that shape Earth.
pages.brief: Paricutín is a cinder cone volcano with a bowl-shaped crater at its top. Lava shoots from a central vent, cools in the air, and falls as rock and ash around the vent, building a cone. Scientists have observed the young volcano’s growth; today it stands about 424 meters tall.

pages.text: AFRICA Zambia Victoria Falls Zimbabwe INDIAN OCEAN Victoria Falls, like the Grand Canyon, was formed by water. Victoria Falls Victoria Falls is the largest mass of falling water on the planet. The water falls 108 meters (354 ft.) into a deep pool. The people of Zambia call the Falls Mosi-oa-Tunya (MOH-see wah TOON-yah) (the smoke that thunders). It’s a perfect name. The thunder refers to the booming sound created by the water crashing over the Falls into the pool below. The smoke refers to the water vapor that comes up from the bottom of the Falls. The colorful mist can be seen from 20 kilometers (12 mi.) away.
pages.brief: Victoria Falls sends a huge mass of water 108 meters down into a deep pool on the Zambezi River. Colorful mist rises from the bottom, visible from far away. The people of Zambia call the Falls Mosi-oa-Tunya, meaning “the smoke that thunders,” for its booming sound and vapor.

pages.text: Victoria Falls is located on the Zambezi River along the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe in Africa. The Falls began forming millions of years ago when a shallow crack in the rock appeared across the path of the river. The crack was caused when parts of the earth shifted about 150 million years ago. Over the years, the river flowed over the rock, eroding away the softer rock, and forming a cliff over which the river now falls. The pool into which the water falls is called a plunge pool. The Scottish explorer David Livingstone visited the Falls in 1855. He was probably the first person from outside of Africa to see the wondrous formations. He named the Falls after Queen Victoria of England. But many people think that Mosi-oa-Tunya is a more accurate name. The Falls is now part of two national parks, one in Zambia and one in Zimbabwe, that draw almost two million visitors each year.
pages.brief: Victoria Falls lies on the Zambezi River along the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe. The river pours over a cliff into a plunge pool. Scottish explorer David Livingstone visited in 1855 and named the Falls after Queen Victoria; today two national parks draw almost two million visitors each year.

pages.text: Victoria Falls Fun Facts • Victoria Falls is actually divided into six waterfalls: Devil’s Cataract, Armchair Falls, Horseshoe Falls, Main Falls, Rainbow Falls, and the Eastern Cataract. • A bridge at the Falls is a popular site for bungee jumping. • During a full moon, the park stays open late so people can enjoy the rainbow that is made when moonlight shines through the water vapor. • People go rafting and kayaking on the water below the Falls. They can even surf on the rapids below.
pages.brief: Victoria Falls is divided into six waterfalls: Devil’s Cataract, Armchair Falls, Horseshoe Falls, Main Falls, Rainbow Falls, and the Eastern Cataract. A bridge at the Falls is used for bungee jumping. Below, people raft, kayak, and even surf the rapids. During a full moon, visitors stay late to see a moonlight rainbow in the mist.

pages.text: CHINA Mount Everest NEPAL PACIFIC OCEAN Mount Everest Mount Everest is named for Welsh surveyor and geologist Sir George Everest. It is the tallest mountain in the world and one of the most amazing sites on Earth. Called “Forehead in the Sky” by the Nepali people, this magnificent landform in the Himalaya mountain range reaches a height of 8,850 meters (29,035 ft.). It lies on the border between Nepal and Tibetan China. The snowcapped Himalayas might appear old, but they are actually quite young for mountains. The mountains formed millions of years ago when two parts of Earth’s crust crashed into each other. Over time, the pressure of the two parts rubbing against each other caused the ground to crumble and rise above the sea. Since Mount Everest is a young mountain, its peaks are still jagged and steep. They haven’t yet been eroded and smoothed down by endless years of wind, ice, and snow.
pages.brief: Mount Everest rises in the snowcapped Himalaya mountain range on the border between Nepal and Tibetan China. Named for Sir George Everest, its jagged, steep peak reaches 8,850 meters. The Nepali people call it “Forehead in the Sky.” The young mountain formed when two parts of Earth’s crust crashed together.

pages.text: Although Mount Everest is beautiful to look at, the conditions on the mountain are very harsh. The average temperature is about −36°C (−33°F) and can drop to −60°C (−76°F) in January. Even in July, the warmest month, the temperature only reaches −19°C (−2°F). It never gets above freezing, and as a result, the ice and snow at the top of the mountain never melt. Because of its elevation, storms can arrive unexpectedly and cause temperatures to drop quickly. Mount Everest’s summit Storms dump more snow on Mount Everest every year.
pages.brief: Mount Everest’s summit stands in harsh, freezing conditions. Ice and snow cover the peak and never melt. The average temperature is about −36°C, and in January it can drop to −60°C. Even in July it stays below freezing. Because of the mountain’s elevation, storms can arrive unexpectedly and temperatures drop quickly.

pages.text: The extreme conditions on Mount Everest make it difficult for animals and plants to survive. One of the only animals that can live on the mountain is the wild yak. This large animal can weigh more than 454 kilograms (1,000 lb.) and grow up to Wild yak grazing 1.8 meters (6 ft.) tall. One of the reasons the yak is able to survive is because its blood can take in more oxygen than the blood of other animals. This adaptation is a lifesaver on Mount Everest, where the air contains little oxygen. The yak also has a dense undercoat of soft hair and a shaggy outer coat that help the animal stay warm. The people who originally settled in the Himalayas believed that the gods made their homes in the peaks. As a result, no one tried to climb Mount Everest until British and other European explorers arrived in the early 1900s. The earliest climbers quickly learned about the harsh conditions on the mountain—freezing temperatures, powerful winds, changing weather, and rough terrain.
pages.brief: A wild yak grazes on Mount Everest, one of the only animals able to live there. Its dense undercoat and shaggy outer coat keep it warm, and its blood takes in more oxygen than other animals’ blood. The earliest climbers learned about freezing temperatures, powerful winds, changing weather, and rough terrain.

Hillary was a beekeeper from New Zealand; Norgay was a Sherpa from Nepal. Stories of the yeti, a legendary Himalayan creature, are also told, but no one has proved the yeti exists.

pages.text: AUSTRALIA Great Barrier Reef A diver explores coral formations on the Great Barrier Reef. Great Barrier Reef The Great Barrier Reef—really a collection of reefs—is more than 2,300 kilometers (1,429 mi.) long. It is located off the northeast coast of Australia and is full of enchanting sea creatures, from sea turtles, sea slugs, and urchins to dolphins, whales, and sharks. More than two hundred species of birds and reptiles inhabit the reef system. A reef is a chain, or range, of rocks that lies at or near the surface of the water. The Great Barrier Reef is the largest system of coral reefs in the world.
pages.brief: A diver explores coral formations on the Great Barrier Reef off the northeast coast of Australia. The reef system stretches more than 2,300 kilometers and is full of sea creatures, including sea turtles, sea slugs, urchins, dolphins, whales, and sharks. More than two hundred species of birds and reptiles live in the reef system.

pages.text: The life and death of coral polyps are responsible for the formation of coral reefs such as the Great Barrier Reef. Coral reefs are found in all tropical oceans of the world, but none is as large as the Great Barrier Reef. Most established coral reefs are between five and ten thousand years old. Many experts agree that the most recent growth of the Great Barrier Reef began between six and eight thousand years ago. At first glance, the Great Barrier Reef might look like a rock, but it’s not. It’s made from the outer skeletons of millions of animals called polyps (POL-ips), which are related to anemones and jellyfish. As the polyps die, new ones grow on top of the old skeletons. The many layers of skeletons form the limestone base of a coral reef. Other kinds of plants and animals also help make up the reef, such as algae, sponges, and shellfish. But the tiny polyp is responsible for most of this natural wonder’s structure.
pages.brief: Coral polyps build the Great Barrier Reef. Their outer skeletons form layers that create a limestone base. As polyps die, new ones grow on top of the old skeletons. Algae, sponges, and shellfish also help make up the reef, but the tiny polyp is responsible for most of the structure. The reef lies in a tropical ocean.

pages.text: Reefs are made from animals, and they supply food and shelter for other animals. They are sensitive to temperature changes in the ocean. Thousands of species live on the reef. They include 1,625 kinds of fish, more than 30 kinds of marine mammals, 50 kinds of seaweed, and 6 kinds of marine turtles. The reef is also an important breeding area for animals, including birds, sea turtles, and several endangered species, such as the humpback whale and the sea cow. As one of the most interesting and beautiful places on Earth, the Great Barrier Reef is a popular destination for scientists, scuba divers, and tourists. In 1981, it was listed as a World Heritage Site by UNESCO, a department of the United Nations. Today, environmentalists work with all of these groups to protect the reef so future generations can learn from it and enjoy its beauty. Look, But Don’t Touch! Reefs are alive and full of delicate creatures. Responsible snorkelers and scuba divers should always follow these • When snorkeling, float over the reef. Never stand on it. • Take pictures, not coral souvenirs. • Stock saltwater aquariums with fish that are raised in captivity, not those taken from a coral reef. • Always pack out your plastics and other trash.
pages.brief: Divers and snorkelers float above a colorful coral reef full of fish. The reef supplies food and shelter to thousands of species, including sea turtles and the humpback whale, and is an important breeding area. People are warned not to stand on coral, take coral souvenirs, or leave trash, so future generations can enjoy the reef.

pages.text: Wonders Everywhere From Arizona to the coast of Australia, natural wonders are everywhere. Whether they formed millions of years ago or within the span of a lifetime, they are all unique. These amazing landforms are some of the largest, highest, and most breathtaking places on Earth. Travelers, scientists, and adventure seekers will continue to visit these special places for generations to come for both study and recreation. The Grand Canyon, Paricutín, Mount Everest, Victoria Falls, and Great Barrier Reef are only five of the many wonders that surround us. Other well-known natural wonders include: • The Northern Lights, a light show that brightens up the skies in the Northern Hemisphere • The Barringer Meteorite Crater, a massive hole in the Arizona desert that is almost a mile wide and 174 meters (570 ft.) deep • Ayers Rock, the world’s largest solid rock, rising 862.5 meters (2,830 ft.) above sea level • Ha Long Bay, Gulf of Tonkin, Vietnam, a large bay that contains more than 1,600 limestone islands.
pages.brief: The Grand Canyon, Paricutín, Mount Everest, Victoria Falls, and the Great Barrier Reef are five natural wonders. The page also names other wonders: the Northern Lights brightening northern skies, the huge Barringer Meteorite Crater in the Arizona desert, Ayers Rock rising above sea level, and Ha Long Bay with more than 1,600 limestone islands.
