books.title: Route 66
books.art_why: Route 66 and every landmark in the book are real places that exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Route 66 takes drivers across the entire American West. Introduction The year is 1957 and you’ve just taken the top down on your cherry-red convertible. Sun glints off the shiny metal fins of your car, rock ’n’ roll music blasts from the speakers, and ahead of you lies nothing but open road. Could this drive get any better? You think not—until you pass a three-story- tall ice cream cone covered in sprinkles. Your mouth waters. Should you stop? Wait, there’s a cheeseburger the size of a bus. Time for a quick lunch instead! When it’s time to retire for the night, you park next to your teepee-shaped hotel room— complete with a bed, bathroom, and shower. What a spectacular day it was on the road! Who knows what tomorrow will bring? If you thought this was a dream or an imaginary road trip, you’d be mistaken. You’ve just taken a real trip down America’s favorite highway, Route 66.
pages.brief: A cherry-red convertible with the top down rolls along an open highway, its shiny metal fins glinting in the sun, music blasting from the speakers. Ahead stand a three-story ice cream cone covered in sprinkles, a cheeseburger as big as a bus, and a teepee-shaped hotel room holding a bed, bathroom and shower.

pages.text: America’s Main Street was soon put to the test. In 1929, the stock market crashed, causing many people to lose their money, jobs, and homes. The dire period that followed was known as the Great Depression. Meanwhile, a series of droughts caused huge dust storms to destroy farms on the Great Plains, especially in Kansas, Colorado, Oklahoma, Texas, and New Mexico. This phenomenon was known as the Dust Bowl. Suddenly, many people were forced to leave their homes to seek a better life elsewhere. Many believed paradise lay out west—especially in California. Thousands packed up their belongings and made the long journey. How did they get there? On a new road named Route 66. Many believed Route 66 would take them away from their troubles and lead them toward opportunity and riches elsewhere. The Dust Bowl The Grapes of Wrath, by John Steinbeck, is a classic novel published in 1939. It is about a family fleeing Oklahoma during the Dust Bowl era and making the long journey down Route 66 to seek work in California. Steinbeck described Route 66 as “the mother road” and “the road of flight.”
pages.brief: Dust storms swallow farm buildings on the dry Great Plains of Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas while a family loads belongings onto a truck. In a city, anxious crowds gather outside a bank after the 1929 stock market crash. The packed truck heads west on an open road toward California.

pages.text: In the 1930s, 1.2 million people moved to California. More than half a million of them went because of difficult conditions during the Dust Bowl era. On December 7, 1941, the Japanese military bombed United States naval ships in Pearl Harbor in Hawaii. The United States entered World War II the following day. Thousands of soldiers, workers, and supplies needed to be quickly mobilized and transported from around the country to military bases in the West. How did they get there? On Route 66, of course. On the long journey, wartime workers needed food, gasoline, and shelter, so restaurants, gas stations, and hotels began to spring up along the route to accommodate them. Times were tough in America, but business on Route 66 was booming. When the war ended in 1945, Americans celebrated. Soldiers came home, started families, constructed houses, and purchased cars. Many wanted to drive their new cars west to see sights like the Grand Canyon and the Pacific Ocean— by way of Route 66!
pages.brief: Soldiers, workers and supplies crowd a convoy rolling west on Route 66, passing newly built restaurants, gas stations and hotels. Later, a family stands beside their new car at the Grand Canyon, looking out over the canyon before driving on to the Pacific Ocean.

pages.text: Route 66 in Popular Culture The years after World War II were glory days for Route 66. Shiny blue roadsters, cherry- red convertibles, bubble gum–pink coupes, and yellow Checker cabs cruised up and down the route. Route 66 was no longer just a way to get somewhere else; it was the new place to be. In 1946, a song called “Route 66” became a top hit. Its most famous line urged listeners to “get your kicks on Route Sixty-Six,” which helped define the highway’s place in popular culture. In 1960, a new TV The original version of the song “Route 66” was performed by show called Route 66 the Nat King Cole Trio in 1946. followed two friends who drove across the country in a Corvette. They weren’t going anywhere in particular; instead, they were looking for adventure on the road. The popular television show Route 66 aired from 1960 to 1964.
pages.brief: Shiny blue roadsters, cherry-red convertibles, bubble-gum-pink coupes and yellow Checker cabs cruise along Route 66. In a recording studio, the Nat King Cole Trio performs the hit song Route 66. On a television screen, two friends drive a Corvette across the country, hunting for adventure.

pages.text: By 1970, most of the original Route 66 was bypassed by a new highway. However, references to Route 66 continued to appear in American popular culture through the end of the century. Fast forward to the year 2000: John Lasseter, the director of Pixar Animation Studios, was driving along Route 66 with his family. He fell in love with the imaginative buildings and colorful art installations he saw. He decided to turn his experiences into a Disney-Pixar movie called Cars, which was released in 2006. Lasseter sent a team down Route 66 to do research for the movie. Some of the roadside art they found inspired characters in Cars, and they used Route 66 landmarks in the movie, too. For example, the Wigwam Motel in Holbrook, Arizona, became the Cozy Cone Motel. Cars was so successful that many families who saw it took their own vacations along Route 66, which helped create a resurgence of the This rusty tow truck (top) in Galena, Kansas, popular route. became the inspiration for the Cars movie character Tow Mater (bottom).
pages.brief: Director John Lasseter drives along Route 66 with his family, admiring imaginative buildings and colorful art installations. His research team photographs the Wigwam Motel in Holbrook, Arizona, and a rusty tow truck in Galena, Kansas, the real places and vehicles that inspired the animated movie Cars.

One thing’s for sure—you won’t be bored on Route 66!
pages.brief: A map of the United States traces the highway from Chicago to Los Angeles. Along it stand oversized roadside figures: the Gemini Giant, Paul Bunyon, Chicken Boy, a giant catsup bottle, the Blue Whale, the Cabazon Dinosaurs and the Wigwam Motel. Dancers perform a Native American ceremony, and rodeo riders compete in Oklahoma.

pages.text: Cadillac Ranch sits in a pasture where cows graze. Cadillac Ranch In 1974, a group of alternative artists from San Francisco buried ten Cadillacs nose down in a field, rear bumpers sticking up toward the sky. The cars have had many colorful paint jobs over the years, but one of the most visible was in 1990, when all the cars were painted pink. Now they appear in every color of the rainbow because visitors have covered them with graffiti. At the nearby VW Slug Bug Ranch in Conway, Texas, five colorful Volkswagen Beetles stick out of the ground.
pages.brief: Ten Cadillacs stand nose down in a grassy pasture where cows graze, their rear bumpers reaching toward the sky, their bodies covered in bright graffiti paint of every color. Nearby in Conway, Texas, five colorful Volkswagen Beetles jut out of the ground at the Slug Bug Ranch.

pages.text: Elmer’s Bottle Tree Ranch When folk artist Elmer Long looks at garbage, he sees a forest. He built Bottle Tree Ranch out of recycled bottles, car parts, and objects of all kinds—including buffalo jawbones. As if feasting your eyes on this forest wasn’t enough, it’s also filled with music: the desert wind blows through all the open bottles, creating a medley Growing up, Elmer Long collected bottles of different tones. and other items people had thrown away. Blue Whale What do you give the woman who has everything? If you are Hugh Davis, you build your wife an 80-foot (24.4 m) blue whale for your anniversary. For many years, kids loved to slide and dive from the Blue Whale’s body into the swimming hole below. Now visitors can climb inside to get a view from tiny windows in the whale’s head. The Blue Whale of Catoosa, Oklahoma, has a boardwalk along its spine.
pages.brief: Elmer Long's Bottle Tree Ranch rises from the desert, built of recycled bottles, car parts and buffalo jawbones, the wind humming through the open glass. Beside a swimming hole stands an 80-foot blue whale built by Hugh Davis, a boardwalk along its spine, tiny windows in its head, children sliding down.

pages.text: Paul Bunyon, Chicken Boy, Gemini Giant, Atlanta, IL Los Angeles, CA Wilmington, IL A Land of Giants Route 66 is truly a land of giants. A California factory called International Fiberglass built thousands of colossal fiberglass statues and sold them to businesses along Route 66 for advertising. The factory created unusual costumes to transform the giants into cowboys, Native Americans, astronauts, and even chickens. Many of the biggest statues on Route 66 are food statues. Humongous oranges, donuts, cheeseburgers, and ice cream cones make for a mouthwatering ride. Look out the window near Collinsville, Illinois, and you may even catch a glimpse of the largest catsup bottle in the world! Brooks Catsup Bottle Water Tower, Collinsville, IL.
pages.brief: Inside a California fiberglass factory, colossal statues are finished and dressed as a cowboy, a Native American, an astronaut and a chicken. Along the roadside stand the Gemini Giant, Paul Bunyon and Chicken Boy, huge oranges, donuts, cheeseburgers and ice cream cones, and the giant catsup bottle water tower in Collinsville, Illinois.

pages.text: Dinny cost $300,000 to build and was made from roadside construction materials. Dinosaurs by the Dozen Dinosaurs may be extinct everywhere else on Planet Earth, but not on Route 66—where you can be greeted by towering prehistoric creatures of all shapes and sizes. At 150 feet (45.7 m) long, Dinny is likely the largest concrete dinosaur in America. He lives at a dinosaur park in Cabazon, California. Claude Bell built the park to lure visitors to his nearby restaurant, the Wheel Inn. The dinosaur park became famous and Mr. Rex, a three-story was even featured in the 1985 Tyrannosaurus rex, is a movie Pee-wee’s Big Adventure. popular feature at Cabazon Dinosaurs.
pages.brief: Dinny, a 150-foot-long concrete dinosaur, towers over a roadside dinosaur park in Cabazon, California, where builder Claude Bell hoped to draw visitors to his nearby Wheel Inn restaurant. Beside him rises Mr. Rex, a three-story Tyrannosaurus rex, greeting drivers traveling along Route 66.

pages.text: Saving Route 66 With Route 66’s popularity came traffic—lots of it. Heavy traffic congestion caused the highway to deteriorate. From 1956 through the 1980s, the United States government began building new interstates—high-speed highways with many lanes—around Route 66. As more and more travelers chose to take interstates, businesses on Route 66 suffered. Peeling paint, faded signs, and boarded-up windows became common sights. In 1999, the United States Congress passed a law to protect Route 66. The government started offering money to help businesses and towns pay the cost of preserving important landmarks. In 2008, the World Monuments Fund declared Route 66 “ endangered ” and put together plans to help attract tourists, such Route 66 Red Rocker, as a virtual reality map. Fanning, MO Now Route 66 is resurging in popularity as many return to seek its amusing artwork and creative spirit. The best way to catch the spirit of Route 66 is to drive it— and have your own classic American experience!
pages.brief: Peeling paint, faded signs and boarded-up windows mark a roadside business losing customers as heavy traffic jams a nearby highway. A wide new interstate carries cars past the old route, while travelers return to see restored landmarks such as the red rocker in Fanning, Missouri.

books.title: Pyramids
books.art_why: Pyramids, tomb building, mummification and burials happened thousands of years ago, so no photographs of these events exist.

pages.text: Over 100 pyramids have been discovered in Egypt. Introduction The country of Egypt sits at the northeastern corner of the African continent. It was once home to the ancient Egyptian civilization. Ancient Egypt was one of the most fascinating cultures ever to exist. Thousands of years ago, the Egyptians studied and practiced agriculture, irrigation, architecture, engineering, and much more. They built great structures, including the pyramids. Learning about these pyramids can help us learn a great deal about this amazing civilization.
pages.brief: A wide desert view of Egypt in the northeastern corner of Africa, with more than a hundred pyramids of different sizes spread across the sand, some whole and some worn down, standing near the green strip of the Nile valley.

pages.text: Paintings in a tomb show scenes of the next life. The ancient Egyptians believed in life after death. They believed that their next life would be similar to their present life and that they would need the same kinds of tools and objects in their next life. Therefore, many people were buried with a collection of some of the things they possessed in their current life. Of all the people living in ancient Egypt, no one was given a more lavish burial than a pharaoh. According to the beliefs of the ancient Egyptians, the pharaoh was the son of the Sun god, Re (or Ra). While the pharaoh was alive on Earth, they were known as Horus. After they died, they were united with Re. The new pharaoh, who replaced the dead pharaoh, became the new Horus.
pages.brief: Inside a painted tomb, wall paintings show a dead pharaoh in the next life surrounded by tools, food and objects, while a wrapped body lies in a decorated coffin with a collection of possessions piled nearby in the dim chamber.

pages.text: The Egyptians believed that in order for a pharaoh to live forever and continue to bless their lives, the pharaoh’s body had to be preserved so that their spirit would stay alive. The Egyptians built pyramids to honor pharaohs who had died. Each pyramid held a pharaoh’s body, as well as riches and treasures meant to travel with them into the next life. The pyramid also protected the pharaoh’s tomb and its treasures from theft. In addition, it served as a monument to the pharaoh’s greatness. Do You Know? The shape of a pyramid represents the Sun’s rays shining on the Earth. Ancient Egyptians believed that a pharaoh who died ascended to heaven on the rays of the Sun.
pages.brief: A pyramid stands over a pharaoh's sealed tomb, holding his body, riches and treasures inside, while above it the Sun's rays slant down through the sky onto the desert sand and the stone slopes.

pages.text: Building a Pyramid A pharaoh planned the construction of their pyramid long before they were expected to die, since finishing it would take many years. A large pyramid could take as long as twenty years to complete. Building a pyramid required thousands of people. Some were skilled workers, such as architects who designed the overall structure on orders from the pharaoh. People with special knowledge were also required to properly remove the stone from a quarry and to shape the stone. After a pyramid was built, skilled sculptors and painters decorated it. A scribe recorded all the materials needed for building the pyramid using the ancient Egyptian writing system, called hieroglyphics. Hieroglyphics consist of a series of small pictures that represent ideas. Samples of.
pages.brief: At a pyramid building site, an architect shows plans to workers while others cut and shape stone blocks in a quarry, and a scribe writes a list of materials in small picture signs on a tablet.

pages.text: Many people were needed to pull each large stone on a sledge. In addition to these specialized tasks, other workers were required to move the heavy stones. They moved some stones from the quarry to the building site by boat. Other stones were put on sledges, or large wooden sleds, which were then dragged across the desert sands. Until recently, historians believed that much of this difficult work was forced on enslaved laborers. But in 1990, a tourist traveling in Egypt stumbled on the remains of an ancient city where workers who helped build the pyramids of Giza were once believed to have lived. Evidence from the city suggests that the people who built those pyramids were not enslaved people, but rather skilled craftspeople—about 15,000 of them. Written records suggest that the workers were treated well while they worked on the pyramids. It is believed that farmers also participated in the building of pyramids, especially during the flood season when they could not farm.
pages.brief: Crowds of workers drag a huge stone block on a wooden sledge across desert sand toward a rising pyramid, while other workers load stones onto a boat at the riverbank and farmers join in during the flood season.

pages.text: Farmers depended on floods to deposit fertile soil for crops. Because the pharaoh was believed to be the son of a god, farmers thought the pharaoh was able to guarantee good floods. They were glad to serve the pharaoh in exchange for the fertile soil brought by the floods. The location of a pyramid had to be determined very carefully. The site needed to be on rocky ground to support the immense weight of the finished pyramid. Do You Know? Each stone in the Great Pyramid weighed up to two tons or 2000 kilograms. This is as much as a car weighs!
pages.brief: Farmers stand in flooded fields where water has left dark fertile soil for crops, and beyond them workers haul enormous stone blocks onto rocky ground chosen to carry a pyramid's great weight, blocks as heavy as a car.

pages.text: The Egyptians sailed heavy stones down the Nile River. The pyramid also needed to be near the Nile River so that some of the stones could be taken by water from the quarry to the building site. The site had to be located on the west bank of the Nile because the west was where the Sun set each night and where the dead were believed to exist. The exact position of the pyramid also needed to be determined carefully, since the sides had to face exact north, south, east, and west. An astronomer-priest was summoned to observe the stars in order to determine true north. During the actual building of a pyramid, many ceremonies were performed to ensure the support of the gods in the endeavor.
pages.brief: Egyptians sail heavy stones down the Nile on boats toward a pyramid site on the west bank, while a priest stands alone at night watching the stars to find true north, and ceremonies are performed near the building works.

pages.text: Several kinds of stone were used in the building of a pyramid. The core of the pyramid was made from local limestone. Other limestone of finer quality, brought from far away, was used to make the outer shell of the pyramid. Granite from even farther away was used for the pharaoh’s coffin, called a sarcophagus, as well as to decorate the burial chamber. After the location and position of the pyramid were decided on, the surface of the ground was leveled. After leveling the ground, the workers began the actual labor of building the pyramid. The tomb of King Tutankhamun (King Tut)
pages.brief: Workers level the ground at a pyramid site and stack rough local limestone for the core while finer limestone is brought for the outer shell, and a granite sarcophagus is prepared for the burial chamber of King Tutankhamun.

pages.text: The internal structure of a pyramid was designed to outsmart thieves and keep them from the burial chamber and its treasures. If the burial chamber was at or below ground level, it was put in place first, and then the pyramid was built around it in horizontal layers. Ramps were built against the sides of the pyramid, and the huge stones were dragged up the ramps and put in position. A series of passageways and rooms included dead ends and empty chambers to confuse anyone trying to loot the tomb. Enormous slabs of stone blocked the entrance to the real tomb. Drawing of the tunnels and passageways in a pyramid.
pages.brief: Inside a pyramid, a cutaway view shows ramps against sloping sides where workers drag up huge stones, and a maze of passageways, dead ends and empty chambers leads toward a burial chamber blocked by enormous stone slabs.

pages.text: Try This! Build a Pyramid Using sugar cubes or cubes fashioned out of clay, build a model pyramid. You can build a pyramid with steps, a flat- sided pyramid, or one of your own design.
pages.brief: On a table, sugar cubes and lumps of clay are stacked into small model pyramids in different shapes — some with steps, some with flat straight sides — being built by hand as a model.

pages.text: Preparing the Body The ancient Egyptians had a special procedure for preparing the body of an important person for burial. This technique, called mummification, preserved the body for thousands of years. The body was taken to an embalmer, who removed the insides and preserved them in canopic jars. Each jar had a lid in the shape of a guardian god. The body then was left to dry for forty days. Then it was washed, rubbed with oil and spices, and packed with preservatives. Afterward, it was wrapped with many layers of linen soaked in resin to hold its shape. A decorative mask was placed on the head, and the entire body was placed in a sarcophagus. Each sarcophagus was ornately painted. This mummy was damaged by thieves looking for souvenirs.
pages.brief: An embalmer works on a body in a workshop, setting aside organs in canopic jars with guardian-god lids, while a wrapped mummy lies drying, then oily, then wrapped in linen layers, given a painted mask and laid in an ornately painted sarcophagus.

pages.text: The Sphinx at Giza. Famous Egyptian Pyramids The first pyramid, built for King Zoser at Saqqâra, is called a step pyramid because it was shaped like giant stairways up the sides. Later pyramids had smaller steps. The design eventually changed into straight-sided pyramids, such as the Great Pyramid at Giza, which was built about 4,500 years ago for King Khufu. The Great Pyramid is 147 meters (482 ft.) tall and contains about 2,300,000 blocks of stone. The Great Pyramid at Giza is part of a complex of pyramids built by King Khufu, his son Khafre, and his grandson Menkaure. Their pyramids are surrounded by other structures. There are pyramids for Queen Meritites and Queen Hetepheres. There are also stone mastabas — tombs made of mud bricks—for the rest of the royal family and members of the court. The Sphinx, a limestone statue with the face of a king and the body of a lion, guards the entire site. The Sphinx represents the Sun god.
pages.brief: The Sphinx with a king's face and a lion's body guards the Giza site, where the straight-sided Great Pyramid of Khufu stands beside the step pyramid of King Zoser, smaller pyramids for queens and mud-brick mastabas for the royal family.

pages.text: All of the ancient Egyptian pyramids have had their treasures looted. Very few tombs have been left intact. The only intact burial of an Egyptian king ever found is that of King Tutankhamun. His tomb, in the Valley of the Kings in Egypt, was built underground, rather than inside a pyramid. Because it was found intact, it has helped archaeologists to learn a great deal about the culture of ancient Egypt. Egyptian archaeologists examine items from King Tutankhamun’s tomb, which was discovered in 1922.
pages.brief: Egyptian archaeologists in the Valley of the Kings examine items from King Tutankhamun's intact underground tomb, its painted coffins and treasures laid out, while looted empty pyramids stand far away in the desert.

pages.text: Pyramids in Other Lands Pyramids were also built in the Americas. They were first built in Central America and in northwestern South America, but soon the practice of building pyramids spread to North America as well. Several of the New World cultures that built pyramids are mentioned below. The Mayan people and other cultures in Central America built stepped pyramids. These pyramids had stairways decorated with sculptures and inscriptions that led to temples at the top. Sometimes, but not always, these pyramids contained the tombs of kings. One of the most Chichén Itzá. Rebuilt over was built just before 1100 bce. Locations of pyramids in the New World.
pages.brief: Across the Americas, stepped pyramids rise from Central American jungle, with stairways carved with sculptures and inscriptions leading up to temples at the top, and other pyramids stand in northwestern and North American lands.

pages.text: Chichén Itzá, the most famous Mayan pyramid The earlier one, built 100 years before, contained a stone sculpture of a jaguar that was painted red and had eyes made of jade. The jaguar, a Mayan symbol of the Earth’s fertility, was worshipped as a god. The Aztecs, another Central American culture, built the Great Pyramid Temple, most likely in the 1300s, in their capital city of Tenochtitlán, on an island in Lake Texcoco in Mexico. The Aztecs believed that the Sun god needed blood from human hearts to stay strong. Without human blood, the Sun would die and the world would come to an end. Human sacrifices of prisoners taken in war were a regular part of Aztec life, and these sacrifices took place at the Great Pyramid Temple.
pages.brief: The famous stepped pyramid of Chichén Itzá rises above the trees, and nearby lies a red-painted stone jaguar with jade eyes, while far away the Great Pyramid Temple of the Aztecs stands on an island in Lake Texcoco where sacrifices take place.

pages.text: Cultures in northwestern South America also built flat-topped, stepped pyramids. The Moche people, who flourished between 100 bce and 800 ce, built the Pyramid of the Sun and the Pyramid of the Moon. About 600 to 700 years later, the Inca people built pyramids. The Temple of the Sun was the most sacred shrine in the Incan empire. It was a pyramid that contained a huge gold disk that represented the Sun god. The Incas believed that their rulers were direct descendants of the Sun. Pyramid of the Moon in Teotihuacan, Mexico.
pages.brief: In northwestern South America, flat-topped stepped pyramids stand on the land, including the Moche Pyramid of the Sun and Pyramid of the Moon, and the Incan Temple of the Sun holds a huge gold disk shining for the Sun god.

pages.text: Meroë Pyramids, Sudan The pyramid shape has been used in building designs in other cultures around the world. The Meroë Pyramids in Sudan are an example of the cross-cultural exchange between ancient Egypt and the empire of Nubia, one of the earliest civilizations of Africa. Cross-cultural exchange is when two cultures help change, develop, or shape each other. Nubian-style pyramids were built between 700 bce and 300 bce. They used Egyptian cultural forms combined with other African influences. Pyramid designs can also be found in parts of Europe, Asia, and the Middle East. The pyramid shape is used in modern architecture in many countries, including France, England, and the United States. A modern pyramid was built in Egypt to honor President Anwar Sadat, who was assassinated in 1981.
pages.brief: Nubian-style pyramids with steep sides rise at Meroë in Sudan's desert, and modern pyramid-shaped buildings stand in France, England and the United States, with a modern pyramid in Egypt honoring President Anwar Sadat.

pages.text: Conclusion Efforts are being made to preserve and protect the pyramids of ancient Egypt, as well as pyramids in other parts of the world. Pollution, urban expansion, tourism, and other problems threaten the pyramids at Giza. The Great Pyramid of Khufu at Giza is the only one of the famous “Seven Wonders of the Ancient World” that still stands. All of the pyramids and tombs are wonders worthy of preservation. By studying pyramids, we learn about complex and fascinating ancient cultures and the accomplishments of humans who lived during those times. We also learn how ancient cultures honored their leaders and worshipped their gods. Millions of tourists from across the world visit the pyramids at Giza each year.
pages.brief: Tourists crowd the desert paths around the Great Pyramid of Khufu at Giza, where city buildings and traffic press close and pollution hangs in the air, while people work at the base to clean and protect the ancient stone.

books.title: Mount Kilimanjaro
books.art_why: Mount Kilimanjaro is a real, present-day place that can be photographed.

pages.text: A line of climbers ascend the slopes of Mount Kilimanjaro on their way to the snow-capped peak.
pages.brief: A line of climbers ascends the slopes of Mount Kilimanjaro, heading toward the snow-capped peak. They walk in single file on a rocky trail, with the white summit rising high above them. The mountain dominates the landscape under a clear sky.

pages.text: Mount Kilimanjaro, Tanzania, Africa The Roof of Africa As the highest peak on the continent of Africa, Mount Kilimanjaro has earned the nickname “the roof of Africa.” The mountain measures 5,895 meters (19,341 ft.) in altitude and rises 4,877 meters (16,000 ft.) above the surrounding land. It is also the world’s tallest freestanding mountain—one not part of a mountain range. Mount Kilimanjaro is located in the country of Tanzania (tan-zuh-NEE-uh), close to its border with Kenya. Kilimanjaro National Park, a World Heritage Site, was established in 1973 to protect the area of the mountain above the tree line. The park was expanded in 2005 to protect the forested areas lower down on its slopes. As a national park, the mountain’s habitats and life forms are under the protection of the Tanzanian government.
pages.brief: Mount Kilimanjaro rises as a freestanding mountain in Tanzania, near the border with Kenya. Its snow-capped peak stands above surrounding land, and lower slopes are covered in forest. Kilimanjaro National Park protects the area above the tree line and the forested lower slopes.

pages.text: The contrast between Kilimanjaro’s black rock and white glaciers is part of its beauty. Glaciers have also helped shape Mount Kilimanjaro. Because of their great weight, they have carved the underlying rock into ridges and valleys as they have moved downhill. It may seem surprising that Kilimanjaro has glaciers at all since it is only about 322 kilometers (200 mi.) from the equator. Lower parts of the mountain have warm weather year-round. The whiteness of the glaciers reflects much of the sunlight that reaches them, allowing their ice to remain cool. Naming the Mountain Kilimanjaro is a name believed to have come from two words. Kilima means mountain in Swahili. Njaro is the Kichagga word for the whiteness of Mount Kilimanjaro’s snowy peaks.
pages.brief: Black rock and white glaciers contrast on Mount Kilimanjaro. Heavy glaciers have carved ridges and valleys into the rock as they moved downhill. The white ice reflects sunlight, keeping it cool even though the mountain is close to the equator. Lower slopes have warm weather year-round.

pages.text: Even so, the mountain’s glaciers are slowly melting because of global warming as well as nearby forests being cut down. The loss of trees reduces the amount of moisture in the air around the mountain. This leads to fewer clouds and less rain in the area, which increases evaporation of moisture from the glaciers. Kilimanjaro’s glaciers have lost more than four-fifths of their mass since 1912, when they were first measured. Some researchers predict that they may disappear completely by 2060. The ice in glaciers holds important historical information about Earth’s atmosphere and climate. Kilimanjaro’s ice holds the only such information for all of Africa. If it melts, that information will be lost forever. So will much of Kilimanjaro’s beauty. Do You Know? Ice cores are cylinders of ice drilled out of an ice sheet or glacier. Bubbles in the ice hold samples of Earth’s atmosphere from thousands or even hundreds of thousands of years ago. Scientists study these air pockets to measure how the makeup of gases in the atmosphere has changed over long periods of time. Ice cores also hold clues about past temperatures and other aspects of the environment.
pages.brief: A glacier on Mount Kilimanjaro shows melting edges and exposed dark rock, with white ice shrinking. A cylindrical ice core sample rests on the ice, holding ancient air bubbles. In the distance below, a patch of forest has been cut down, leaving bare ground.

pages.text: The Chagga people live around the base of Mount Kilimanjaro. Traditional Chagga culture is kept alive in small villages. The Chagga People People have lived on or near Mount Kilimanjaro for centuries. At the beginning of the eleventh century, many people from across Africa migrated to northern Tanzania. Many of tribes these people were from various Bantu. They settled the southern and eastern slopes of Mount Kilimanjaro, Mount Meru, and the nearby town of Moshi. They established themselves as a new community, the Chagga people. Several different tribes were already living in the area when the Chagga arrived. In time, however, only the Chagga remained. The Chagga make up the third-largest ethnic group in Tanzania. While the Chagga have remained Bantu speakers, their language has several dialects that can sound like whole separate languages.
pages.brief: Chagga people live in a small village around the base of Mount Kilimanjaro. Traditional homes and village life are shown, with the mountain rising behind. The Chagga have lived on the southern and eastern slopes for centuries, keeping their culture alive.

pages.text: Before German colonists and missionaries arrived in the late 1800s, the many Chagga chiefdoms were often at war. But after German colonial rule imposed order, the Chagga banded together. They developed advanced methods to farm the mountain slopes and prospered. They continued to improve their farming methods after Tanzania gained independence in 1961. Today, the Chagga are the wealthiest and the most highly organized communities in Tanzania. Bananas are their main crop, but they also grow yams, beans, and maize in Kilimanjaro’s rich volcanic soil. Around the world, the Chagga are famous for a type of coffee that is now important to Tanzania’s national economy. Over time, ways of life have changed, but they still have a strong sense of pride in their cultural identity. Moshi Town in Tanzania has a beautiful view of Kilimanjaro.
pages.brief: Chagga farmers work on the fertile slopes of Mount Kilimanjaro, tending rows of banana plants, yams, beans, maize, and coffee bushes in rich volcanic soil. In the background, the town of Moshi sits with a clear view of the mountain.

pages.text: Uhuru Peak is the highest point on the rim of Kibo’s crater. Visiting Kilimanjaro At least twenty-five thousand people from around the world climb Mount Kilimanjaro each year. As the tallest mountain in Africa, Kilimanjaro is one of the Seven Summits— the highest peaks on Earth’s seven continents. Climbing these seven peaks is a goal of many mountaineers. Kilimanjaro is one of the easiest of the Seven Summits to climb. Most of the routes to Kibo’s peak (the highest point of Mount Kilimanjaro) do not require training. Climbers don’t need ropes or mountaineering gear—just good hiking boots and camping equipment. Still, Kilimanjaro is not an easy climb. To avoid altitude sickness, climbers must be careful to adjust slowly to the thinner air as they move up the mountain. A round-trip climb typically takes between five and nine days. About two-thirds of the people who attempt it succeed.
pages.brief: Climbers in hiking boots and with camping backpacks ascend a rocky trail on Mount Kilimanjaro toward Uhuru Peak, the highest point on Kibo’s crater rim. They walk slowly to adjust to the thinner air. The snow-capped summit rises ahead.

pages.text: Reaching Kibo’s summit isn’t the only reason to travel to Kilimanjaro. Many nature hikes are available for less ambitious visitors. These include day trips to Lake Chala, a beautiful crater lake, and Shira Plateau, which formed when Kilimanjaro’s first volcano collapsed. Trout fishing is popular in Kilimanjaro’s rivers, and the entire area is great for photography. Tourism brings more than $20 million each year into the local economy. Mountain climbing and other activities create jobs for guides, porters, hotel staff, food producers, travel agents, construction workers, and others. The economy of the entire region benefits. Lake Chala looks blue, turquoise, or green, depending on the time of year.
pages.brief: Lake Chala, a crater lake near Mount Kilimanjaro, glows turquoise. A guide and two visitors hike along its shore, one carrying a camera. Nearby, a person fishes for trout in a river. The Shira Plateau, formed by a collapsed volcano, lies in the background.

pages.text: Plants and Animals One of the amazing parts of the experience of climbing Kilima njaro is the changing scenery. Climbers pass through several different ecosystems as they move up the mountain. • The cultivated zone is 800 to 1,800 meters (2,625–5,906 ft.) above sea level. It receives the most rainfall and has many rivers formed by melted ice from glaciers. Due to the The cultivated zone is plentiful water, this zone located around the base of the mountain. contains farmland and small villages. • The montane forest is 1,800 to 2,800 meters (5,906–9,186 ft.) above sea level. This is where the climb begins. The south and east sides have because they get the most rainfall. Monkeys, elephants, rhinos, and other animals are present Elephant’s trunk flower grows in the but hard to spot. forest on the cool upland slopes. It is Mount Kilimanjaro’s semiofficial symbol.
pages.brief: At the base of Mount Kilimanjaro, the cultivated zone shows farmland and small villages with rivers fed by melted ice. Above, the montane forest begins, where climbers start their ascent. An elephant’s trunk flower blooms on the cool upland slopes, and monkeys and elephants are hidden among the trees.

pages.text: • Above the tree line, the heather and moorland zone is 2,800 to 4,000 meters (9,186–13,123 ft.) above sea level. It’s sometimes listed as two separate zones. This zone is drier and windier than the forest below. Temperatures can reach 40° Celsius (104°F) during the day and drop below freezing at night. Climbers often see clouds at eye level. Wild Giant groundsels live in the moorland grasses and giant zone. These plants in the sunflower family can live at high altitudes. heathers are the main vegetation. The most common animal is the four- striped grass mouse. Larger animals sometimes wander up the slopes but don’t stay long. • The alpine desert is 4,000 to 5,000 meters (13,123–16,404 ft.) above sea level. It receives less than 20 centimeters (8 in.) of rain each year. The few plants that can survive at this altitude must be able to withstand strong sunlight as well as subzero temperatures. Animals include birds of prey and a high-altitude spider. • Kibo’s summit is 5,000 to 5,895 meters (16,404– 19,341 ft.) above sea level. Almost nothing lives here because of the lack of water. Lichens are the main life forms.
pages.brief: In the heather and moorland zone above the tree line, giant groundsels and heathers grow among the grasses. A four-striped grass mouse scurries past. Clouds drift at eye level, and the temperature swings from hot sun to freezing night. In the distance, the alpine desert and Kibo’s summit rise, where only lichens survive.

pages.text: A Symbol of Freedom Tanzania, where Mount Kilimanjaro is located, was called Tanganyika (tang-guh-NYEE- kuh) before it gained independence from Britain in 1961. Two years earlier, the country’s future president, Julius Nyerere (nih-RAIR-ee), said, “We, the people of Tanganyika, would like to light a candle and put it on the top of Mount Kilimanjaro.” He envisioned the candle shining beyond the country’s borders, offering love in place of hate and hope and respect where neither existed before. Because of Nyerere’s words, Kilimanjaro has become a symbol for independence for all of Africa. Kibo’s summit, called Uhuru Peak, gets its name from the Swahili word for “freedom.” Julius Nyerere served as president of Tanzania from 1964 to 1985.
pages.brief: A single candle burns brightly on the snowy summit of Uhuru Peak, casting light beyond the borders of Tanzania. Below, Julius Nyerere stands speaking, his hand raised as he shares his vision of hope and respect. The mountain rises as a symbol of independence for all of Africa.

pages.text: Author Ernest Hemingway described Mount Kilimanjaro as “wide as all the world, great, high and unbelievably white in the sun.” The Jewel of Africa Mount Kilimanjaro is a rich natural area that is home to a wide variety of plants and animals, some found nowhere else on Earth. It is also a dramatic example of the creative force of volcanoes and a fascinating part of Earth’s geologic history. To travelers who come from every corner of the world, Kilimanjaro is a mountain to climb and a personal goal to reach. To local people, it is a source of prosperity and pride as well as a powerful symbol of freedom and self-government. And to people from all walks of life who are lucky enough to see it, Mount Kilimanjaro is a place of stunning beauty.
pages.brief: Mount Kilimanjaro stands wide and unbelievably white in the sun, its snow-capped peak rising above the surrounding land. Below, a rich natural area holds a variety of plants and animals found nowhere else. Travelers gaze at the mountain, a personal goal and a symbol of freedom, prosperity, and pride for local people.

books.title: Amazing Migrations
books.art_why: Real animals, real places and real scientists that exist today; no named famous person, so no cartoon art.

pages.text: Caribou cross a river in Alaska’s Arctic National Wildlife Refuge.
pages.brief: A herd of caribou wades and swims across a wide river in Alaska's Arctic National Wildlife Refuge. Their antlers and dark bodies stand out against the shallow water as they push through the current, moving together in a long line toward the far bank.

pages.text: African elephants migrate through Kenya. During a very dry season, they may cover more than 100 kilometers (62 mi.). The Journey Begins It has been said that a journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step. It may also begin with a swish or a flutter. Traveling by land, sea, and air, many animals journey hundreds and even thousands of miles yearly to feed and breed. This seasonal or annual relocation is known as migration. Such long hauls are not only impressive because of their great distance and exact routes. They are also amazing because of the many challenges migrating animals face as they travel.
pages.brief: A herd of African elephants walks across dry Kenyan grassland during a very dry season. Dust rises around their legs as the huge animals travel in a line, adults and younger elephants together, covering more than 100 kilometers in search of food and water.

pages.text: A road closing helps Christmas Island red crabs cross safely during their annual migration. Some migratory animals travel a relatively short distance. Australia’s Christmas Island red crabs, for example, make an annual 8-kilometer (5 mi.) journey. They travel from the island’s forests to breed on nearby beaches at the start of the rainy season. Compare their migration to that of North America’s monarch butterflies. These beautiful insects fly up to 4,800 kilometers (3,000 mi.) in the fall and again in the spring! Monarch butterflies pollinate many types of they need milkweed plants to reproduce and lay their eggs.
pages.brief: Christmas Island red crabs swarm across a road that has been closed to traffic. The bright red crabs carpet the ground, crawling in a dense crowd from the island's forests toward the beaches at the start of the rainy season, while the empty road stays clear.

pages.text: Timing Is Everything All animal migrations take place regularly at certain times of the year. How animals know just when to begin their migrations is a bit of a mystery, however. Getting started before food supplies run out is key, but what triggers migrators to get moving? Day length cues some birds to begin migrating. These migrators are called obligates —they are hardwired to go at a certain time, no matter what. One example of such a migrator is semipalmated sandpipers. These birds breed and nest on Arctic coasts in summer. There, they feast on coastal marine life to build up fatty reserves. Gaining weight is important to these long-distance migrators. As the days begin to shorten, the sandpipers set out on an amazing 4,000-kilometer (2,500 mi.) nonstop journey. They fly south to their winter homes in South America. Most of the route is over open waters with nowhere to stop for a snooze or a snack!
pages.brief: Semipalmated sandpipers stand and feed along an Arctic coast in summer, probing the wet shoreline for marine life to build up fat reserves. The small shorebirds gather in numbers on the mud and sand before setting out over open ocean without stopping.

pages.text: Half a million migrating sandhill cranes are common along Nebraska’s Platte River in early spring. Other bird species, such as sandhill cranes, seem to start their spring and fall migrations based on changes in temperature and weather. The cranes’ long migration between the Arctic Circle and Mexico may be delayed or advanced by days or even weeks. That’s because the cranes use tailwinds and rising columns of warm air called thermals to carry them up to 650 kilometers (400 mi.) in a single day. Waiting for optimal conditions reduces the birds’ effort as they journey over North America.
pages.brief: Half a million sandhill cranes gather along Nebraska's Platte River in early spring. The tall gray birds stand in shallow water and on sandbars, some with wings spread, packed closely together as they rest and feed on their journey between the Arctic Circle and Mexico.

pages.text: Gray Whale Migration Gray whales mate and give birth in the warm waters off Mexico’s Baja Peninsula. Mothers wait until their calves get strong enough. Then the pairs make the long journey back toward the cold seas of the Arctic, where food is plentiful. It is the longest annual migration of any mammal on Earth. Optimal conditions may also trigger migration in other animal species. For instance, gray whales summer in the cold waters between Siberia and Alaska. There, they spend up to twenty hours a day eating. The whales begin to migrate south when ice cover over the sea increases in the fall. Gray whales seek warmer water where pregnant females can safely give birth to calves. The whales eat very little as they migrate between 16,000 and 23,000 kilometers (10,000–14,300 mi.). They live off the fatty blubber they have built up during the summer.
pages.brief: An adult gray whale swims with her calf in the warm, calm waters off Mexico's Baja Peninsula. The huge mother stays close beside the smaller calf, guiding it through the sea before the pair begins the long journey back toward the cold, food-rich seas of the Arctic.

pages.text: Which Way Do We Go? Humans use memory, maps, and technology to help them find their way. Long-distance migrators use a mix of navigational tools as well. Airborne migrators like birds and insects have a built-in sense of direction that is based on something called celestial bearings. During daylight hours, they determine their position in relation to the Sun’s position in the sky. Migrating birds that travel at night, such as warblers and blackcaps, use the stars. One scientist projected images of night skies on a domed ceiling to study how some of these night direction. He beneath a display of the night sky. They fluttered and in the direction normally migrate. When he rotated the starry display, the birds turned as well. The experiment showed that birds use the position of the stars as a guide.
pages.brief: Inside a darkened domed room, a researcher watches small warblers and blackcaps flutter beneath a projected display of the night sky. The birds turn and shift direction as the starry pattern rotates above them, showing that they steer by the position of the stars.

pages.text: What do birds do when skies grow cloudy? Birds and some other animals use Earth’s magnetic field to navigate. Earth is sort of like a giant magnet surrounded by this field. Certain animals can sense the pull of the magnetic field at their location and use it to guide them. Researchers are still studying just how animals do this. One theory is that animals such as sockeye salmon have an internal compass that points them to their destination. When salmon are born, they can somehow sense exactly where they are within Earth’s magnetic field. This location becomes imprinted in their memory. After spending up to four years in the Gulf of Alaska, the salmon return to their freshwater birthplace. They travel thousands of kilometers to release eggs, or spawn, at this exact spot. The salmon are able to sense this point as they make their way back from the sea. Sockeye salmon return to their birthplace in British Columbia to spawn.
pages.brief: Sockeye salmon swim upstream in a river in British Columbia, returning to the exact freshwater birthplace they left years before. Their red bodies crowd the shallow water as they push against the current to release their eggs at the same spot where they hatched.

pages.text: But what accounts for the multigenerational migration of monarch butterflies? The round-trip migration from Hudson Bay to Mexico takes longer than a monarch’s life span. The generation that is born in Mexico must find its way back to a place it has never been. Just as some animals have the instinct to begin migration on specific days, monarchs have the instinct to follow the same routes taken by previous generations. The idea of a magnetic “map” stored within their genes may explain this instinct. Genes are basic units of heredity that transfer a trait from one generation to the next. In the case of monarchs, their genes somehow code their destination in their memory. Thousands of monarch butterflies cover a single tree in the oyamel fir forest of central Mexico. They pack in tightly for warmth, wait out the winter, then fly north in spring.
pages.brief: Thousands of monarch butterflies cover a single oyamel fir tree in the forest of central Mexico, packing tightly onto branches and trunk for warmth through the winter. Their orange and black wings overlap in thick clusters before they fly north again in spring.

pages.text: Wildebeest Migration Wildebeest arrive on the short-grass plains of the Serengeti in late November. Their calves are born in February. In April, the herd starts its great migration back north. They cross the Mara River in September. By October, they are heading south again. Many migrating mammals depend on landmarks and a sharp sense of smell to guide them. Africa is home to two of the largest mammal migrations known. The great Serengeti wildebeest migration takes place yearly when 1.5 million wildebeest make their way between feeding grounds in Tanzania and Kenya. Their journey takes them 2,900 kilometers (1,800 mi.) across grassy plains and the rushing Mara River. As they follow the rain and greener pastures to the north, the wildebeest are often joined by zebras and gazelles.
pages.brief: A vast herd of wildebeest crosses the rushing Mara River, with zebras and gazelles among them. The animals plunge through the water and climb the far bank on the Serengeti plains, following the rain and greener pastures north toward Kenya.

pages.text: The bats that come to Kasanka National Park each fall bring their appetites. By the time they leave in late December, they have consumed more than a billion fruits! Just as impressive is the Kasanka bat migration. In fact, it is the biggest mammal migration on Earth. From almost every corner of sub-Saharan Africa, ten million straw-colored fruit bats gather on a patch of swamp forest in northern Zambia. For several weeks, they feast on the fruit that grows after the start of the rainy season. By day, they cover the trunks of the trees and fly out to forage at dusk. Math Minute The sooty shearwater is a dark seabird that migrates great distances over ocean waters. Its migration route can stretch 14,000 kilometers (8,700 mi.) between New Zealand and the North Pacific Ocean. If it takes a shearwater 29 days to make the trip, how far does the bird travel in an average day?
pages.brief: Straw-colored fruit bats hang in dense clusters on tree trunks in Kasanka National Park, Zambia, then stream out over the swamp forest at dusk to forage for fruit. Far out over the ocean, a dark sooty shearwater glides on long wings during its migration.

pages.text: Overcoming Obstacles Knowing when and where to go are just two of the problems migratory animals face. An increasingly bigger problem is dealing with both natural and constructed hazards. Many migrators are prey animals that must be wary of predators as they travel. The wildebeest of the Serengeti are a main food source for lions and jackals as well as crocodiles lurking in lagoons and rivers. Hawks and humans hunt African fruit bats, which grow plump from eating dates and figs. Hawks also hunt the migratory routes of songbirds that travel North America’s flyways. Bad weather presents other challenges to migrating species. Sudden storms can disrupt the flight plans of migrating birds and force large flocks to land in unusual locations. This type of event is known as a fallout. One songbird fallout occurred in South Texas in April 2013. Thousands of tired and hungry migrating songbirds landed on South Padre Island, off the coast of Texas. Island residents put out fruit and worms to help the birds gain enough strength to resume their migration north.
pages.brief: On South Padre Island, Texas, residents set out fruit and worms for thousands of tired, hungry songbirds that landed after a storm. The small birds rest and feed on the ground and in low shrubs, regaining strength to continue their migration north.

pages.text: Shifting weather patterns have sometimes interrupted land and water migrations as well. Warm spells can cause early snowmelt, leading to flooding that complicates the migration of animals such as elk. Flooded rivers can overrun their banks and send migrating salmon off course, leaving them high and dry when waters recede. Droughts can make food scarce and can also spark wildfires that put migrating herds in danger. Human-made barriers threaten long-distance migrators as well. Dams block waterways that migrating fish once used. Highways that cross migration routes put animals and people on a collision course. Fences block migrating range animals from following established trails that lead to important feeding grounds. A herd of migrating pronghorn encounter a barbed wire fence in Wyoming. A closer look at the bottom wire, however, reveals that it is not barbed. Pronghorn can slide under it without cutting themselves.
pages.brief: A herd of migrating pronghorn in Wyoming stops at a barbed wire fence. The animals crowd along the wire, and the smooth bottom strand lets them slide underneath. Beyond the fence lie the established trails that lead to important feeding grounds.

pages.text: Even useful and important structures harm migrators. The huge blades of giant wind turbines used to produce clean electricity are deadly to migrating birds and bats. Large-scale solar farms, such as the Ivanpah solar plant in California’s Mojave Desert, are responsible for killing thousands of birds that fly into the concentrated beams of sunlight and are instantly burned to death. To address these problems, researchers use tracking devices to monitor migratory animals. They include the information in studies showing the impact of construction on the environment. This information may be helpful in placing new construction away from migration routes. New awareness of these routes and the behavior of migrators has inspired people to find ways to help rather than hurt them. A young loggerhead sea turtle in Florida is tagged by a scientist before it sets out on a journey of 7,250 kilometers (4,500 mi.). Even more incredible, turtles make the trip in just seventy days.
pages.brief: On a Florida beach, a scientist carefully tags a young loggerhead sea turtle before it begins its long ocean journey. The small turtle rests in the scientist's hands near the water, fitted with a tracking tag that will follow its travels across thousands of kilometers of sea.

pages.text: The Grand Champion of Migration If any one species deserved to be crowned the grand champion of migration, it would be the arctic tern. Tiny tracking technology enabled scientists to follow the flight of this bird on its long migration between the North and South Poles. What researchers learned was astounding: the tern’s journey was twice as long as once thought, an unbelievable 70,800 kilometers (44,000 mi.)! Instead of following a straight north-south line, many Arctic terns zigzag from Greenland to Antarctica and back again. They do this to take advantage of swirling wind currents that carry them on their way. The saves these birds effort of having to fly directly into the wind.
pages.brief: An arctic tern flies low over the open ocean, its white body and long pointed wings tilted against the wind. Instead of a straight north-south line, it zigzags across the water between Greenland and Antarctica, riding swirling wind currents that carry it on its way.

pages.text: Some regions now have wildlife overpasses and underpasses where roadways and land migration routes cross. These wildlife bridges and tunnels help keep migrators and drivers away from each other and safe. Engineers are working to improve clean-energy devices that unintentionally harm migrators. Vertical wind turbines in development may one day replace the giant horizontal propellers on wind farms. Specially constructed “fish ladders” have been placed next to dams on salmon migration routes. These ladders help the fish safely reach their spawning grounds. Information about how pollution affects stressed from their long journeys could lead to A salmon leaps up a fish ladder in Alaska. to keep migrators safe. What’s most impressive about amazing migrators is how, despite these obstacles, they set out on their epic journeys year after year. These migrations across land, in the air, and through the sea are critical to the survival of these species. Understanding their importance can inspire us to take action to ensure that these important journeys continue for many years to come.
pages.brief: A salmon leaps up a fish ladder beside a dam in Alaska, its body arched above the rushing water as it climbs step by step toward its spawning grounds. The concrete ladder channels river water upward, helping the fish pass the dam safely.

books.title: Dust Storms and Sandstorms
books.art_why: The book describes modern, dated real-world events and places that can be photographed.

pages.text: People walk through a sandstorm in China to celebrate a festival in 2008.
pages.brief: A group of people walks through a thick sandstorm in China during a festival in 2008. Dust fills the air and reduces visibility as they move together through the storm. The scene shows the people outdoors in the dusty conditions.

pages.text: Dust in the Sky In September 2009, the people of eastern Australia watched their world change color. Strong winds had whipped up bone-dry dirt. The storm rolled eastward, building a moving cloud of dust measuring more than 500 kilometers (311 mi.) 1,000 kilometers (621 mi.) long. Dust covered towns and cities. It painted the sky Australians said the sky during a 2009 and landscape an dust storm reminded them of scenes eerie reddish-orange. from a disaster movie. Meteorologists called it the worst dust storm the area had seen in almost seventy years. Poor visibility forced drivers to slow down and turn on their headlights. Airlines canceled flights due to hazardous conditions. Doctors warned people with asthma and other health issues to stay inside. By the time the dust settled, the storm had dumped about 2.5 million metric tonnes (2.75 million tn.) of dust into the ocean. Meteorologists categorize the dramatic dust storm that struck Australia as an SDS event (sandstorm/dust storm). These extreme weather systems pose a serious threat to human health and even the land itself.
pages.brief: In eastern Australia in 2009, a huge moving cloud of dust covers towns and cities. The sky and landscape turn an eerie reddish-orange. Drivers slow down and turn on headlights as visibility drops. The storm stretches across the land after strong winds whipped up dry dirt.

pages.text: A sandstorm blows across the Middle Eastern country of Jordan. The different types of storms are sometimes lumped together. However, some meteorologists and other scientists distinguish between types of SDS events. What are the different types? As their name suggests, sandstorms occur in sandy regions, such as the Gobi Desert, in Asia, and the Arabian Desert, in the Middle East. A large gust of wind picks up the top layer of sand from the ground. Sandstorms stay close to the ground, rarely rising more than 15 meters (49 ft.) in the air. Since dust weighs less than sand, sandstorms usually include dust as well. On the other hand, dust storms can happen wherever the ground is dry, especially areas parched by drought. Without moisture, dirt doesn’t stick together and breaks down into smaller dust particles. These particles are smaller and lighter than sand grains. That means winds can carry dust farther and faster than sand. In fact, dust storms often carry dust 10 kilometers (6 mi.) or higher into the atmosphere!
pages.brief: A sandstorm blows across Jordan in the Middle East. The storm stays low, with sand lifted only a short way above the ground. The sandy desert landscape is partly hidden by blowing sand. The scene shows one kind of storm that scientists separate from dust storms.

Gusts traveling downward can pick up a large amount of sand and dust from the ground. The winds create giant walls of these materials measuring 457 to 1,524 meters (1,500–5,000 ft.) high. The walls may even block out the Sun, which makes visibility very low. Because they can make daytime seem like night, haboobs are also called “black blizzards.” The storms can cover very large areas—up to 160 kilometers (100 mi.) wide. They can also travel as far as 320 kilometers (200 mi.).
