pages.text: Each year, dust storms carry orange dust from the Sahara Desert across the Atlantic Ocean to North and South America. That’s a distance of about 2,600 kilometers (1,616 mi.). How frequent and how severe SDS events are depends on the location and conditions. Sandstorms and dust storms generally occur during the driest seasons. In much of China and other parts of Asia, that period may last from November to April. SDS events in North Africa’s Sahara Desert most often occur from June to September. In Arizona and other parts of the American Southwest, haboobs are common during the summer months, when heavy rains are frequent. A massive haboob moves across Phoenix, Arizona, in 2012.
pages.brief: A massive haboob moves across Phoenix, Arizona, in 2012. The storm forms a huge, dusty wall over the city, reducing visibility. The scene shows the severe weather system in an American Southwest city during the summer months.

pages.text: Health Threats When sandstorms and dust storms strike, they can make life very unpleasant. Blowing dust forces people to stay indoors. High winds can knock out electrical power. Drivers may also face great risk. The blinding dust from Drivers in Kuwait, in the Middle East, faced dangerous conditions a sudden storm can during a sandstorm in 2014. result in car accidents. To stay safe, officials ask vehicles to pull off the road until a dust storm clears. However, the worst effects of SDS events usually appear after storms pass. Around three million people die each year due to air pollution. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that some of those people become sick as a result of SDS events. However, it is difficult to tell the number of people who suffer as a direct result of sandstorms and dust storms. As a preventive measure, WHO recommends that people wear masks if they must walk or work outdoors during an SDS event. In particular, those with asthma or lung and heart problems are asked to stay indoors.
pages.brief: Drivers in Kuwait face dangerous conditions during a sandstorm in 2014. Blinding dust sweeps across the road, making it hard to see. Vehicles are shown in the storm as officials would ask them to pull off the road until it clears. People may need masks outdoors.

pages.text: Other major threats from SDS events are bacteria, viruses, and fungal spores that sand and dust particles can carry. Once lifted into the atmosphere, these particles become easier to inhale. Research indicates that SDS events can spread serious infections great distances. In North Africa, for example, these storms have been linked to thousands of cases of meningococcal meningitis (muh-nin-juh-KAH-kuhl meh-nin-JY-tiss). This serious bacterial infection of the brain and spinal cord can result in death. In the American Southwest and northern Mexico, dust storms sometimes carry fungal spores that cause an illness called valley fever. Symptoms include chest pain, coughing, rashes, and respiratory infections. A woman in Beijing, China, In some cases, valley fever protects herself during can also result in death. a sandstorm in 2010. Africa in the Amazon Not all dust storms bring bad news. Each year, winds carry about 18 million metric tonnes (20 million tn.) of dust from Africa’s Sahara Desert across the Atlantic Ocean. Much of it settles in South America, including around the Amazon River. The African dust delivers important nutrients that the Amazon area lacks. Without that dust, the Amazon would not be a lush rainforest.
pages.brief: A woman in Beijing, China, protects herself during a sandstorm in 2010. She wears a mask and covers her face as dust blows around her. The scene shows a person outdoors in the storm. Dust particles can carry bacteria, viruses, and fungal spores that people may inhale.

pages.text: Losing Soil Sandstorms and dust storms pose a different kind of threat to farmland and food production. The most vulnerable areas affected have little plant life to prevent erosion —the process of soil being washed away by water or ice or blown away by wind. The roots of trees, bushes, and grasses usually hold soil in place. Without them, erosion can cause soil to disappear once a sandstorm or dust storm blows through. Dry conditions can turn topsoil into dust. Plants need this layer of earth to get the nutrients they need to grow. When winds strip away topsoil, the remaining land is bare and impossible to cultivate. In the United States, Bowl in the 1930s offers The Dust Bowl was one of the major causes of the Great Depression. During that time, many Americans faced hunger and homelessness. do to land. Farmers in the Plains states, located in the middle of the country, suffered a severe drought throughout the 1930s. Beginning in 1934, major dust storms made conditions even worse.
pages.brief: Farmers in the Plains states of the United States suffer through a severe drought in the 1930s. Dry conditions turn topsoil into dust, and winds strip it away. The bare land is left impossible to cultivate. The Dust Bowl is shown as a threat to farmland and food production.

pages.text: In the most affected areas, animals died because they couldn’t breathe. Houses were also half buried in dirt. By 1940, some 2.5 million people had left Dust Bowl areas to start fresh somewhere else. In response to this crisis, the U.S. government started programs to help rural areas. Efforts included education to teach farmers better ways to protect the soil and prevent erosion. Another major threat of SDS events is the spread of deserts, a process known as desertification. Every year, topsoil near the edges of deserts dries out and blows away. This causes desert areas to expand. Frequent and severe SDS events cause this process to intensify. China’s State Environmental Protection Administration has noted that the country is losing almost a million acres of farmland each year. In parts of Asia, Africa, and the Middle East, desertification is forcing farmers and villagers off their land. Without healthy soil, fields and gardens can no longer grow food. A farmer in Yemen, in the Middle East, herds his animals during a drought in 2014.
pages.brief: A farmer in Yemen, in the Middle East, herds his animals during a drought in 2014. The land is dry and bare. In other affected areas, animals died, houses were half buried in dirt, and millions of people left Dust Bowl areas. Desertification forces farmers and villagers off their land.

pages.text: Ways to Settle the Dust The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) monitors sandstorms and dust storms around the world. It warns that the number and intensity of these storms are rising. It worries that the increase in storms is a troubling sign of climate change. Normal, gradual climate change is a natural process. Over a long period of time, the amount of energy produced by the Sun changes. However, Earth is currently warming at an alarming rate. Most scientists blame certain human activities for causing climate change. The mass destruction of forests and the burning of fossil fuels, such as oil and coal, are two major examples. As long as global temperatures continue to rise, the threat of stronger and more frequent SDS events remains constant. Wowser!!! Scientists are fascinated by dust storms on planets other than Earth, such as Mars. Some of these storms grow so large that they go around the entire planet. They can even be seen through telescopes on Earth. Martian dust can make space missions to the Red Planet difficult. It sticks to equipment and blocks solar panels An artist made this image of that recharge electrical batteries. what a dust storm on Mars might look like.
pages.brief: An artist imagines what a dust storm on Mars might look like. A huge storm covers the Red Planet, with dust filling the sky. Martian dust can stick to equipment and block solar panels that recharge batteries. Scientists study these storms through telescopes and space missions.

pages.text: WMO officials encourage communities and countries to do more to prepare for SDS events. One way to reduce the negative effects of future SDS events is to protect vulnerable land, mainly by reducing erosion. People and governments are fighting desertification by planting and reforesting at-risk areas. Well-placed rows of trees and shrubs serve as windbreaks capable of blocking strong winds. They also hold dirt and moisture in place. Farmers in West Africa have been planting and caring for trees that help preserve soil and crops, and help prevent the Sahara Desert from encroaching on more farmland. Efforts have restored millions of acres of trees to hold back the desert. Improved forecasting and A woman plants a tree monitoring of SDS events can for the Great Green Wall project. This project also help limit the damage they cause. Like other types along the Sahara Desert. of weather reports, forecasts can alert people of storm conditions so they can take precautions. Monitoring sandstorms and dust storms also leads to the collection of valuable data about where and how they form, their behaviors, and their impacts.
pages.brief: A woman plants a tree for the Great Green Wall project along the Sahara Desert. She works to help hold soil and moisture in place. Rows of trees and shrubs can act as windbreaks that block strong winds. Farmers in West Africa plant and care for trees to protect soil and crops.

pages.text: A sandstorm from the Sahara Desert turned snow in Russia and eastern Europe orange. When the Dust Blows Climate scientists have noted a rise in sandstorm and dust storm activity in the last fifteen years. They have also reported an alarming growth of arid regions around the world. Warmer global temperatures are causing more frequent and more powerful thunderstorms and winds. With these strong winds come more frequent SDS events. The stage has been set for a sandier, dustier, and stormier future in the driest parts of the world. Changing the conditions that contribute to this surge in SDS events will require substantial global efforts, including new ideas and long-term planning.
pages.brief: A sandstorm from the Sahara Desert carries dust that turns snow in Russia and eastern Europe orange. The colored snow lies on the ground. Climate scientists note a rise in sandstorm and dust storm activity and a growth of arid regions. Warmer global temperatures bring more powerful thunderstorms and winds.

books.title: Mount Fuji
books.art_why: Drawing suits the volcano diagrams, legend, and historical artwork in this book.

pages.text: Mount Fuji gets unusual cloud formations because of wind blowing off the ocean that hits the mountain and is forced upward. This one is known as a cap cloud.
pages.brief: Mount Fuji rises above the land with a broad cap cloud around its peak. Wind blows in from the ocean, strikes the mountain, and is forced upward. Snow lies on the upper slopes, and the sky around the summit shows the cloud spreading outward.

pages.text: Important religious shrines and cherry blossoms dot the landscape around Mount Fuji. Peaceful Mountain Earth’s tallest mountains are known for their high winds, cold temperatures, and steep cliffs of rock and ice. They often look like harsh, unwelcoming places. The opposite is true of Japan’s highest mountain. Although scientists consider it an active volcano, Mount Fuji conveys a sense of peace and calm. Snowcapped for most of the year, it is considered one of the most beautiful mountains in the world. For many Japanese people, Mount Fuji is not just a mountain, however. It’s also a symbol of their country and a place of worship. Throughout history, Mount Fuji has been a source of inspiration. It continues to inspire people today.
pages.brief: Mount Fuji, snowcapped for most of the year, rises calmly above a landscape dotted with religious shrines and cherry blossoms. The mountain looks peaceful rather than harsh. Around it, the scene suggests a place of worship and inspiration, with cherry trees in bloom near the base.

pages.text: The Formation of Mount Fuji The eruption of Old Fuji covered Komitake with lava. The eruption of New Fuji covered both of the older volcanoes. Geology Mount Fuji is a cone-shaped volcano. It is located where three huge plates in Earth’s crust meet. Its volcanic activity is caused by the Pacific Plate moving beneath the Philippine Plate and melting from the heat below. According to a Buddhist legend, an earthquake created Mount Fuji in 286 bce. In reality, it formed over a very long period of time. Its base is thought to have formed about sixty-five million years ago. The modern-day mountain mainly formed as a result of lava building up over hundreds of thousands of years.
pages.brief: A cutaway view shows Mount Fuji as a cone-shaped volcano where three huge crustal plates meet. Layered lava from Old Fuji covers Komitake, and lava from New Fuji covers both older volcanoes. The Pacific Plate moves beneath the Philippine Plate and melts from heat below.

pages.text: Mount Fuji has erupted more than seventy times in the last 2,200 years. The largest eruption in recorded history took place in 864 ce. The most recent large eruption occurred in 1707, less than two months after a massive earthquake. It caused enormous clouds of volcanic ash to fall on the city of Edo (modern-day Tokyo). It also destroyed villages and farmland nearby and caused a ten- year famine. Mount Fuji has been dormant since then. However, it is considered active, meaning that scientists expect it to erupt again. Mount Fuji’s base is roughly 50 kilometers (30 mi.) in diameter. The crater is about 500 meters (1,600 ft.) from one side to the other.
pages.brief: Mount Fuji erupts, sending enormous clouds of volcanic ash over the city of Edo and nearby villages and farmland. Lava and ash spread across the slopes. The mountain’s broad base and wide crater are visible, and the scene suggests the long history of eruptions and the mountain’s dormant but active state.

pages.text: After an enormous earthquake struck Japan in 2011, scientists became concerned that Mount Fuji might erupt. Large earthquakes near volcanoes often signal that an eruption is coming. An increase in volcanic activity was measured, but no eruption followed. However, since Mount Fuji is so close to Tokyo, one of the world’s largest cities, officials put new safety measures into effect. These include a new evacuation plan for more than a million people who might need to escape quickly. In addition, careful monitoring of Mount Fuji and a warning system are in place. Lava, airborne ash, and fast-moving masses of hot rocks and gases are all hazards if the mountain erupts. Mount Fuji is visible from Tokyo on clear days.
pages.brief: Scientists monitor Mount Fuji after a large earthquake, watching for signs of an eruption. A warning system and evacuation plan are in place for more than a million people near Tokyo. Lava, airborne ash, and fast-moving masses of hot rocks and gases are shown as hazards, while the mountain stands visible from the city on a clear day.

pages.text: Mount Fuji’s Vegetation Zones Plants and Animals Many different kinds of plants grow on Mount Fuji’s slopes. The steady increase in elevation creates ever colder habitats going up the mountain. Temperature is an important factor in which kinds of plants can grow in each vegetation zone. The mountainous zone contains trees such as beech, oak, maple, cedar, and fir. A dense forest known as Aokigahara (ou-kee-gah-HAH-rah) (“Sea of Trees”) and the Asagiri (ah-SAH-gee-ree) highland—grasslands with cattle ranches—are both located here. Hemlock and fir trees grow at lower altitudes, and birch and larch grow higher up. No trees grow above roughly 2,200 meters (7,218 ft.) in elevation. The alpine zone usually has snow and subzero temperatures. Only mosses and lichens grow here.
pages.brief: Mount Fuji’s slopes rise through changing vegetation zones. Dense forest with beech, oak, maple, cedar, and fir covers the mountainous zone, along with Aokigahara’s Sea of Trees and the Asagiri highland grasslands. Hemlock and fir grow lower, birch and larch higher, and above roughly 2,200 meters only mosses and lichens survive in snow and subzero cold.

pages.text: Mount Fuji is home to thirty- seven types of mammals. These include the Japanese serow, a type of well as Japanese deer and occasional Japanese serows (suh-ROHS) live in forests in the mountainous zone. Asiatic black bears. More common are Japanese squirrels and foxes. They live in many habitats, from the base of the mountain to near the top of the subalpine zone. More than a hundred types of birds breed around Mount Fuji’s base because of the wide variety of habitats. A few kinds of birds live on the mountain year-round. Others migrate through the area or are summer or winter residents. The few amphibians and reptiles include one kind of tree frog. The mountainous zone contains the most insects, including many kinds of butterflies. Japanese paradise flycatchers live on the lower slopes of Mount Fuji. A male’s tail can be three times as long as its body.
pages.brief: Forests on Mount Fuji’s slopes are home to Japanese deer, occasional Japanese serows, Asiatic black bears, squirrels, and foxes. Many birds breed around the base, including Japanese paradise flycatchers with males’ very long tails. A tree frog represents the few amphibians and reptiles, while butterflies and many insects live in the mountainous zone.

pages.text: This Shinto shrine is devoted to the spirit of Mount Fuji. Sacred Symbol Mount Fuji is Japan’s sacred symbol. It has been seen as a sacred mountain for as long as people have lived in Japan. Early people built a shrine around 800 ce near Mount Fuji’s base. They hoped it would calm the god they believed was responsible for the volcano’s eruptions. Japan’s two main religions, Shinto and Buddhism, both consider Mount Fuji sacred. Shinto practitioners believe the mountain is the home of the goddess Konohana Sakuya Hime (koh-noh-HAH-nah SAH-koo-yah HEE-meh). Her name means “the Goddess of the Flowering Trees,” and her symbol is cherry blossoms. Many shrines built in her honor are located at the base and summit of Mount Fuji as well as at the bottom of the crater. Buddhists refer to Mount Fuji’s summit as zenjo, which means “a perfect state of meditation.” Both religions consider it important for worshippers to climb the mountain as a religious pilgrimage.
pages.brief: A Shinto shrine near Mount Fuji is devoted to the spirit of the mountain. Shinto practitioners honor Konohana Sakuya Hime, goddess of flowering trees, whose symbol is cherry blossoms. Shrines stand at the base, summit, and bottom of the crater. Buddhists call the summit zenjo, a perfect state of meditation, and worshippers climb as a pilgrimage.

pages.text: Naming the Mountain No one knows for sure how Mount Fuji got its name. A Japanese folktale links the mountain with the concept of eternal life, or fu-shi (foo-SHEE) (“not death”). Another possibility is that it is named for Fuchi, the goddess of fire of the Ainu, Japan’s first people. Today, people in Japan call the mountain Fuji-san, Fujiyama, or Fuji no Yama (san and yama both mean “mountain”). Artist Katsushika Hokusai (kaht-SOOSH-kah HAWK-sie) (1760–1849) focused on Mount Fuji as a symbol of everlasting life. His woodcut prints titled Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji (1826–1833) are Japan’s best-known artwork. Hokusai later added ten more prints to that collection and also created One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji in 1834. The Great Wave off Kanagawa by Katsushika Hokusai features Mount Fuji in the background and is one of the most famous pieces of art in the world.
pages.brief: A woodcut-style scene recalls Katsushika Hokusai’s famous artwork. A great wave rises off Kanagawa with Mount Fuji small in the background. Hokusai focused on Mount Fuji as a symbol of everlasting life in Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji and later One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji. The mountain also appears in a Japanese folktale about eternal life.

pages.text: Many people report that Mount Fuji is much more beautiful when seen from a distance. Much of its surface is barren volcanic rock and dust. Visiting Mount Fuji Mount Fuji is one of Japan’s most popular tourist sites and may be the most climbed mountain in the world. As many as four hundred thousand people climb Mount Fuji each year. Close to two-thirds are Japanese. Climbing Mount Fuji is not difficult by mountain-climbing standards, and no special equipment is required. The hike up is more like backpacking than mountain climbing. It’s still challenging, though, as the trails are rocky and the weather changes often and is windy. Paved roads go halfway up the mountain, and public transportation is available to the 5th station, at 2,305 meters (7,562 ft.). Four main trails go up from there. Depending on the trail, it can take between four and ten hours to ascend and about half that time to descend.
pages.brief: Many visitors climb Mount Fuji along rocky trails, carrying backpacks rather than special equipment. Paved roads and public transportation reach the 5th station, where four main trails begin. Hikers ascend and descend through windy, changeable weather. It is a popular tourist site: as many as four hundred thousand people climb each year, close to two-thirds of them Japanese.

pages.text: Lakes often create stunning views of Mount Fuji, as this reflected sunset shows. Mount Fuji’s official climbing season is early or mid-July to mid-September. During that time, trails and services are open, the weather is fairly mild, and the mountain is usually free of snow. The mountain is crowded during climbing season, and people often must line up and wait to get through certain areas. Winter climbing conditions are very difficult and are only recommended for the most experienced climbers. Reaching the summit isn’t the only reason to travel to Mount Fuji. Visitors also enjoy seeing the lakes and shrines along the way. Other popular activities include visiting Shiraito Falls, which is considered one of Japan’s most beautiful waterfalls. Nearby Mount Tenjo offers a great view for photographing Mount Fuji.
pages.brief: A lake reflects Mount Fuji at sunset, creating a stunning view. During the official climbing season, trails and services are open, the weather is fairly mild, and the mountain is usually free of snow, though people may line up in crowded areas. Visitors also enjoy lakes, shrines, Shiraito Falls, and the view from nearby Mount Tenjo.

pages.text: So Much to Offer Mount Fuji is a symbol of peace and calm around the world. At the same time, it is an active volcano, which makes it a symbol of nature’s power and danger as well. For some, seeing Mount Fuji is a spiritual experience. Its ever- changing beauty inspires artists, photographers, and poets. Its natural habitats make it an ideal spot for many different plants and animals to live. Its habitats also make Mount Fuji a place of great interest to hikers and nature lovers. With so much to offer to so many different people, it’s no wonder that Mount Fuji is one of the most beloved places on Earth. Special Views of Mount Fuji A few times a year, Mount Fuji’s summit lines up with the rising or setting Sun, creating a dramatic star-shaped flash of light known as a Diamond Fuji. When viewed from the far side of a lake, the reflection creates a Double Diamond Fuji. And when the Moon lines up with the peak, that’s a Pearl Fuji. Pearl Fuji.
pages.brief: Mount Fuji is a symbol of peace and calm, and of nature’s power and danger. Artists, photographers, and poets draw inspiration from its changing beauty; hikers and nature lovers value its habitats. A rare star-shaped flash at the summit is Diamond Fuji, a lake reflection creates Double Diamond Fuji, and the Moon creates Pearl Fuji.

books.title: Rachel Carson
books.art_why: A named famous person from history is best shown in cartoon-style biography illustrations.

pages.text: AN EARLY WARNING For months, Rachel Carson had been reading the research coming across her desk. The year was 1945, and she worked as a scientist and editor in chief for the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service. It was her job to edit the department’s reports. Other wildlife biologists were raising concerns about a common pesticide known as DDT. DDT killed mosquitoes and other pests. However, researchers reported that wherever it was sprayed, birds and other wildlife were also dying. Tests raised concerns about its long-term effects on humans as well, but government officials ignored these reports. That July, Carson wrote to Reader’s Digest, a popular American magazine. She proposed writing an article about DDT and its negative effects. The publication was not interested, so Carson turned to other work. Twelve years later, DDT was being used more than ever, and it again came to Carson’s attention. By this time, however, she was a best-selling author. She would use her new fame to help protect the natural world she loved. How? By telling people the truth.
pages.brief: In a 1945 office, Rachel Carson sits at a desk of research reports, editing for the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service. Reports warn that DDT kills pests but also birds and wildlife. Carson writes to Reader’s Digest proposing an article; the magazine declines. Twelve years later, now a best-selling author, she returns to DDT to tell the truth.

pages.text: In 1925, Rachel Carson enrolled at a nearby college. She arrived there planning to study English, but a biology course changed her life, and the professor became a mentor to Carson as well as a lifelong friend. Carson switched her degree to zoology—the study of animal life—and excelled. She graduated with high honors in June 1929. As a teenage girl, Carson had fallen in love with the sea through books. The summer after graduation, she visited the ocean for the first time. She was invited to do research at a marine biology lab on the coast of Massachusetts. Carson attended the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, which is dedicated to the study of marine science.
pages.brief: At a nearby college in 1925, young Rachel Carson arrives planning to study English. A biology course changes her life; she switches to zoology and graduates with high honors in June 1929. That summer she visits the ocean for the first time, joining research at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution on the Massachusetts coast.

pages.text: Once there, she studied marine creatures up close and in their natural habitats. For Carson, it was a summer of bliss surrounded by aquatic scientists. She later credited her time there as inspiration for her work. Carson had already been accepted at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, Maryland, for further studies in zoology. However, money problems continued to weigh on her family. Rachel’s parents moved to Baltimore to live with her. Working as a lab assistant, she became the family’s as she continued her studies. In 1932, Carson master’s degree. She had hoped to go on and get her Carson in 1932 highest degree possible—but two years later she was forced to quit the program for financial reasons. Carson’s love of writing soon came into play.
pages.brief: At Woods Hole, Carson studies marine creatures up close in their natural habitats, surrounded by aquatic scientists. She is accepted at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore but family money problems continue. Her parents move in with her while she works as a lab assistant. She earns her master’s degree in 1932, then leaves further study for financial reasons.

pages.text: HEROINES of ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE Rachel Carson and other female ecologists have often had to struggle for respect and recognition. Despite this, women have made great contributions to the environmental movement. Here are a few. Marjory Stoneman Douglas (1890–1998) Douglas was a determined defender of Florida’s wetlands. Her 1947 book The Everglades: River of Grass helped save that important ecosystem from development. Margaret Thomas Murie (1902–2003) For almost forty years, Murie studied the wilderness and wildlife of Alaska and Wyoming. She helped establish the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and campaigned for federal protections Murie in 1974 of other wilderness areas. Wangari Maathai (1940–2011) Maathai was a biologist from Kenya who founded the Green Belt Movement. The program trained Kenyan women to plant trees and restore deforested areas. For her work in conservation and women’s rights, she was awarded the 2004 Nobel Peace Prize. Jane Goodall (1934–2025) Goodall pioneered the study of wild chimpanzees in Tanzania. She was an international champion for the preservation of wildlife and animal habitats. Greta Thunberg (2003–) The young activist has inspired an international student movement demanding that governments address climate Thunberg in 2019 change.
pages.brief: Rachel Carson appears with other female ecologists who struggled for respect. Marjory Stoneman Douglas defends Florida’s wetlands; Margaret Thomas Murie studies Alaska and Wyoming wilderness; Wangari Maathai plants trees with Kenyan women; Jane Goodall observes wild chimpanzees in Tanzania; Greta Thunberg leads a climate protest.

pages.text: THE WRITER AND THE SEA In 1936, Carson took a part-time position in Washington, D.C., in what would become the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service (FWS). She was first tasked with writing short radio scripts about marine life. A year later, she was named an assistant aquatic biologist. The position allowed Carson to combine her scientific knowledge and writing talent. She explained complex environmental science in ways the average reader could not just understand but also enjoy. Carson excelled and soon rose to the position of editor in chief of all publications. On the side, she wrote science articles for magazines and newspapers to bring in extra cash. Her father had died in 1935, but Carson was still supporting her mother and other family members. In 1941, Carson published her first book, Under the Sea Wind. With poetic style, it described marine life in the sea and along Under the Sea Wind the seashore. Book critics praised it for being beautifully written and scientifically accurate. However, Americans had turned their attention to fighting World War II (1939–1945), and it did not sell as well as Carson had hoped.
pages.brief: In 1936 Washington, D.C., Rachel Carson writes radio scripts about marine life for the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service. She becomes an assistant aquatic biologist and later editor in chief, explaining complex science clearly. She supports her family after her father’s 1935 death. Her first book, Under the Sea Wind, is praised in 1941, but World War II distracts readers.

pages.text: Carson did not realize it yet, but she was in an ideal place for her life’s work. Her projects sharpened her writing skills to a fine point. At the same time, she was studying the latest research by expert scientists. When vacations were possible, she and her mother escaped to the seashore. There, Carson would lose herself watching birds, exploring tidal pools, and tramping across mud flats in search of natural wonders. In 1951, Carson published The Sea Around Us. Like her previous title, it took readers on a voyage across and into the ocean using clear yet graceful language. Experts and nonexperts loved it, and critics praised it in glowing terms. This time, her book was a huge success. The Sea Around Us landed on the New York Times best-seller list, where it stayed for eighty-six weeks. Carson won the National Book Award for Nonfiction as well as other important prizes. Carson receives the National Book Award for Nonfiction in 1952.
pages.brief: At work, Carson sharpens her writing while studying new scientific research. On vacations she and her mother escape to the seashore, where she watches birds, explores tidal pools, and crosses mud flats. In 1951 The Sea Around Us becomes a huge best-seller, stays on the New York Times list for eighty-six weeks, and wins the National Book Award.

pages.text: Her earnings allowed her to leave the FWS in 1952 to write full-time. She also built a cottage on the rugged coast of Maine. There, the ocean was right outside her door. Carson had many Carson in 1952 other subjects she wished to write about. One in particular would turn out to be her most important work of all. RACHEL’S REFUGE The Rachel Carson National Wildlife Refuge was established in 1966, not far from the cottage where Carson spent her summers. The refuge stretches along 50 miles (80 km) of coastline near Kennebunkport, Maine. It protects important wetlands and coastal habitat used by migratory birds and other wildlife. The refuge welcomes about three hundred thousand bird-watchers and other nature lovers each year.
pages.brief: With her earnings, Carson leaves the Fish & Wildlife Service in 1952 to write full-time and builds a cottage on Maine’s rugged coast. Nearby, the Rachel Carson National Wildlife Refuge is established in 1966. It stretches along fifty miles of coastline near Kennebunkport, protecting wetlands for migratory birds and welcoming about three hundred thousand nature lovers yearly.

pages.text: A BOOK THAT STARTED A MOVEMENT The future of science and technology seemed bright after World War II. Scientists had released the power of atoms to create atomic bombs and nuclear energy. In medicine, antibiotics were saving countless lives by killing infections. There seemed to be no challenge that science couldn’t meet. Controlling destructive insects was one of those challenges. Pesticides such as DDT were the main weapon in this battle. Trucks would roll down neighborhood streets and spray the chemical over houses and gardens. Aircraft dropped it on forests and fields. Government officials said there was nothing to worry about. In July 1945, a young beachgoer is sprayed with DDT as a new machine is tested for the first time.
pages.brief: After World War II, science seems bright: atomic power and antibiotics save lives. Controlling destructive insects becomes a challenge, with DDT as the weapon. Trucks spray neighborhoods and aircraft drop chemicals on forests and fields. Officials say there is nothing to worry about. In July 1945, a young beachgoer is sprayed with DDT during a new machine’s first test.

pages.text: Salmon and butterflies were among the many victims of DDT. By 1957, though, Carson’s doubts about pesticides had been renewed. She had read the reports about DDT during her time with the FWS. Now she was hearing reports from biologists and naturalists. They described dead and dying bird populations in places where DDT was used. Fish were being poisoned. Helpful insects like butterflies and bees were dying, too. Carson began collecting information for a new book. Her research revealed the likelihood that the chemicals in pesticides and herbicides could cause serious illness in humans, too, including cancer. Still, Carson knew her evidence had to be rock solid. She would be questioning whether huge chemical companies were poisoning people as well as wildlife. Her friends warned her that these giant businesses would do everything in their power to destroy her reputation. As she finished her drafts, she sent every chapter to experts for them to fact-check.
pages.brief: Salmon and butterflies are among DDT’s victims. By 1957 Carson’s doubts are renewed as biologists report dying birds, poisoned fish, and dead helpful insects wherever DDT is used. She begins a new book, gathers evidence that the chemicals may seriously harm humans, and sends each chapter to experts for fact-checking. Friends warn that chemical companies will attack her reputation.

pages.text: Even as she continued this work, Carson faced serious personal challenges. In 1957, one of her nieces died, leaving Carson to care for her young great-nephew. A year later, her beloved mother passed away. Then in 1960, Carson learned she had cancer. Progress on the book was slowed by surgery, treatments, and periods of intense pain. In September 1962, Silent Spring was released. The title described a world where birds and insects no longer sang or buzzed because chemicals had wiped them out. In the book, Carson carefully laid The chickadee is one of many birds discussed in Silent Spring. out the scientific evidence about the impact of pesticides and herbicides on the environment. It also raised questions about ways they might harm human health. Silent Spring stayed on the best-seller list for more than a year. It ignited a national debate about the safety of using chemicals to control nature. Carson’s third book has been translated into more than thirty languages.
pages.brief: Carson faces personal challenges: a niece dies in 1957, leaving her to care for a young great-nephew; her mother dies in 1958; and in 1960 she learns she has cancer. Surgery and treatments slow her work. In September 1962 Silent Spring is released, describing a world without birdsong or buzzing insects, laying out pesticide evidence, and igniting a national debate.

pages.text: Carson testifies before a Senate subcommittee in June 1963. Carson did not call for a total ban on these chemicals. However, she did urge the government to test them more carefully and regulate them more closely. She also urged readers to consider the long- term dangers of poisoning the environment. Again, she displayed her talent for explaining complex science in ways that nonscientists could grasp. As predicted, chemical manufacturers attacked. They criticized Carson’s research and qualifications—some simply because she was a woman. She was accused of being antibusiness and a nature fanatic. They said she would rather see people starve than use chemicals to make sure there was enough to eat.
pages.brief: In June 1963, Rachel Carson testifies before a Senate subcommittee. She does not call for a total ban but urges closer testing and regulation of pesticides and asks readers to consider the long-term dangers of poisoning the environment. Chemical manufacturers attack her research and qualifications, some because she is a woman, calling her antibusiness and a nature fanatic.

pages.text: In the months that followed, Carson calmly explained her position in speeches and interviews. Other scientists defended her research and conclusions. Despite her failing health, Carson testified before members of the U.S. Senate. President John F. Kennedy and other political leaders pointed to Silent Spring as proof that the government needed to study environmental policies more carefully. In the summer of 1963, Carson and her great- nephew returned to the coast of Maine for a much- needed break. Her cottage there was her favorite place in the world. It would be her last visit. Carson looks down the coast in 1961.
pages.brief: In speeches and interviews, Carson explains her position while other scientists defend her research. Despite failing health, she testifies before the U.S. Senate; President John F. Kennedy and political leaders point to Silent Spring as proof the government must study environmental policies more carefully. In summer 1963, Carson and her great-nephew return to her Maine cottage for a last visit.

pages.text: THE TROUBLE WITH DDT In 1939, the Swiss scientist Paul Müller developed what seemed like a miracle pesticide: dichloro-diphenyl- trichloroethane, or DDT for short. It killed insects but seemed to leave birds and other animals unharmed. It helped stop large outbreaks of insect-spread diseases such as malaria and typhus. Müller was awarded the Nobel Prize for his research. DDT was used widely to control insect pests in the 1940s and 1950s. However, biologists eventually found that its poisons built up in BIOMAGNIFICATION OF DDT the tissues of animals, a process called seemed harmless at first caused problems over time. For birds, it left their eggs brittle and prone to breaking. Some bird populations fell by more than 80 percent, including bald eagles, the U.S. national bird. pages.brief: In 1939 scientist Paul Müller develops DDT, which kills insects but seems harmless to animals and helps stop malaria and typhus. DDT is used in the 1940s and 1950s. Biologists find its poisons build up in tissues, making bird eggs brittle and causing bald eagles to decline. Silent Spring spotlights DDT; the U.S. bans it in 1972, and species rebound.

pages.text: A ROLE MODEL FOR TODAY “ Conservation is a cause that has no end,” Carson said in a 1963 speech. “There is no point at which we will say ‘our work is finished.’” She died the next year, but her vision of protecting the natural world lived on. In fact, it took on a life of its own. It is no exaggeration to say that Silent Spring helped inspire the environmental movement that followed. More Americans questioned the use of pesticides as well as uncontrolled pollution. Carson’s writing contributed to new laws to protect wilderness and wildlife as well as people. They included the Clean Air Act (1963), the Wilderness Act (1964), the Clean Water Act (1972), and the Endangered Species Act (1972). The pesticide DDT caused the number of bald eagles in the continental United States to plummet. By 1963, just 417 pairs were found nesting there. Today, thanks in part to Rachel Carson, that number is nearly 10,000.
pages.brief: Carson says conservation is a cause with no end; she dies the next year, but her vision lives on. Silent Spring helps inspire the environmental movement. More Americans question pesticides and pollution, and her writing contributes to laws protecting air, water, wilderness, wildlife, and people. DDT reduced bald eagle nesting pairs to 417 by 1963; today nearly 10,000 nest.

pages.text: Carson’s environmentalism grew out of her love of nature. She was fascinated by the beauty and science of ecosystems. Her life’s work was communicating that joy, believing that people would protect what they loved. She thought of humans as belonging to the natural world, not as its enemies. Carson and a cat keep company at her home in Maine in 1961. Today, wilderness areas and wildlife populations continue to shrink. Threats to the environment are greater than ever, including the global danger of climate change. At the same time, environmental awareness and activism have grown. With her determination, courage, and passion, Rachel Carson remains a hero and role model for the challenges we face.
pages.brief: Carson’s environmentalism grows from her love of nature. She spends her life communicating that joy, believing people will protect what they love and humans belong to the natural world. At her Maine home in 1961, she keeps company with a cat. Today wildlife shrinks and climate change threatens the planet, but environmental awareness makes Carson a hero and role model.

books.title: Money, Money, Money
books.art_why: Real money, banks, mints and museum coins all exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Money is worth much more than the paper it’s printed on. An ordinary piece of paper isn’t worth a lot, but a piece of paper money can be worth thousands of dollars. A check can be worth millions. Each printed bill is worth much more than the paper it’s printed on. But why? Where did money come from, and what makes money so valuable? Money is valuable because the people who make and use it agree that it is valuable. The government that issues it, the mint that strikes or prints it, the banks that hold it, and the people who buy and sell things with it all agree that money is worth something. The history of money is the fascinating story of how people changed from trading valuable objects to trading objects that represented their valuables. It also tells how technology creates “invisible money” that allows people to trade goods and materials around the world.
pages.brief: A plain sheet of paper lies beside a thick stack of printed bills and a single check on a desk, showing how one small piece of paper can stand for a fortune. Behind it, a mint prints bills, a bank holds them, and people buy and sell goods in a busy market.

pages.text: Currency let people trade objects without carrying them around. In order to get around the problems of bartering, people invented currency, or objects that represented certain values. For example, a group of people might agree that a cow was worth twenty shells and a large fish was worth two shells. People could trade goods for currency and vice versa. Each culture around the world chose a different item to represent the value of its goods. The objects people used for currency were almost always light enough to carry, but rare enough that people couldn’t just pick them up off the ground. The rarer the currency was and the more work it took to find it, the more valuable it was.
pages.brief: Two traders meet in an open marketplace and swap a cow for a pile of twenty shells, while a large fish is traded for two shells. Nearby, people carry strings of small, rare objects instead of hauling goods, showing how currency replaced bartering.

pages.text: Some of the items used as currency in ancient times were bright or colorful stones, shells, leaves, feathers, lumps of silver and gold, salt, spices, and gems. In ancient Rome, soldiers got paid with bags of salt. From Africa to Asia, people traded with rare speckled shells that were only found on a few islands in the Indian Ocean. Some Native Americans used wampum, or beads made from clam shells, to trade and make treaties. Other Native Americans used eagle feathers. The Chinese used bundles of tea leaves, and European colonists in North America used tobacco leaves as their currency. The problem with currency of this type was that it was hard to decide how much a particular object was worth. If one shell was much larger than another shell, shouldn’t it be worth more? And what if you met somebody who didn’t think your shells were worth anything at all? Do You Know? The biggest currency in the world is used by the Yap Islanders, who live on an equatorial island near Indonesia. They make coins of giant stones that weigh as much as full-grown Asian elephants. The stones have holes in them, and the Yap Islanders move the stones by putting sticks through the holes and rolling the coins.
pages.brief: Ancient traders display their currency: bright stones, speckled shells, eagle feathers, lumps of salt, spices and gems. Roman soldiers receive bags of salt, Native Americans hold clam-shell wampum beads and feathers, Chinese carry bundles of tea leaves, and colonists hold tobacco leaves. On a far island, huge stone coins with holes are rolled on sticks.

pages.text: These old coins were stamped with the king’s picture. One solution to the problems of using ordinary objects as currency was to make coins from precious metals. Precious metals are rare and valuable across cultures, and they are easily shaped and weighed. The first coins were minted, or produced, 2,600 years ago in Lydia, which is now a part of Turkey. From Lydia, coins quickly spread into the neighboring countries of Greece and Persia (now known as Iran). The earliest coins were hammered out of a natural combination of gold and silver called electrum. These coins were very rough and crude, with no patterns on the sides or standard sizes and weights. Later, coins were made from either pure gold or pure silver. They had standard weights, and the king’s seal was stamped on one side to confirm the coin’s quality.
pages.brief: A Lydia mintworker hammers a rough lump of electrum into one of the first coins, 2,600 years ago, in a workshop in what is now Turkey. Finished coins stamped with a king's seal stack beside him, and traders carry them onward to Greece and Persia.

pages.text: Early European coins usually had a god’s head on one side and a seal from the maker on the other. Later coins pictured the heads of kings and rulers, with elaborate symbols on the other side. These pictures helped establish when, where, and by whom the coin was made. Even today, you can see the faces of presidents, kings, and queens on modern coins. These Greek coins had words, a picture of an owl, and a portrait of the goddess Athena. The Chinese melted copper and poured it into molds where it hardened into coins. Chinese coins had holes in their centers, so thousands could be easily carried on a ribbon or a stick. Instead of pictures, the Chinese coins, called cash, had words telling their worth, or denomination. Only the government could produce coins. Chinese cash could be held on a string or stick for easy carrying.
pages.brief: A Greek silver coin rests beside an image of the goddess Athena and her owl, while a Chinese mint pours melted copper into molds. Rows of Chinese coins with square holes hang from a ribbon and a stick, ready to be carried.

pages.text: Coins are harder to make than you might think. Once the government decides to produce new coins, these are just some of the steps that must happen. 1 A designer draws a picture of the coin’s two sides on a large piece of paper. 2 Sculptors make a large, three-dimensional model of the coin. An engraving machine uses the model to make a die, or coin stamp. The die is sent to mints, or factories that produce coins. 3 Mints cut blank coins, called blanks, from a rolled-up sheet of the right kind of metal. The sheet can be as long as five football fields. 4 The blanks are heated, cooled, washed, and dried. 5 A machine called an upsetting mill creates the raised edge of the coin. 6 The coin press stamps the pattern from the die into the coin. 7 Inspectors make sure that there are no mistakes in the coin. Incorrectly made coins get melted down and recycled. 8 The coins are sent out to banks in armored trucks.
pages.brief: Coin makers work through their steps: a designer sketches, sculptors build a large model, an engraving machine cuts a die, and a long metal sheet is cut into blanks. Blanks are heated, washed and dried, an upsetting mill raises the edge, a press stamps the pattern, inspectors check, and armored trucks leave for banks.

pages.text: A Chinese man named Ts’ai Lun invented paper 1,900 years ago. But it wasn’t used for money until 700 years later when the Chinese government ran out of copper to produce coins. They switched to printing paper money. The earliest paper money was printed by hand by with ink onto rectangles of paper. Although coins were still available, the lighter paper popular. Early Chinese paper money In Europe, another invention changed the shape of money. Johannes Gutenberg invented the movable-type printing press in the mid-1400s. Gutenberg’s press allowed people to print paper money by machine, rather than by hand.
pages.brief: Ts'ai Lun presses wet pulp into a sheet of paper in ancient China. Centuries later, Chinese printers brush ink onto rectangles of paper money by hand. In Europe, Johannes Gutenberg stands at his movable-type printing press, running off printed sheets.

pages.text: The Value of Money Unlike gold or silver coins, paper money is worth very little by itself. It costs only four cents (U.S.) to print a bill, including the cost of the paper, ink, and the printer’s pay. So why is one piece of paper worth a hundred dollars? And why is another worth only one? Because the government says so. A hundred years ago, for each dollar in circulation, the government had one dollar’s worth of gold in a bank. This system was called the gold standard, because it ensured that every dollar represented its face value, or the number printed on it, in gold. Back then, you could trade your dollars for the same amount of gold at the bank. Banks used to keep bars of gold. They represented the sum of everyone’s money.
pages.brief: A printing press runs off a bill that costs only four cents in paper, ink and wages, while a bank vault behind holds stacked gold bars. A customer hands dollars across a counter to trade them for the same amount of gold.

pages.text: Do You Know? Travel from country to country has become so easy, and it can be a bother to change one country’s money to another country’s money every time you travel. Most of Europe’s nations have joined together to form the European Union. Many of them standardized their money so that the euro is worth the same amount in each nation. Each country mints euros. The tail side of the euro has a picture that symbolizes the country that made it. Most countries do not maintain the gold standard anymore. There are simply too many bills in circulation. They represent more wealth, goods, and valuables than there is gold in the world. Britain stopped using the gold standard in 1931, and the United States stopped forty years later. Today, governments keep track of how many goods and resources there are in a country and circulate enough money to represent those goods and resources. Depending on how many goods and resources the country produces and how successful its businesses are, the value of a country’s money can rise and fall compared to other countries’ currencies. This is called a floating currency system.
pages.brief: Travellers cross Europe with a pocket of euro coins and notes, each showing a different national symbol on its tail side. In a bank office, officials retire the gold standard and compare piles of different nations' notes to see whose value is rising or falling.

pages.text: Keeping Money Real Many agree that only the government can make currency because the government keeps track of the actual goods and resources that the currency represents. But what if people try to produce money on their own? Fake money, called counterfeit, isn’t worth anything because it isn’t backed up by goods or resources. Banks, stores, restaurants, and companies will not let you use counterfeit money. Worse, having counterfeit money in circulation hurts the value of everyone’s money—if there is fake money around, how do you know if your money is real or not? Try This! Get a dollar bill and pieces of paper, construction paper, cloth, and tissue paper. Cut the pieces of paper and cloth so that they are the same size and shape as the dollar bill. Now close your eyes and try to tell the real bill from the fake bills by touch. Cashiers and bank tellers who handle a lot of money can tell a real bill from a counterfeit just by feeling it. Could you do the same thing?
pages.brief: A cashier at a store counter and a bank teller both rub a bill between their fingers, checking whether it is real, while a counterfeiter's fake notes lie rejected to one side. On a table, a real dollar bill sits among cut paper, cloth and tissue copies.

pages.text: In order to defeat counterfeiters, most countries make their money using special, hard-to-copy tricks. Bills are printed on paper made with a secret formula. U.S. dollars are made of a mixture of about one-quarter linen and three-quarters cotton, with some red and blue fibers sprinkled throughout. However, the government keeps the exact formula a secret, the way Coca-Cola protects the secret recipe for their famous soda pop. A special thread below the portrait glows in ultraviolet, or “black,” light. Banks and some stores use special pens with ink that turns from black to yellow on real money, but stays black on fake money. The pictures and print on bills are designed to prevent easy copying. The portrait is large and detailed, placed slightly off-center, and made of very thin dashed lines. The patterns on the bill are small and complicated. Each bill has a serial number that shows when and where the bill was printed. In addition, many bills also have colored inks, magnetic inks, and inks that change color depending on the angle you look at them. Some bills have holograms or watermarks that produce an image only when you hold the bill up to the light.
pages.brief: A bill is held up to the light, showing a watermark and a security thread that glows under ultraviolet light. A bank teller draws a special pen across a note and the ink turns from black to yellow, beside a large portrait of fine dashed lines and tiny complicated patterns.

pages.text: Invisible Money: Checks and Credit Cards Most adults have checking accounts. Banks keep track of how much money a person has saved, and the person writes checks, or official notes, that stand for a certain amount. Checks can represent a large amount of money on one piece of paper. Many checking accounts also have debit cards that people can use to take cash from their accounts at ATMs or pay for things at shops and restaurants. Credit cards work like debit cards and checking accounts, except that instead of saving money in the bank, a person borrows the money from the bank. People use credit cards to buy items that cost more than they have in the bank. Then, they have to pay the money back, plus a fee called interest. If someone takes a long time to pay the money back, the interest gets bigger. Automatic teller machines, or ATMs, allow people to get cash from their accounts at any time.
pages.brief: An adult writes a check at a kitchen table, then uses a debit card at a shop counter and takes cash from an ATM on the street. Beside them, a shopper hands over a credit card to pay for something that costs more than the money in the bank.

pages.text: Debit and Debit and credit cards are made of durable plastic. The person’s name and an individual number are stamped onto one side, along with the name of the bank where the account is. A magnetic strip on the top has special encoded information about the person’s bank account. When the card is swiped through a card-reading machine, the machine electronically calls the bank to make sure that the account has enough money in it. If the money is there, the price is taken from the person’s account and moved to the store’s, restaurant’s, or company’s account. It is easier to carry around one piece of plastic than it is to carry many bills. Plus, since cards have your name and information on them, the money is harder to steal than bills are.
pages.brief: A plastic debit card lies face up with its magnetic strip along the top, and a customer swipes it through a card-reading machine at a store counter. The machine connects to the bank, moving the price from the shopper's account into the store's account.

pages.text: However, credit cards can be dangerous because people forget that they must pay back the money they borrowed. Many people who use credit cards irresponsibly owe so much money to the banks that the banks take back, or repossess, the things the person bought. Plastic cards are less visible than money, but they still buy the same goods. Our invisible money allows us to trade with people around the world. With the help of catalogs and the Internet, you can use a credit card to buy goods from a person or company in another country. Your money is changed into a currency the other person can use. Shopping online with a credit card can instantly send money across oceans.
pages.brief: A person sits with a stack of catalogs and a laptop, typing a card number to buy goods from a company overseas, while money changes into another country's currency. Nearby, a bank officer repossesses furniture from someone who borrowed too much and could not pay it back.

pages.text: Three thousand years ago, people bartered one good for another. Today, people trade with each other using bills, coins, and even invisible money. What sort of money do you think we’ll have in another three thousand years? At a stock market, people buy and sell stock. Stocks are pieces of companies. Stock costs more or less depending on the value of the company. But until the stock is sold, the money in it is not real.
pages.brief: Long ago, two people swap one good for another in an open marketplace. Today, a shopper taps a card and a trader in another country is paid. On a stock market floor, people buy and sell pieces of companies, and the price rises and falls with the company.

books.title: Special Effects
books.art_why: The book is about real filmmaking techniques and movie history, not a biography of one named famous person.

pages.text: Introduction The gigantic ape stands high above New York City on the very top of the Empire State Building. He holds a woman in one of his massive hands. The ape gently puts the woman inside the building, thumps his chest, and roars menacingly at the squadron of planes circling just outside his reach. He strikes out at one of the planes, sending it spiraling to the ground in a ball of fire. The other planes attack, firing bullets at the huge creature. Some of the bullets hit and the ape is badly wounded. He lets out one last roar and lets go of the building, falling to the street.
pages.brief: A gigantic ape stands high above New York City on top of the Empire State Building, holding a woman in one massive hand. He gently puts her inside the building, thumps his chest, and roars at circling planes. He strikes a plane, it spirals down in fire; bullets wound him and he falls.

pages.text: The scene we’ve described is from the movie King Kong and was made many decades ago! The movie would never have been possible if it hadn’t been for Willis O’Brien. A master of movie special effects in the 1920s and the 1930s, he helped create special-effects movies that audiences still love. A close-up of the gorilla model used in the 1933 film King Kong.
pages.brief: Willis O’Brien, a master of 1920s and 1930s movie special effects who helped create special-effects movies audiences still love today, stands beside a close-up of the gorilla model used in the 1933 film King Kong.

pages.text: So, what are special effects? Special effects are the part of moviemaking that creates, or makes, pictures and sounds that can make movies seem real. Special effects allow a superhero to rescue anyone, anywhere, at any time. Special effects can create alien spacecraft soaring toward Earth at an alarming speed. Special effects can make buildings crumble, tornadoes twist, and dinosaurs, long extinct, come alive. Movies, or moving pictures, work by capturing a series of still images and replaying them quickly one after the other. Dinosaurs appear to come to life in this special-effects scene from Jurassic Park III (2001).
pages.brief: Special effects create superhero rescues anywhere, alien spacecraft soaring toward Earth, crumbling buildings, twisting tornadoes, and extinct dinosaurs coming alive. Movies capture a series of still images and replay them quickly one after the other. A dinosaur appears to come to life in a special-effects scene from Jurassic Park III (2001).

pages.text: Stop-Motion Animation So, how did O’Brien make King Kong possible? First, he constructed several gorilla models using a metal skeleton with joints like those found in human knees and shoulders. He padded the joints with cotton and foam rubber. He then covered them with rabbit skins to resemble the beast’s fur. Next, O’Brien studied the movements of gorillas in zoos. He also attended professional wrestling matches looking for ideas of how to make his creature battle the dinosaurs and other huge animals on Skull Island, King Kong’s home.
pages.brief: O’Brien constructs several gorilla models with metal skeletons and joints like human knees and shoulders, padded with cotton and foam rubber, covered in rabbit skins to look like fur. He studies gorillas in zoos and attends professional wrestling matches for ideas of battles on Skull Island.

pages.text: O’Brien’s special-effects team then constructed detailed miniature sets, like a New York City street, to provide the backdrop for the animated models. Now it was time for O’Brien to use the process he invented: stop-motion animation. With stop-motion animation, the miniature models were photographed one frame at a time and put into different positions for each frame. When each frame of the developed film was projected in sequence, the models appeared to move with the illusion of being alive.
pages.brief: O’Brien’s special-effects team builds detailed miniature sets, including a New York City street, as backdrops. O’Brien uses stop-motion animation: miniature models are photographed one frame at a time and repositioned for each frame. Projected in sequence, the developed film makes the models appear to move with the illusion of life.

pages.text: Award-winning special effects The following films were either nominated for or won the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences award for Visual Effects. The year each film was released is listed. Have you seen any of these movies? 2012 Life of Pi (winner) 2014 Interstellar (winner) 2015 Star Wars: The Force Awakens 2016 The Jungle Book 2017 Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 2018 Avengers: Infinity War 2019 The Lion King Special effects have been used in movies for more than 100 years. Georges Méliès, a French magician, invented some of the earliest special effects. In 1899 he directed a movie called The Conjurer and used special effects to make himself disappear. Some members of his audience were so terrified by what they saw that they actually fainted! Since then, many types of special-effects tricks have been created.
pages.brief: Georges Méliès, a French magician, uses special effects to make himself disappear in The Conjurer in 1899; some terrified audience members faint. Around him are scenes from award-winning films released from 2012 to 2019, including Life of Pi, Interstellar, and The Lion King.

pages.text: Rear Projection Rear projection is a type of special effect that creates fake scenery behind an actor. For example: to make it look like a person is driving a car on a beach, the beach scene is filmed first. Then the beach scene is projected onto a screen. A car and a driver are placed in front of the screen and filmed.
pages.brief: Rear projection creates fake scenery behind an actor. A beach scene is filmed first, then projected onto a screen. A car and a driver are placed in front of the screen and filmed, making it look like the person is driving on a beach.

pages.text: An actor flies through the air in front of a green screen. In the final shot, the background will be replaced with images of a busy market. Color-Replacement Photography With color-replacement photography, the movement of an actor or an animal, such as someone falling, is filmed in front of a chroma blue screen or a green screen. The background is shot at a different time. Then the action of an actor pretending to fall is layered on top of the colored screen. The color is then erased and the background becomes visible wherever the color was. This special effect is like cutting out the shape of an animal or an actor from a sheet of paper and pasting it onto different scenery, except the image is moving and so is the scenery!
pages.brief: An actor flies through the air in front of a green screen; in the final shot the background will be a busy market. With color-replacement photography, an actor or animal falling is filmed before a chroma blue or green screen, then layered over a separately shot background.

pages.text: This technique is used every day on most weather portions of the news on TV. The weather anchor stands in front of a color screen while a technician puts the image of a map behind the anchor. The image brought into the picture shows up on any area that is the same color as the screen. You will never see a weather anchor on TV dressed in the screen’s color. That might cause a weather map to appear where their body should be! The cast of Emmerdale goes white water rafting in front of a green screen. The background will be replaced with wild rapids.
pages.brief: A weather anchor stands before a color screen while a technician places an image of a map behind the anchor. The map appears on any area the same color as the screen. The cast of Emmerdale goes white water rafting in front of a green screen; wild rapids will replace the background.

pages.text: Animatronics The huge shark crunching Quint’s boat in Jaws and the endearing creepiness of E.T. are unforgettable images. The process known as animatronics was used to create E.T. as well as the shark in Jaws. Animatronics is a type of special effect that creates characters using electronic robots. A special-effects crew controls the robots’ movements through remote control.
pages.brief: The huge shark crunching Quint’s boat in Jaws and the endearing creepiness of E.T. are unforgettable images on film. Animatronics creates characters using electronic robots, and a special-effects crew controls the robots’ movements by remote control.

pages.text: Animators study the movements of real animals and people and try to copy the movements electronically. Because animatronic creatures appear to move like living creatures, they can be filmed interacting with the actors and real animals. The dinosaurs in Jurassic Park were just as scary as E.T. was endearing, due to effective animatronics. Word Wise The word animatronics was coined in 1961 by Walt Disney and comes from the words animate and electronics.
pages.brief: Animators study the movements of real animals and people and copy them electronically. Animatronic creatures move like living creatures and can be filmed interacting with actors and real animals. The dinosaurs in Jurassic Park are as scary as E.T. is endearing. Walt Disney coined the word animatronics in 1961 from animate and electronics.

pages.text: The actors riding the dragon highlight its size in Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows, Part 2 (2010). Miniature Models Miniature models are often used in place of real buildings or other large objects. On film, the models look life-size. Sets and props can be made extra large or small to make people seem tiny or large. Sets include such things as houses, cities, or jungles—anywhere the acting takes place. Props are objects like chairs or swords that actors use.
pages.brief: Actors riding a dragon highlight its size in Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows, Part 2 (2010). Miniature models replace real buildings or large objects and look life-size on film. Sets and props can be extra large or small to make people seem tiny or large; sets include houses, cities, or jungles, and props are objects like chairs or swords.

pages.text: Weather Special Effects Special effects are often used in movies to create weather conditions and natural disasters. For example, to film a violent storm at sea, actors do not need to go out in a real storm. That would be very dangerous. Instead, they can sit safely in a boat in a large pool or pond. A machine creates crashing waves in the water, huge fans produce powerful winds, and giant overhead sprinklers send down pouring rain. Filmmaker Ang Lee’s Life of Pi (2012) won an Academy Award for Visual Effects. One of the most challenging scenes to create was the storm scene. The tiger and the storm were created separately and then had to be meshed together. The scene is filmed in front of a blue screen, which can later be replaced with film of an actual storm. When snowstorms are needed in a movie, snowflakes can be made from bleached potato flakes, plastic flakes, or powdered laundry detergent.
pages.brief: To film a violent storm at sea, actors sit safely in a boat in a large pool or pond. A machine makes crashing waves, huge fans produce powerful winds, and giant overhead sprinklers send pouring rain. In Life of Pi, the tiger and storm are created separately and meshed in front of a blue screen.

pages.text: Encanto (2021) features amazing CGI to create the mountain landscape of Colombia and the characters’ fantastical abilities. Computer-Generated Images (CGI) Computer-generated images can be used to create almost any imaginable effect in a movie— blazing fires, giant waves, or talking dinosaurs. Once the images are created on the computer, they can be changed, moved, copied, and combined with other images for the movie. Computers helped revolutionize the world of special effects in movies. With computers, special-effects artists can create movie scenes never thought possible. Now, computer-generated images can be used to create an entire movie like The Polar Express.
pages.brief: Encanto (2021) uses amazing CGI to create the mountain landscape of Colombia and the characters’ fantastical abilities. Computer-generated images create blazing fires, giant waves, or talking dinosaurs. Once made on computers, images can be changed, moved, copied, and combined. Computers revolutionized special effects, and CGI can create an entire movie like The Polar Express.

pages.text: Conclusion Audiences in 1933 were awestruck by the special effects used in King Kong. And audiences of today are equally awestruck as they watch volcanoes erupt in cities, spaceships engage in battle, and huge ocean liners crack in half and sink to the bottom of the ocean. But today’s audiences know a little more about special effects than audiences of years ago. Does this mean that today’s audiences are bored with today’s movies? Not a chance! They still enjoy the “magic” they see on the screen. They love being frightened, amazed, and entertained. So, what’s left for movie special effects? Computer special- effects artists want to perfect a way to make a computer- generated human being look completely real. Will they achieve their goal? They probably will, because with special effects anything can happen, right? CGI-rendered human character.
pages.brief: 1933 audiences are awestruck by King Kong’s effects, and today’s audiences watch volcanoes erupt in cities, spaceships battle, and ocean liners sink. Today’s audiences know more but still enjoy the screen magic, loving being frightened, amazed, and entertained. Computer artists want a computer-generated human to look completely real; a CGI-rendered human character.
