books.title: Threats to Our Atmosphere
books.art_why: The book covers real Earth science, current environmental issues, and observable places and technology.

pages.text: Layers of Earth’s atmosphere as seen from a satellite Earth is surrounded by a protective blanket called the atmosphere. The atmosphere is a mixture of many gases. The three most important are nitrogen, oxygen, and carbon dioxide. Living things need these gases in order to survive. Earth’s atmosphere filters out the Sun’s harmful rays. It also prevents heat from escaping too rapidly into space. Living things on Earth survive within a narrow range of conditions. All living things need the right amount of gases, the right range of temperature, and the right balance of sunlight. The atmosphere helps to maintain proper conditions for life on Earth.
pages.brief: A satellite view of Earth from space shows the planet wrapped in its atmosphere, a protective blanket of mixed gases. Nitrogen, oxygen, and carbon dioxide surround the globe. Sunlight reaches Earth, with harmful rays filtered and heat held near the surface so living things can survive in suitable conditions.

pages.text: The Ozone Layer Ozone is a special form of oxygen gas. Different amounts of ozone are found in each of the five layers of Earth’s atmosphere. A lot of ozone is in the upper part of the stratosphere, so it is considered a sublayer called the ozone layer. This sublayer absorbs harmful ultraviolet rays from the Sun. It is called “good ozone” because it protects us. Do You Know? Atoms are the tiny particles that make up all matter in the universe. There are ninety-four natural substances on Earth, called elements. Each element has its own type of atom. Atoms join together to make all the things found on Earth. Combinations of atoms are called molecules. For example, one molecule of the oxygen we breathe is made up of two atoms of oxygen, or O₂. Ozone is an oxygen of three atoms of oxygen, or O₃.
pages.brief: A cutaway view of Earth’s atmosphere shows five stacked layers, with a concentration of ozone in the upper stratosphere. Ozone molecules absorb incoming ultraviolet rays from the Sun. Tiny atoms join into molecules, including two-atom oxygen and three-atom ozone, showing how this special oxygen gas forms.

pages.text: UV rays break down normal oxygen molecules into two separate atoms. These atoms then combine with other oxygen molecules to make ozone. Ozone in the ozone layer is always being created and destroyed. Under normal conditions, the amount of ozone remains fairly constant, which means that the balance does not shift too greatly one way or the other. The part of sunlight known as ultraviolet (UV) light is responsible for both creating and destroying ozone. UV light creates ozone by splitting molecules of oxygen gas (O ) into two individual oxygen atoms (O). If one of these oxygen atoms joins with a molecule of oxygen gas, a three-atom ozone molecule forms. UV light can also change an existing ozone molecule by removing one of its oxygen atoms. The freed oxygen atom then reacts with an ozone molecule (O ), causing it to split into two oxygen molecules (O + O ).
pages.brief: High above Earth, ultraviolet sunlight strikes oxygen molecules and splits them into separate oxygen atoms. Some freed atoms join other oxygen molecules to form three-atom ozone. At the same time, ultraviolet light removes atoms from existing ozone, splitting it back into oxygen molecules, so creation and destruction continue in balance.

pages.text: Do You Know? Sunlight is actually a mixture of visible and invisible light of various wavelengths. The visible light is made of different colors from red to violet. Long wavelengths, which are less powerful, produce red light. Shorter wavelengths, which are more powerful, produce blue and violet light. Light eventually becomes invisible as the wavelengths decrease. Powerful ultraviolet light is invisible. It can cause skin cancer and damage the eyes. It can hurt plants and kill ocean life. Some biologists think that an increase in ultraviolet light is bleaching the color out of corals around the world. Light Wavelengths Ultraviolet light The colors of the rainbow make up the shorter than those range of visible light, of visible light and or the light humans cannot be seen. can see.
pages.brief: Sunlight streams toward Earth as a mixture of visible and invisible wavelengths. A rainbow-like spread shows red light with long, less powerful waves and blue-violet light with shorter, stronger waves. Beyond visible light, powerful ultraviolet rays reach Earth, harming skin, eyes, plants, ocean life, and possibly bleaching corals.

pages.text: Because ozone is always being created and destroyed, the amount of ozone in the ozone layer is fairly constant. The layer of ozone created keeps harmful UV light from reaching Earth’s surface. Ozone also forms near the ground. This ozone is harmful to plants and animals. It is called “bad ozone.” It forms when cars and factories release chemicals called pollutants into the air. On hot days, sunlight starts a reaction between the pollutants and oxygen, causing the formation of harmful ground-level ozone. When air becomes polluted, outdoor activities might be limited. If levels of ground-level ozone rise to dangerously high levels, a warning is sent out. People with breathing problems are told to stay inside.
pages.brief: Above Earth, a steady ozone layer blocks harmful ultraviolet light from reaching the surface. Near the ground, sunlight reacts with pollutants from cars and factories, forming harmful ozone on hot days. People with breathing problems stay indoors when ground-level ozone rises to dangerous levels.

pages.text: Discovery of the Ozone Hole In the 1970s, scientists in Antarctica measured an increase in the ultraviolet (UV) light reaching Earth. Later, satellites confirmed that UV light in some areas was not being absorbed by the ozone layer as much as in previous years. From the satellite data, scientists made maps that showed a hole in the ozone layer over the South Pole. By 1994, the ozone level had dropped to one-half of what it was in the 1970s. There were signs that the ozone hole above Antarctica was expanding past the polar region toward the equator, where more people lived. The ozone hole was becoming a threat to people and the environment. Math Minute A one-percent decrease in ozone in the stratosphere will cause a two-percent increase in UV-B light that reaches the ground. If ozone in the stratosphere decreases by ten percent, what is the increase in the percentage of UV-B light reaching the ground?
pages.brief: Scientists in Antarctica measure rising ultraviolet light reaching Earth. Satellite observations help them map a thinning area in the ozone layer over the South Pole, a hole that grows toward the equator. By 1994, ozone levels there had fallen to half of what they were in the 1970s.

pages.text: Ozone destruction is greatest around the North and South Poles during winter, due to the winds and low temperatures common to polar regions. The ozone layer rebuilds during warmer months. (Winter in Antarctica, or the South Pole, occurs during summer in the Arctic, or North Pole.) Scientists in Antarctica launch an instrument that will measure the ozone layer. NASA ozone charts record the amount of ozone on a daily basis. The lowest ozone level ever recorded was in 2006.
pages.brief: In polar winter, cold temperatures and winds make ozone destruction strongest near the North and South Poles. Scientists in Antarctica launch an instrument to measure the ozone layer, while satellites record daily ozone amounts. The ozone layer rebuilds during warmer months. The lowest ozone level ever recorded occurred in 2006.

pages.text: Chemical Causes of the Ozone Hole Scientists searched for causes of the changing ozone levels. They discovered that some factories release chemicals called CFCs, or chlorofluorocarbons, that could destroy ozone. The element chlorine in CFCs was the main problem. CFCs were used in air conditioners, insulating foams, and spray paint. As a result, large amounts of chlorine were regularly released into the atmosphere. Scientists also learned that another chemical, bromine, could destroy ozone. Bromine is found in substances that are known as ODCs, or Ozone Depleting Chemicals. Bromine can destroy forty-five times more ozone than an equal amount of chlorine found in CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons). ODCs are frequently found in chemicals used to control fires. Planes drop chemicals to slow down or stop forest fires.
pages.brief: Factories release chemicals called chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs, used in air conditioners, insulating foams, and spray paint. Their chlorine can destroy ozone. Another chemical, bromine, found in ozone-depleting chemicals used to control fires, can destroy even more ozone. Planes drop fire-control chemicals over burning forests.

pages.text: Erupting volcanoes are one natural source of harmful chemicals that destroy ozone. CFCs and ODCs rise into the stratosphere, where sunlight breaks these molecules into chlorine and bromine atoms. The chlorine and bromine then break down ozone molecules. One chlorine atom can destroy one hundred thousand ozone molecules. The process stops when the chlorine and bromine drift into space. Natural sources of chemicals can also destroy ozone. One such source is erupting volcanoes. They spread hydrochloric acid high into the stratosphere, where it breaks down into chlorine gas, which destroys ozone. Volcanoes and other natural events destroy some ozone, but CFCs and ODCs from industry cause most of the damage.
pages.brief: An erupting volcano sends hydrochloric acid high into the stratosphere, where it breaks into chlorine gas that destroys ozone. CFCs and ozone-depleting chemicals also rise into the stratosphere, and sunlight releases chlorine and bromine atoms. One chlorine atom can destroy one hundred thousand ozone molecules until it drifts into space.

pages.text: The World Responds Even after ozone destruction was connected to CFCs and ODCs, many countries continued to produce them. These chemicals were so useful that nobody wanted to give them up. It took cooperation between the governments of many nations to address this global problem. Countries joined together in 1987 and signed the Montreal Protocol. This agreement called for reducing and later banning the production of CFCs and ODCs by 1996. This is a success story because it is the first time that many nations have tackled an environmental issue on a global scale. As a result, since the year 2000, CFCs and ODCs in the atmosphere have been decreasing. However, it may take years to tell whether or not the ozone layer will fully recover. Researchers and scientists from many countries share the satellites that monitor the atmosphere.
pages.brief: Representatives of many nations meet and sign the Montreal Protocol in 1987, agreeing to reduce and later ban CFCs and ozone-depleting chemicals by 1996. Since 2000, those chemicals in the atmosphere have decreased. Scientists from many countries share satellites to monitor the atmosphere and watch for recovery.

pages.text: Engineers quickly developed alternative chemicals to CFCs and ODCs in hopes of restoring the ozone layer. However, some of these ozone-friendly alternative chemicals are also powerful greenhouse gases. Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane, when released into the atmosphere, trap heat near Earth’s surface in the same way that glass traps heat in a greenhouse. The result is a condition known as the greenhouse effect. Some scientists think an increase in gases that create the greenhouse effect has caused the temperature of the air around Earth to gradually rise.
pages.brief: Engineers develop replacement chemicals for CFCs and ozone-depleting substances, but some alternatives are powerful greenhouse gases. Carbon dioxide and methane trap heat near Earth’s surface just as glass traps heat in a greenhouse. This greenhouse effect may gradually raise the temperature of the air around Earth.

pages.text: If Earth becomes hotter, polar ice on land might melt and break off into the sea, raising the oceans’ water levels. Earth has warmed by one degree over the last one hundred years. That may not seem like a lot, but scientists are concerned. Over time, a persistent warming trend might cause Earth’s temperature to rise higher and higher. A hotter Earth may lead to the melting of the polar ice caps and warming of the oceans. If ice on land melts, the world’s oceans would rise and flood land near the coast, destroying habitats of living things. A warmer Earth would also create changes in weather patterns that could lead to habitat destruction and the deaths of some plants and animals. Some living things that don’t move around, such as the oceans’ corals, would be trapped and doomed. The sea life that depends on the coral reefs for shelter and food would also die.
pages.brief: A warmer Earth could melt polar ice on land, breaking it into the sea and raising ocean levels. Coastal flooding would destroy habitats, while changing weather patterns harm plants and animals. Corals trapped in warming oceans would be doomed, and sea life depending on reefs for shelter and food would also die.

pages.text: Four different greenhouse gases contribute to global warming when they are released into the atmosphere. The four gases are carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, and fluorocarbons. Most scientists think that carbon dioxide causes about three-fourths, or 76 percent, of the increase in global warming. Machines using gas-powered motors, as well as power plants, produce carbon dioxide by burning fossil fuels such as coal, oil, and natural gas. The carbon dioxide released into the atmosphere by our cars, planes, trucks, and trains may contribute to greater global warming. Most scientists think these four gases are responsible for current trends in global warming.
pages.brief: Four greenhouse gases contribute to global warming: carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, and fluorocarbons. Carbon dioxide causes about 76 percent of the increase. Gas-powered engines in cars, planes, trucks, and trains, along with power plants burning coal, oil, and natural gas, release carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.

pages.text: Methane is responsible for about 13 percent of global warming. Methane is produced naturally in swamps and by livestock passing gas. It is also a product of rotting garbage. Nitrous oxide is the third-worst contributor to global warming. Nitrous oxide is found mostly in fertilizers. The nitrogen in fertilizers is an important plant food, but when it mixes with soil it produces nitrous oxide. Nitrous oxide is also produced when animal waste decomposes. The final contributor to global warming is fluorocarbon gases. Fluorocarbons also contribute to the destruction of ozone. Fluorocarbons rarely occur in nature. They are almost totally human- made, so their production can be prevented. Rotting garbage at landfills produces methane, a greenhouse gas.
pages.brief: Methane, about 13 percent of global warming, rises from swamps, livestock passing gas, and rotting garbage in landfills. Nitrous oxide comes mostly from fertilizers and decomposing animal waste. Fluorocarbons are almost entirely human-made, contribute to global warming, and also destroy ozone.

pages.text: Carpooling and taking public transportation would reduce the amount of carbon dioxide released into the atmosphere by gas-powered cars and trucks. Not everyone agrees on the seriousness of the global-warming problem. Some say that a one-percent rise is nothing to be concerned about. Others think that the problem will worsen and that people ought to take steps now to prevent future global warming. These people believe that we should find ways to reduce greenhouse gas production before it is too late. Reducing the amount of greenhouse gases may also slow down the destruction of the ozone layer. Global warming of the lower atmosphere actually cools the upper atmosphere. This cooling leads to conditions that can cause.
pages.brief: People carpool and use public transportation to reduce carbon dioxide from gas-powered cars and trucks. Some people consider a one-percent rise unimportant, while others urge action now to cut greenhouse gas production. Reducing these gases may also slow ozone destruction, because warming in the lower atmosphere cools the upper atmosphere.

pages.text: Riding bicycles, skateboards, and scooters instead of riding in a car helps to reduce production of greenhouse gases. further breakdown of the ozone layer. So, if we can learn how to decrease the production of greenhouse gases, we might prevent further destruction of the ozone layer. There are no definite answers to the problem of global warming, but many scientists around the world are looking into effective solutions. They say it is in everyone’s best interests to understand as much as possible about decreasing the release of greenhouse gases.
pages.brief: Riders use bicycles, skateboards, and scooters instead of traveling in cars, helping reduce greenhouse gas production. Scientists continue looking for effective solutions to global warming. They say decreasing greenhouse gas releases may prevent further breakdown of the ozone layer, though no definite answers exist yet.

pages.text: What You Can Do to Help Governments and industries around the world have taken steps to reduce chemicals that destroy ozone. They are cooperating in programs to measure and monitor the ozone layer. There are also things we can each do to protect the atmosphere. We can stop producing more ground-level ozone by reducing the use of automobiles. And we can use hand-powered mowers instead of mowers that burn gasoline. Protecting the upper-level ozone layer means trying to avoid releasing CFCs and ODCs into the atmosphere. Recycle the chemicals that cool old refrigerators and air conditioners. Avoid foam packaging, if possible. Write letters to industries that still use CFCs and ODCs, and ask them what they are doing to find alternatives. Using public transportation is better for the ozone layer.
pages.brief: People take steps to protect the atmosphere by reducing automobile use, using hand-powered mowers, recycling chemicals from old refrigerators and air conditioners, and avoiding foam packaging. They write letters asking industries about alternatives to CFCs and ozone-depleting chemicals. Governments and industries cooperate in programs to measure and monitor the ozone layer.

pages.text: Factories and certain products we use release chemicals that are destroying part of the protective blanket surrounding Earth. The chemicals being released into the air may be causing Earth’s atmosphere to warm up. Actions taken by governments from all around the world have helped ban certain chemicals. However, more action is needed to prevent future harm to our atmosphere. The ozone problem has taught us many things. We now know that we need to control the use of certain chemicals. Scientists, politicians, and concerned citizens work common goals. Perhaps the most important thing it has taught us is that we need to start our current activities. We need to think about how they will affect our future well-being and the health of our planet.
pages.brief: Factories and certain products release chemicals that destroy part of Earth’s protective atmosphere and may warm the planet. Governments around the world have banned some chemicals, but more action is needed. Scientists, politicians, and concerned citizens work toward common goals, thinking about how current activities will affect future well-being and planetary health.

pages.text: Mariachi copper sculpture.
pages.brief: A polished copper sculpture of a mariachi band stands in a sunlit plaza, instruments raised. The scene opens a fifth-grade travel brochure about Mexico, with a sense of music, history, and welcome. The sculpture honors Mexico’s mariachi traditions and invites readers into the country.

pages.text: A mariachi band My Travel Brochure By Juan Rodriguez Ms. Brown’s Fifth-Grade Class Welcome to Mexico! I love my beautiful country and am so happy we can explore it together. Mexico has a lot of rich history and culture. The people who live here are very kind, and their hospitality is out of this world! There is so much here to see and do. The question is not what you want to do, but whether you will have the time to do it all. You might want to relax on the shores of Mexico’s many beaches or visit some of our wonderful museums, historic sites, or ancient ruins. You could even go for a horseback ride in the mountains, a boat ride through the wetlands, or listen to local mariachi music. Whatever you want to do or see, Mexico has something for you!
pages.brief: A mariachi band in embroidered jackets plays guitars and trumpets in a lively Mexican plaza. Juan Rodriguez, a fifth-grade student in Ms. Brown’s class, shares his love for Mexico’s history, culture, kind people, beaches, museums, historic sites, ancient ruins, mountains, wetlands, and local music.

pages.text: Mexico’s States The land in Mexico covers 756,066 square miles (1,972,550 sq km). How big is that? Well, you could fit about five countries the size of Mexico into the United States. I bet you didn’t know that Mexico has states, too. It has 31 states and a federal district. All of these areas have cool places to visit! Mexico’s blue water and landforms are as diverse as its people and culture.
pages.brief: A broad view of Mexico reveals blue water along the coasts and many different landforms across the country. The land covers 756,066 square miles and is divided into 31 states and a federal district, with varied places to visit. Its diverse geography mirrors the diversity of its people and culture.

pages.text: Mexico’s many unique landform regions include the Mexican plateau, the central plateau, Gulf Coastal Plain, Pacific Coastal Lowlands, southern highlands, Chiapas Highlands, Tabasco Plain, the Yucatán (yoo-kah-TAHN) Peninsula, Sierra Madre Occidental and Sierra Madre Oriental, and the Sonoran Desert. If you review that list, you’ll notice that very few sound alike. Chihuahuan Sonoran Desert Desert.
pages.brief: A wide view of Mexico shows its varied landform regions: the Mexican and central plateaus, Gulf Coastal Plain, Pacific Coastal Lowlands, southern highlands, Chiapas Highlands, Tabasco Plain, Yucatán Peninsula, and the Sierra Madre Occidental and Oriental. The Sonoran and Chihuahuan Deserts stretch across dry ground, each region looking different from the next.

pages.text: When to Visit One thing to keep in mind is that Mexico’s climate along the coast is hot and humid. If you don’t like hot and humid weather, you should plan your trip from October through May. Of course, the temperatures are almost always milder inland and in the mountains. If you love dry weather, try visiting Baja (BAH-hah) California or the Sonoran or Chihuahuan Deserts. It is dry in these places year-round. Cacti in the Sonoran Desert in Baja California.
pages.brief: Tall cacti stand in the dry Sonoran Desert in Baja California under bright sun. In the distance, a hot, humid coastline and cooler inland mountains show Mexico’s varied climates, with dry desert weather lasting year-round in Baja California and the Sonoran and Chihuahuan Deserts.

pages.text: My Country’s History Before the Spanish conquered the Aztecs in 1521, Mexico was part of what is called Mesoamerica. The Olmecs, Maya, Teotihuacán (tay-oh-tee-wah-KAHN), Toltec, and the Aztec peoples lived in Mesoamerica for a long time before the Spanish arrived. You can visit some of the buildings they left behind such as temples, pyramids, and even ball courts! The Aztecs were the most powerful of the Mesoamerican civilizations. The Spanish invasion of the Aztecs changed the people and the land. Spain sent some of its people to live here. Spanish colonizers forced many Indigenous peoples to abandon their own religions to become Catholic. Colonizers also forced Indigenous peoples to learn Spanish. Although many Indigenous languages are no longer spoken, about 1.5 million people speak Náhuatl, the language of the Aztec Empire. Today Spanish is the official language of Mexico. Mexico was a colony of Spain until 1810. Many Mexicans revolted against Spain, and in 1821, Mexico officially won its independence. It is now a republic.
pages.brief: Ancient Mesoamerican temples, pyramids, and ball courts stand across the land, with Olmec, Maya, Teotihuacano, Toltec, and Aztec peoples gathered nearby. Spanish colonizers arrive with Catholic religion and the Spanish language, while Indigenous people preserve Náhuatl. Later, Mexican rebels celebrate independence in 1821 and form a republic.

pages.text: Templo Mayor in Tenochtitlán, capital of the Aztec Empire Mexico City Now, let’s begin our tour of some of the great cities to visit. We’ll begin in the heart of Mexico— Mexico City. When the Aztecs ruled, it was called Tenochtitlán (tay-nohch-teet-LAHN). Many of the ancient ruins in and around Mexico City were built by the Aztecs. The Templo Mayor (Great Temple) was actually the site of the capital of the Aztec Empire. It was built during the 1300s and 1400s. The Spanish tried to bury it, but in 1978 the amazing temple’s ruins were uncovered. It is now a museum.
pages.brief: The Templo Mayor ruins rise in Mexico City, once the Aztec capital Tenochtitlán. Built during the 1300s and 1400s, the great temple was buried by the Spanish and uncovered in 1978. Today its ancient stone walls stand as a museum in the heart of the modern city.

pages.text: In Mexico City, there are many cathedrals and other examples of Spanish architecture. The largest cathedral in Latin America is Catedral Metropolitana. Would you believe it took nearly 300 years to build? Throughout the city you can see painted or sculpted art by famous Mexican artists. One of the most well known is muralist Diego Rivera. From 1929 to 1935, he painted murals showing Mexican history in the courtyard of the Palacio Nacional (pah-LAH-see-oh nah-see-oh-NAHL). The site of the palace has been home to many rulers. Moctezuma, who was an Aztec emperor, lived on the same site before the Spanish conquest. After the Spanish conquest, it was home to Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés (air-NAHN kor-TESS). Today, the offices of Mexico’s president are inside. The palace faces the Plaza de la Constitución (often called the Zócalo). This is one of the world’s largest public squares. Mexico City’s largest park is another major attraction. This was where the Aztecs used to spend their summer vacations! You can spend a part of your vacation at Bosque de Chapultepec (BOHSS-keh DEH chah-pool-teh-PEK), too. You can visit a zoo or botanical garden, buy a balloon or a snack, and then visit museums or art galleries and not even leave the park!
pages.brief: The Catedral Metropolitana towers over Mexico City, its construction taking nearly 300 years. Inside the Palacio Nacional, Diego Rivera’s murals show Mexican history in the courtyard, while the building faces the vast Plaza de la Constitución. Nearby, families visit Bosque de Chapultepec to enjoy a zoo, botanical garden, balloons, snacks, museums, and art galleries.

pages.text: There are other art museums and centers throughout the city, including the Palacio de Bellas Artes, Museo Dolores Olmedo Patiño, Museo Mural Diego Rivera, Museo Frida Kahlo, and many, many more. Frida Kahlo was a Self-portrait with Monkey by Frida Kahlo known for her bold self-portraits. My favorite painting of hers has a monkey in it! However, if shopping is what you want to do while in Mexico City, you won’t be disappointed at the Bazar del Sábado (Saturday Market) in the Plaza San Jacinto in the San Ángel neighborhood. You can buy Mexican fruits, vegetables, or even candy, at the Mercado de la Merced. Candy at the Saturday Market.
pages.brief: Colorful art museums and centers fill Mexico City, including the Palacio de Bellas Artes and the Museo Frida Kahlo. Frida Kahlo’s bold self-portrait with a monkey hangs on view. At the Bazar del Sábado in Plaza San Jacinto, shoppers browse Mexican fruits, vegetables, and candy, while more candy fills the Mercado de la Merced.

pages.text: Central and Southern Mexico Just northwest of Mexico City, you can find more examples of Spanish colonial architecture. Sometimes this area is called the Colonial Heartland. It is also the heart of Mexico’s rich agriculture. The Spanish built many cities and towns here to take advantage of the silver deposits. If you visit the city of Taxco, southwest of Mexico City, you can find many beautiful silver shops. Farther west there are many beaches. One place known for its beaches is Acapulco Spanish colonial (ah-kah-POOL-koh). Decades ago, Puerto Vallarta became a popular beach resort for Hollywood stars. If you get tired of the beach, you can visit the city of Colima. Colima has been rebuilt over and over again because frequent earthquakes continually damage it.
pages.brief: Northwest of Mexico City, Spanish colonial architecture marks the Colonial Heartland, a rich agricultural region built near silver deposits. In Taxco, silver shops line the streets, while Acapulco and Puerto Vallarta draw visitors to western beaches once popular with Hollywood stars. In Colima, rebuilt buildings show the city’s repeated rebuilding after earthquakes.

pages.text: Guadalajara is the country’s second largest city after Mexico City. There are many great places to visit in Guadalajara (gwah- The Cathedral at dah-lah-HAH-rah). Guadalajara There is the city’s famous Cathedral, which took more than two centuries to build. You can take a short walk from the Cathedral and see a lot of Spanish colonial architecture. But like many regions in Mexico, you can also just enjoy being outside! The country’s largest lake, Lago de Chapala, is a great place to go boating. You may want to check out the waterfalls, tropics, and mountains at Huasteca Potosina (wahss-TEH-kah poh-toh-SEE-nah) located in the state of San Luis Potosí. I also recommend that you take a boat ride to see Tamul waterfall. It drops 344 feet into a canyon! Fishermen at Lago de Chapala, Mexico.
pages.brief: Guadalajara’s famous Cathedral rises above Spanish colonial streets, its construction spanning more than two centuries. Outside the city, fishermen work on Lago de Chapala, Mexico’s largest lake, where boats glide across the water. Farther away, a boat carries visitors to Tamul waterfall, which drops 344 feet into a canyon in Huasteca Potosina.

pages.text: Central and southern Mexico have many ancient ruins of Mesoamerican civilizations. Teotihuacán is probably one of the greatest examples of all Mesoamerican cities. It has two great ancient temples: the Pyramids of the Sun and the Moon, which people visit more than any other Mesoamerican site. Pyramid of the Sun So what was Teotihuacán? It was once a place where about 125,000 people lived in about ce 400. The word Teotihuacán means “the place where gods were created.” People who lived there were called Teotihuacanos, but many different Indigenous peoples inhabited Teotihuacán. At that time, it was one of the world’s largest cities. Monte Albán (MOHN-teh ahl-BAHN) in the state of Oaxaca (wah-HAH-kah) was a city of the Zapotec people. You can visit what was their ceremonial site on Pyramid of the Moon á n top of a mountain! at Teotihuac At one time, this was also a cultural center for the Olmec and the Teotihuacanos.
pages.brief: The Pyramids of the Sun and Moon rise at Teotihuacán, once a great Mesoamerican city where about 125,000 people lived. Its name means the place where gods were created. Farther south, Monte Albán sits on a mountain in Oaxaca, a Zapotec ceremonial site that was also a cultural center for Olmec and Teotihuacano peoples.

pages.text: El Tajin in Veracruz The Gulf Coast and Yucatán Peninsula Moving out to the tropical plains and jungle of the Gulf Coast, we find land that was once home to several Mesoamerican cultures, including the Maya, Olmec, and Totonac. Olmec artifacts are all over this region, especially in the Parque-Museo de La Venta. Mayan hieroglyphics You can visit ancient pyramids at El Tajin. This was a major religious center for the Totonac who lived here between ce 900 and 1150. Or you can check out Quiahuiztlán (kee-uh-weet-ZLAN), a hilltop city where some 15,000 Totonac people once lived.
pages.brief: Tropical plains and jungle cover the Gulf Coast, where Maya, Olmec, and Totonac cultures once lived. Olmec artifacts rest in the Parque-Museo de La Venta, and Mayan hieroglyphics mark the region. At El Tajin, ancient pyramids form a major religious center, while Quiahuiztlán sits on a hilltop where Totonac people lived.

pages.text: Mayan ancient ball court The Mayan ruins at Chichén Itzá are the best preserved of anything the Maya left behind. There are temples, Mexico’s largest ancient ball court, and an observatory. The Maya were fascinated with looking at the stars, just like me! They even had their own writing system. Uxmal is another Mayan site that you should visit. Most of the Spanish cities and towns in the Yucatán were actually built on top of Mayan ruins. What other cool things are there to see and do on the Gulf Coast? Just about everything! There are many museums, cathedrals, and churches. Don’t forget to stop in the city of Veracruz! The waterfront promenade and arcades are a lot of fun. Like the Colonial Heartland, this region is also a center for agriculture. Sugarcane, cacao (yum!), and coffee are grown here. Coffee beans.
pages.brief: At Chichén Itzá, a Mayan ball court, temples, and an observatory stand among well-preserved ruins. Maya writing and star knowledge are suggested by the site, while Uxmal rises nearby. In Veracruz, a waterfront promenade and arcades face the Gulf, with sugarcane, cacao, and coffee growing in the tropical region.

pages.text: The Yucatán Peninsula is also well known for its white sand beaches, and has plenty of them considering it’s surrounded by water on three sides, like Baja California. The world’s second longest barrier reef (after Australia’s) is located near the islands of Cozumel and Scuba lessons Isla Mujeres (EESS- lah moo-HEH-ress). It is a popular place to snorkel and scuba dive. Cancún is probably the most popular spot to get a suntan. This region is well known for its breathtaking natural wells called cenotes. Probably the most visited one is the Cenote de Dzitnup (si- NOH-tee day ZEET-nup) near Valladolid (bah-yah- doh-LEED). Can you believe that it was discovered only a half century ago? Great Mesoamerican Reef near Cozumel and Isla Mujeres.
pages.brief: White sand beaches line the Yucatán Peninsula, with clear water on three sides. Near Cozumel and Isla Mujeres, divers explore the world’s second longest barrier reef. At Cancún, sunbathers relax, while nearby the Cenote de Dzitnup opens as a breathtaking natural well near Valladolid.

pages.text: Copper Canyon in Northern Mexico Northern Mexico Many of Mexico’s deserts, mountains, and canyons are located here. You might have heard of the Grand Canyon in the United States, but did you know that Copper Canyon is even bigger? It is more than one mile deep and part of the Sierra Madre Occidental range. You can take a train to get a close-up view of this deep canyon, its waterfalls, and lakes. The Rarámuri (rah-RAH-moo-ree) people who live there are famous for the drums and violins they make. If you are looking for great beaches and resorts, like Cabo San Lucas, then Baja California is the place for you. It is a peninsula, so water is around three of its sides. In the winter, you can even spot along the shore as south! Cabo San Lucas in Baja California.
pages.brief: Copper Canyon cuts deep through the Sierra Madre Occidental, with waterfalls and lakes below. A train winds along the canyon for a close-up view, while Rarámuri people make drums and violins nearby. Farther west, Cabo San Lucas in Baja California shows beaches and resorts surrounded by water on three sides.

pages.text: You won’t find any Aztec ruins in Baja. Why? Because the Aztecs didn’t live here! But you can find some ancient cave paintings. Many believe the ancestors of the Cochimi painted the cave pictures. They show people and animals in black and red. Cave paintings at Baja California Probably the most amazing ancient ruins in this region are the adobe buildings at Paquimé (pah-kee-MEH). Adobe is a brick made with mud and grass. Often many bricks were used to create buildings that look like today’s apartment buildings. Between the 900s and 1300s, more than 3,000 people lived in adobe buildings near the Casas Grandes river. pages.brief: Inside a Baja California cave, ancient paintings show people and animals in black and red, believed to be made by ancestors of the Cochimi. Nearby, the adobe ruins of Paquimé rise like apartment buildings, built from mud and grass bricks near the Casas Grandes river.

pages.text: A whale dives, showing its tail in the Sea of Cortés. If you’re not interested in ruins or the beach, you may enjoy whale watching in a boat. In Guerrero Negro, blue whales are often spotted along the Sea of Cortés. If you get seasick, you can visit them and many other sea mammals on land at the nearby Laguna San Ignacio, Bahia de Magdalena. Cultural center in San Miguel de Allende Mexico has delicious food. You have to agree: Mexico has much to offer—so come visit!
pages.brief: A whale dives, lifting its tail above the Sea of Cortés while a small boat watches. Along the shore, the cultural center in San Miguel de Allende stands near delicious Mexican food, inviting visitors to enjoy the country’s wildlife and culture.

Around them are symbols of the country’s economy: petroleum, silver, crops, clothing, cars, computers, and tourism, with natural resources and industries spread across the land.

books.title: Energy Sources: The Pros and Cons
books.art_why: Real-world power plants, dams, solar panels, and energy sources exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: The Endless Need for Energy The United States is a modern society. Like all modern societies, it uses a lot of energy. Scientists define energy as the ability to do work. Many kinds of things can be called work. Getting an automobile to move down a road or an airplane to fly is work, and so is producing in a factory. The energy used by the United States sources. Much Machines in this car factory need energy to build cars. of it comes from the burning of fuels, such as coal and gasoline. Other energy comes from the power of flowing water, from the light of the Sun, the wind, or from the splitting of atoms.
pages.brief: Inside a large car factory, machines build automobiles. The busy industrial scene shows one kind of work that requires energy. The factory represents the many ways a modern society uses power, from moving automobiles and airplanes to producing goods.

pages.text: Fossil Fuels Fossil fuels —coal, oil, and natural gas—are a leading energy source around the world. They are called fossil fuels because they were formed from the remains of plants and animals that died many millions of years ago. Over time, great heat and pressure underground changed the remains into materials we use as fuel. About 85 percent of energy used each year in the United States comes from fossil fuels. Coal is burned in many power plants to produce electricity. Fuels made from fuel, and jet fuel— power our cars, airplanes. Most homes use natural Gasoline is a common fossil fuel. gas to provide power for stoves and water heaters.
pages.brief: A power plant burns coal to produce electricity. Gasoline fuels cars and airplanes, and natural gas provides power for home stoves and water heaters. The scene connects fossil fuels—coal, oil, and natural gas—to the everyday work they do.

pages.text: Flood prevention is good for people, but not so good for the environment. Rivers are supposed to flood. Flooding produces sediment, which is a mixture of gravel, sand, and topsoil. Sediment deposited by floods keeps the soil rich in farmlands located near rivers. When a river is dammed, it cannot renew the soil on the land around it. Salmon swimming upstream Dams also block the route for fish that swim up and down rivers. In the U.S. Pacific Northwest, dams have been a serious problem for salmon. Every three to five years, salmon swim from the ocean up rivers to their birthplaces to lay eggs. Dams make it difficult for salmon to swim up and down rivers. As a result, salmon populations have severely declined in the past 100 years.
pages.brief: A river flows past farmlands, where floodwaters would normally spread sediment—gravel, sand, and topsoil—and keep the soil rich. Upstream, a dam blocks the river’s flow, and salmon struggle to swim upstream to their birthplaces to lay eggs.

pages.text: This solar water heater is one of many used to heat water for a town. A solar heat collector uses the Sun’s energy to heat water. These solar heat collectors are often placed on rooftops. Water circulates through pipes in the panels, and the Sun’s radiant energy heats the water. The heated water is pumped into a building through more pipes. The heat leaves the water and heats the inside of the building. Then the cooled water returns to the rooftop to be heated again.

pages.text: Rooftop solar panels provide this house with energy. In some areas of the world, such as the southwestern United States, there are many sunny days. In these places, solar cells and solar panels can produce lots of electricity and heat. Since the Sun sends abundant free energy streaming toward Earth 24 hours a day, people in many parts of the world, not just the sunniest places, have mounted solar cells and solar panels on the roofs of their houses or businesses to lower their energy costs. Experts say that huge installations of solar panels in sunny regions could generate enough electricity to supply an entire country. Capturing this energy can help overcome our diminishing energy supply. New ways to capture this energy are being developed all the time to maximize efficiency.
pages.brief: A house has solar panels mounted on its roof, capturing sunlight to produce electricity and heat. The home is in a sunny area where solar cells can lower energy costs. The panels are part of a system that uses abundant free energy streaming from the Sun.

pages.text: There are two main problems with solar cells. One is that they are very expensive to manufacture. Their cost makes hydroelectric and fossil-fuel power plants a cheaper source of energy. Until inexpensive manufacturing is developed for solar cells, this free energy source will continue to come at a high cost to capture and convert to electricity. The second problem is that not all areas of the world get abundant sunlight. Other sources of energy would be needed as a backup to the solar cells, which adds to overall energy costs. Some people who live near houses that use solar cells and solar panels think the rooftop systems are ugly. They believe the look of the solar systems will decrease the value of their homes. Power plants could serve as backups for solar farms.
pages.brief: Rows of solar panels form a solar farm. Nearby houses have rooftop solar systems, and some people consider the systems ugly. A power plant stands ready as a backup for the solar farm when sunlight is not abundant.

pages.text: Nuclear Power Nuclear power plants unlock the energy inside atoms to generate electricity. Each splitting of an atom releases energy. An atomic bomb explodes by creating a very rapid chain reaction. A nuclear power plant uses the radioactive element uranium to create a slow, controlled chain reaction. The energy released by breaking apart uranium atoms is used to heat water into steam. The steam is then used to generate electricity in much the same way that coal power plants produce it. Cooling towers keep the core of a nuclear power plant at a safe temperature.
pages.brief: A nuclear power plant uses uranium to create a slow, controlled chain reaction. The energy released by splitting atoms heats water into steam, which is used to generate electricity. Cooling towers rise above the plant, keeping the core at a safe temperature.

pages.text: Nuclear waste is handled very carefully. Uranium releases an incredible amount of energy. One kilogram (2.2 lbs) of uranium can produce more energy than 3 million kilograms (6.6 million lbs) of coal. Nuclear power plants have another advantage over coal power plants: They do not produce gases that can pollute the skies or add to global warming. Many people oppose nuclear power because of its dangers. One danger is the possibility of an accident. A nuclear power plant can’t explode like an atomic bomb. However, it can have a steam explosion if the core (the area containing the uranium) gets too hot. This would spew out a lot of dangerous radiation. A second danger is the waste material nuclear power plants produce. Even when uranium is no longer useful for generating electricity, it is still highly radioactive. It remains dangerous for thousands of years.
pages.brief: Nuclear waste is handled very carefully. The radioactive material remains dangerous for thousands of years, even after uranium is no longer useful for generating electricity. A nuclear power plant nearby shows where the waste comes from.

pages.text: Wind turbines could provide more energy in the future. Looking to the Future In years to come, we will have to find substitutes for oil. Hydroelectric power may also be replaced, too. Many people are concerned about the environmental effects of dams and would like to see many dams torn down. The use of solar energy will probably continue to grow. Energy experts also say that more nuclear power plants will have to be built to meet growing energy needs.

More nuclear power plants may be built to meet growing energy needs. The scene shows a mix of energy sources and changing choices.
